News.title: Navy SEALS blew up dozens of deadly Iranian mines in ‘secret, four-month special op mission’ to clear Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
NAVY seals waged a secret four-month underwater blitz to hunt down and blow-up dozens of Iranian mines lurking in the Strait of Hormuz.

The covert US mission saw elite divers plunge into the perilious waterway as they battled to clear a route vital to the world’s oil supplies.



Operating largely under the cover of darkness, the SEALs used drones, robotic vessels and high-tech sonar to track down the explosive traps.

It comes as Iran is accused of plotting a terrifying October 7-style assault on Israel using its sprawling network of terror proxies.



Trump has meanwhile vowed that the bloody conflict will ultimately send oil prices crashing as he insisted Iran will never be allowed to get its hands on a nuclear weapon.

Writing on Truth Social, the US president said: “Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran.



“Three Dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below Two Dollars a gallon. It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon. MAGA! President DJT”.

Israeli intelligence has reportedly claimed Tehran has held meetings and training exercises with Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis and Iraqi militias as it looks to bolster its forces and weapons stockpiles.

The four-month operation was carried out amid a terrifying barrage of strikes between the US and Iran, according to a report by the Financial Times.

It was aimed at reopening the strategic strait to commercial shipping after vessels largely abandoned the treacherous route following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February.



But even after sophisticated technology has pinpointed suspected mines, the most dangerous job could still fall to a human being.

A retired US Navy captain Bill Hamblet, who often operated in the Gulf, told the FT: “That is usually followed up by a navy diver who’s got to get in the water and approach the mine, and then put a charge on it and destroy it.”



The underwater bomb squad could also unleash robotic drones to approach and destroy the mines with explosives – a safer option for the divers but a painfully slow one.

Among the weapons in the Navy’s technological arsenal was the Common Uncrewed Surface Vessel, or CUSV – a drone boat capable of towing unmanned submersibles through the deadly waters.

One of those, the MK 18 Mod 2 Kingfish, is fitted with sonar technology capable of scanning the ocean floor for suspicious objects.

Despite the treacherous operation, no US casualties have been reported in connection with the mine-clearing mission.



It comes as US forces launched a blistering attack on three Iranian oil tankers last week after Tehran reportedly fired missiles at American warships.

US Central Command said it “permanently disabled” two tankers and “completely destroyed” a third, claiming the vessels were part of a shadow network funnelling cash to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies.

The scale of the underwater menace was laid bare in June when the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization estimated that around 80 mines had been planted along the Strait.

The strategic waterway handles around 20 per cent of the world’s oil transports, making the explosive threat a potential nightmare for global energy supplies.

Iran has repeatedly claimed its mines remain active in the Strait and its military has claimed two attacks on oil tankers in the past week.



US President Donald Trump last week declared that “all mines” in the international waters of the Strait had been removed or destroyed.

The US military subsequently confirmed the claim.

But fears of a fresh Iranian mining blitz have continued to stalk ships attempting the dangerous crossing.



The threat has also sparked fierce uncertainty among shipping firms over whether the entire waterway is truly safe.

Shipping companies and maritime analysts believe areas close to the Omani coast – where US forces have been escorting ships – are likely to have been cleared.

But there is far less certainty over the rest of the Strait.

“It’s hard to know what to believe,” Ethan Connell, assistant director of Taiwan Security Monitor and an expert on mines, told the FT.

“Iran is certainly trying to re-mine.”



The latest mine scare comes as the Strait has been hammered by missile and drone attacks, sending visible shipping traffic crashing to its lowest level since May, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler.

Just two ships crossed the Strait on Saturday, while only six made the perilous journey on Sunday.

Most of those vessels travelled through a route approved by Iran.

But the true scale of traffic remains shrouded in mystery, with some ships reportedly switching off their transponders and creeping through the Strait under the protection of US military escorts.

The danger facing the crews is compounded by the sheer difficulty of hunting mines beneath the waves while a war rages around them.



The secret mission involved small teams of Navy divers operating from inflatable-hulled boats, backed by unmanned surface vessels and specialised underwater equipment.

Sonar-equipped submersibles were used to scour the seabed for suspected explosives before the dangerous process of destroying them began.

And despite the robotic technology, some mines still had to be tackled at close quarters by Navy divers.

The painstaking operation amounted to an underwater bomb disposal mission carried out in the middle of a war zone.

“It is an extremely time-consuming process,” said Nitya Labh, an associate fellow at Chatham House.



“They are doing, essentially, active bomb detonation underwater.”

The mission was carried out despite a twist that raised fresh questions over the US mine-clearing effort.

Three American vessels normally assigned to mine-countermeasure operations in the Gulf had reportedly been operating in the Indian and Pacific oceans since at least early June.

Mine clearance is already a notoriously slow and dangerous business in peacetime.

News.title: Protesters ‘launched rocks & bricks’ at police during anti-migrant clashes in Portsmouth after ‘catching cops off guard’
News.content:
PROTESTERS have been accused of launching rocks and bricks at cops who were “caught off guard” during anti-migrant clashes on Sunday.

Around 200 people – some wearing face coverings – descended on Eastney ferry port in Portsmouth after 140 migrants were brought to shore.



Several vans and cars were reportedly damaged as multiple officers were injured during the chaos which went deep into the night.

Cops guarded coaches parked on a roadside not far from the marina, as protesters blocked the flow of traffic and stopped RNLI teams from accessing the port.



Policing Minister Sarah Jones told the House of Commons that the chaos was “intimidating and thuggish”.

She said protesters would face the “full force of the law”.



The migrant boat from Normandy which sparked the chaos was thought to have been the longest-ever Channel crossing by people smugglers.

It was intercepted in the Solent between the Isle of Wight and Portsmouth earlier on Sunday.

Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had “serious questions to answer” over the decision to bring migrants to shore in the area.

Council leader Steve Pitt said the move had caused “needless disruption”.



In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

“No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched.”

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: “I’ve seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I’ve seen pictures of police vehicles damaged.



“It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest.”

Border Force confirmed that the coaches leaving the dock in the early hours of Monday were transporting “individuals from the boat” for “processing”.

Protesters claim they were trying to stop authorities from ferrying migrants to the Manston centre in Kent.

Reform leader Nigel Farage said the country was on the precipice of “serious civil disturbance” and called on the protests to remain peaceful.

Posting to social media, he said: “Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution.”



His remarks prompted Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, to urge the Reform leader to be “careful” with his words.

Livestreaming the mayhem, the far-right figure had called on his supporters to “get down to Eastney”.

Danny later barged into the frame during a Sky News interview with Reform’s spokesperson for home affairs, Zia Yusuf.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp also condemned the violence in Portsmouth.

But he added: “This should also be a wake-up call for the government because it’s not just those protesters in Dover and Portsmouth who feel so angry about large-scale illegal immigration.



“It is millions and millions of people up and down this country who feel angry as well.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It follows a similar incident on Saturday, which saw some 625 masked men assemble at the Port of Dover to protest against small-boat crossings.

A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK on small boats up until September 1, 43 per cent less than the same period the previous year.

News.title: Elderly woman, 80, forced to lay on the ground for over FOUR hours as she waited for ambulance after nasty fall
News.content:
OAP'S TORMENT Elderly woman, 80, forced to lay on the ground for over FOUR hours as she waited for ambulance after nasty fall

AN ELDERLY woman was forced to lay on the pavement for more than four hours as she waited for an ambulance after a nasty fall.

Kathleen Bryson was wrapped in blankets provided by neighbours who tried to make her comfortable while she lay there helpless.



The 80-year-old fell outside her home in County Durham at 11.20am on Monday morning.

By 3.30pm she was still lying in the same position on the pavement, waiting for medical help.



Speaking to ChronicleLive Kathleen’s son, Karl Bryson, said: “It’s been nearly three hours that she’s been lying on the concrete floor.

“She’s just lying there in the same position. She’s 80 years old.”

Karl was doing some gardening work when he received a call from his sister saying their mum had had a fall.

They believe she may have tripped on a pothole in the pavement.

When he arrived, neighbours had already contacted the North East Ambulance Service and Karl waited almost an hour before calling back at 12.10pm.

When no ambulance had arrived by 2pm, Karl and a neighbour called back for an update.



At this point the wait had exceeded two hours, which he says he was told would be the maximum wait.

However, their wait continued until 3.34pm when an ambulance eventually arrived on scene to assist Kathleen, according to ambulance service logs.

Vicky Court, deputy chief operating officer for North East Ambulance Service, said: “We are sorry for the delay experienced by Ms Bryson and for the distress this has caused her and her family.

“We recognise that Ms Bryson waited far longer than we would like and this is not the service we would have wanted to provide for her.

“Our teams work hard to respond to patients as quickly as possible, but at times of high demand, our resources must always be prioritised by clinical need for patients whose lives are immediately in danger.



“We will review this incident and would encourage Ms Bryson or her family to contact our patient experience team through our formal complaints process so that the circumstances can be fully investigated and we can feed back to her directly.”

News.title: Moment police ram driver, 35, off road and cuff him after 3 week ‘crime spree’ saw thief steal cars, coffee & whiskey
News.content:
THIS is the moment police ram a stolen car off the road following a city-centre chase, as the driver is locked up for a “crime spree”.

The disqualified driver has been jailed for a number of offences, including stealing two cars, five jars of coffee, and two bottles of whiskey.



Video footage shows Liam McDonald, 35, swerving through Cardiff lanes after being confronted head-on by police.

Officers were searching for a stolen car when it was spotted driving towards them in July.



Despite McDonald attempting to escape, officers were eventually able to box in the car and safely arrest McDonald.

McDonald, of no fixed abode, committed several crimes in and around Cardiff across three weeks in July.

After being arrested, he was linked to earlier offences, including stealing five jars of coffee from inside a B&M in Leckwith.

A few days earlier, a different car was reported stolen from an address in Cardiff.



Following CCTV enquiries, a man on a bike – now known to be McDonald – was identified as being responsible for stealing the car.

McDonald then stole two bottles of whiskey worth £119 from a Waitrose in Pontprennau on July 21.

He previously pleaded guilty to numerous offences, including two counts of driving while disqualified, aggravated vehicle taking and dangerous driving, and using a vehicle without third-party insurance.

On Friday, McDonald was sentenced to a year and nine months at Cardiff Crown Court.

He was also banned from driving for three years.



Investigating officer PC Paul Griffiths said: “McDonald committed a spate of offences that had a big impact on the people and businesses in his communities.

“He also put people on the road at risk that day driving in the manner that he did and without a license. I’m pleased to see this sentence handed down today.”

News.title: US accuses Labour of ‘censorship’ over plans to force social media giants to promote ‘trustworthy’ news outlets
News.content:
THE US has accused Labour of seeking to punish critical media outlets with “viewpoint-based censorship”.

Donald Trump’s administration condemned the Government’s plans to force social media sites to promote only news providers deemed “trustworthy”.



The plans would require tech platforms to make stories from public service media such as the BBC more prominent.

The US embassy in London responded by saying: “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.



“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government- disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than ­outright removal.

“Furthermore, such a mandate could establish a template authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content.”



PM Andy Burnham is hoping to meet the President for the first time at the United Nations General Assembly later this month.

The News Media Association, which represents the media industry, lashed out at the plans for the government to define which outlets are trustworthy.

It said: “This would be incompatible with a free press, and represent press regulation by the back door.”

A DCMS spokesperson said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper.



“We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

News.title: Fury as UN reveals migrants are being granted asylum in Britain even when they may NOT be entitled to it
News.content:
MIGRANTS are being granted asylum even when they may not be entitled to it, UN investigators have warned.

A probe by the organisation’s Refugee Agency found serious flaws in Home Office interviews used to decide who is allowed to stay in the UK.



Officials warned rushed questioning meant asylum was at risk of being wrongly granted to people who do not qualify — while genuine refugees could be rejected.

UN officials examined 60 interviews and cases and found the full basis of an applicant’s claim was still unclear after questioning in nearly a third of interviews studied.



They uncovered a “failure to probe material facts”, too many closed questions and interpreters summarising migrants’ answers instead of translating them fully.

They warned this created a “real risk” of genuine refugees being rejected while others were granted asylum despite not qualifying.



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “The UN — hardly a hostile witness — has told the Home Office that it is granting asylum to people who are not entitled to it.

“Last year alone 58,000 people were granted asylum or leave to remain, a ten per cent increase on the year before, and the highest number of initial decisions since records began.”

Meanwhile, a Government whistleblower has claimed just one in 100 asylum claims are genuine and many “use the same script”.

The Home Office insider, who has assessed thousands of applications, said he and his colleagues have encountered hundreds of Iraqi Kurds purporting to be in a relationship with the daughter of Kurdistan’s prime minister.



The number is so high that it has allegedly become a “running joke” among officials.

He also told The Times that hundreds of Pakistanis claim to fear for their lives because they are in a gay relationship with the same man.

Multiple claims feature photos of “topless guys in a club with their arms around each other trying to prove they’re gay”.

News.title: Andy Burnham braced for Donald Trump clash as he prepares to hit Israel with sanctions
News.content:
ANDY Burnham is bracing for a fresh row with Donald Trump as he prepares to unveil Israeli sanctions as soon as today.

The PM is expected to impose a punishment package on Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over illegal West Bank settlements.



Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to make the announcement today as Labour seeks to win back pro-Gaza voters it has lost in recent years.

But it risks a backlash from the Americans who are understood to be furious with Britain’s hardening approach against Israel.



Washington’s ambassador to Israel recently blasted Labour for being consumed with “Jew hate”.

Mike Huckabee said: “The Brits have lost it.

“The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.”

A Number 10 spokesperson completely rejected the claim.

They said: “We’re committed to protecting Jewish communities in the UK, and continue to engage with community leaders and groups.

“The government is investing almost £318 million over three years to protect Jewish communities, crack down on antisemitic extremism and hostile state activity, and tackle antisemitism in schools, universities, and local communities.”



Mr Trump and Mr Burnham spoke last night about the Israel-Gaza war.

A Downing Street spokesman said: “On the Middle East, the Prime Minister set out the UK’s commitment to working towards peace and security in the region, stressing the importance of the Two-State Solution, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.”

News.title: Brit hols hotspot dubbed ‘Devil’s Island’ as 88 of Italy’s most dangerous mafia bosses and terrorists moved to new jail
News.content:
DOZENS of Italy’s most notorious criminals have been moved to a jail in a Brit holiday hotspot which has now been dubbed “Devil’s Island”.

The group of 88 infamous mafia bosses and feared terrorists has been sent to a new high security wing at Uta prison.



The criminals are among 746 inmates who are forced to follow Italy‘s strictest solitary confinement rules known as 41-bis.

Prisoners held under these terms are forbidden from talking to each other – limiting their ability to run gang operations from behind bars.



The crooks were transferred to the island via two ATR 42 jets owned by Italian police.

Only eight or nine were allowed to board each flight at a time and cops separated them to prevent communication.

Sardinia’s governor Alessandra Todde complained about the move which she said posed a risk to the island’s safety.

The latest decision has nearly doubled the number of 41-bis prisoners in the island to 183 – about a quarter of the national total.



Todde said: “The government has moved in a unilateral and arrogant way, treating Sardinia like the Cayenne of Italy.”

The Cayenne prison – also nicknamed “Devil’s Island” – was run by France off the coast of French Guiana before being closed in 1953.

Earlier this year, hundreds of protesters swarmed the streets of Cagliari, the Sardinian capital, to demonstrate against the looming arrivals.



Todde warned the island’s jails are already understaffed – a factor which was magnified by the escape of a Puglia mafia boss from one of their jails in 2023.

Prisoners are being sent to Uta jail as part of a plan to concentrate inmates serving life sentences into a smaller number of jails, one prisoner officer told The Times.

He said the law favoured them being sent to islands to keep them isolated.

The officer said: “We can’t send them to Sicily because many of them come from there in the first place.”

Italy‘s junior justice minister Alberto Balboni called Todde, who represents the opposition party, a hypocrite.



She said: “The new wing of Uta jail for these prisoners was ordered by a minister in a previous government who belonged to the [opposition] Five Star party.”

Balboni argued claims that families of mafia prisoners would move to Sardinia to be closer to their relatives were baseless.

She added: “They do not do this since you can only visit prisoners once a month for a few minutes.”

In the 1990s, Sardinia started to host more and more mob prisoners following a crackdown on Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian mafia.

Many criminals were jailed on the small island of Asinara – nicknamed the Alcatraz of Italy – off Sardinia’s coast.



This included Raffaele Cutolo, a crime boss from Naples, and Salvatore “Toto” Riina, the head of Cosa Nostra.

Toto was linked to 150 killings and orchestrated the murder of anti-mafia officials Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino in 1992.

Asinara only saw one prisoner escape from its facilities during its 112 years of service before it closed in 1997.

The 41-bis system is designed to entice prisoners to give up mafia secrets in return for better living conditions.

Some human rights groups have criticised the standard of living.



Inmates are locked in nine-square-metre cells for 23 hours per day – only being allowed 60 minutes outside for exercise in a tiny yard.

Conversations are closely monitored by prison guards who are familiar with codes used by mafia heads.

Officers also have to make sure bosses who mix don’t kill each other.

The prison source added: “You don’t want mafiosi from the same organisations together but if they are from opposing clans they might try to kill each other.”

News.title: Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurt
News.content:
Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".

Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.

Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.

The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".

News.title: What we know about anti-migrant protests and organiser Danny Thomas
News.content:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend in protests against small boat crossings.

But what is the connection between the two protests?

The answer is one man - Danny Thomas, more often known as Danny Tommo.

UK correspondent Daniel Sandford looks into the background of Danny Tommo and how he has galvanised these protests through social media and local support.

News.title: King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals
News.content:
The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.

Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.

This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.

It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.

This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.

The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.

The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.

This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.

The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case.

"The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.

The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".

News.title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
News.content:
The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.

It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).

In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.

Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.

The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.

So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.

In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.

The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos.

"Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely.

It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?

The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years.

"Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th".

OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?

This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.

"The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said.

Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
News.content:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save Â£1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to Â£22.9bn from Â£29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party" in terms of electric vehicles.

Jaguar launched the I-PACE, a fully-electric SUV, in 2018. But the electric Range Rover announced last week will be its first electric vehicle launch since then.

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

News.title: Self-described 'genocidal racist monster' jailed after BBC investigation
News.content:
"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't send you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killedâ¦ Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as wellâ¦ and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

News.title: Police forces failing investigation basics, says inspectorate report
News.content:
Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC).

In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.

Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.

There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.

The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.

HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.

Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.

The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.

The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".

Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report also highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.

It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing.

News.title: Ecclestone stopped by police for taking shotgun into Portugal
News.content:
Former Formula 1 boss Bernie Ecclestone has denied being arrested at an airport in Portugal after arriving with a shotgun he intended to use in a clay pigeon shooting competition.

Ecclestone, 95, said he was stopped and questioned by four police officers and customs officials at the Tires Aerodrome in Cascais on Monday after arriving from Switzerland.

The British businessman told the Press Association he had to "surrender" the weapon he travelled with as he did not have the right documents to correctly import it.

Ecclestone, who was in charge of F1 for nearly 40 years until 2017, said the Portuguese police were "very helpful" and rejected reports he had been arrested.

"I was going to take part in a clay pigeon shooting competition in Portugal," said Ecclestone.

"I went to see the police and said, 'What can I do for you?' And they said, 'We would like some information on this gun you brought in'."

Ecclestone added he had already taken his shotgun from England to Switzerland and said he anticipated no problems as the airport officials know him "very well".

However, on arrival he was questioned by police for about an hour and was asked to hand over the weapon as he did not have the official documents to bring it into the country.

The incident marks the second time Ecclestone has encountered airport issues regarding firearms. In 2022, he was arrested in Brazil for illegally carrying a gun while boarding a private plane to Switzerland and was ordered to pay 6,000 Brazilian reals (Â£1,000) to the local authorities.

News.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
News.content:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."

Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."

He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."

Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government.

He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."

Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman ZÃ¶e Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."

Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."

A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".

The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.

Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.

In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.

Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.

In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.

The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.

In July â just days before Burnham became prime minister â Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

News.title: Chancellor calls for 'confidence about Britain' despite 'historic high' borrowing costs
News.content:
Asked about the impact of higher borrowing costs, which have surged this month, the Chancellor said that the government was responding to "extreme pressures in the wider market," and reiterated that he wanted to "bring down welfare costs."

Earlier, in his first major speech as chancellor, Healey said his mission was to "make Great Britain growth Britain" again.

Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, he said,

"My defining mission as chancellor is growth, good growth in every postcode. And I've set out today the way this government will set about it: more devolution, more public leadership and control, more investment, more innovation, more jobs."

Healey said he is in "lockstep" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the need for fiscal discipline and having a buffer in the government's spending plans "against the sort of uncertainty that the JLR decision locally has shown".

It came as Healey offered an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of the Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

Speaking in Coventry, he set out a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

With seven weeks until the Budget, Healey said the government will stick to Labour's manifesto pledge, made under Sir Keir Starmer and former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, to not "increase taxes on working people".

He repeatedly refused to comment on possible tax rises or spending cuts ahead of 28 October, stating only: "Staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending."

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, said: "Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises."

He added that Healey "sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves".

In his speech from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in the Midlands, Healey described the UK as "turning the corner" and said greater devolution would spread economic growth more evenly across the UK.

But recent ructions in government debt markets have piled fresh pressure on already-stretched public finances, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs and the need to fund higher defence spending.

News.title: Murder arrest after two people found dead at house
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people were found dead in a house in Blackburn.

Lancashire Police said the bodies of a man and woman were found at the home in Hardman Street in the town at about 08:20 BST, and a man aged in his 40s had been arrested.

The man and woman, who have not been named, were both pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said they were unable to confirm the victims' ages but local residents told the BBC they were elderly.

Police said a dedicated team of officers had been assigned to the case, and were carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic inquiries.

News.title: Barrister jailed over revenge plot with client
News.content:
A barrister from West Yorkshire who plotted a revenge attack with her "career criminal" client has been jailed for more than three years.

Samreen Akhtar had represented Tabish Ali, who had been shot and injured in Blacker Road in Huddersfield on 14 September 2021.

The following day, the 38-year-old barrister, of Sufton Street, Huddersfield, was recorded on a telephone call to Ali putting forward a plan to find the person responsible for the shooting so they could be caused serious injuries, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Akhtar was convicted of encouraging or assisting the commission of an indictable offence, namely inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent.

At Manchester Crown Court on Monday, she was given a prison term of three years and three months.

Police said Ali was part of a drugs gang and was later charged with the murder of Jamal Nedd.

Nedd had been shot and killed outside his Huddersfield home as he was driving his mother to work on 19 December 2020.

Ali, of Clare Road, Cleckheaton, was charged with his murder in 2021 and later convicted and given a life sentence along with two other men in July 2022.

News.title: Murder arrests over baby girl's death in woodland
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a baby was found dead while camping with her family in Staffordshire.

The three-month-old girl died after emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest in woodland off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, at 08:45 BST on Saturday.

The people arrested were a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

All four were detained at the scene and have since been bailed while inquiries continue, Staffordshire Police said.

Det Insp Josh Lee said officers were working to gather further evidence around the circumstances of the girl's death and were "keeping an open mind".

He said it was being treated as an isolated incident and urged people not to share "unconfirmed and speculative" claims online.

News.title: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest told
News.content:
A 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died nearly two weeks later, an inquest has heard.

Philip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following an incident at the Crows Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

He is understood to have been visiting the pub for a drink when he went on to a stage in the venue to complain about the volume of the music.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains on bail under investigation.

The senior coroner Caroline Saunders said the former design engineer "sustained a fall at the pub", adding that it happened "following an allegation that he was pushed".

The inquest heard he was taken to the Grange hospital with a fractured hip, however his condition deteriorated and he died on the 12 August.

The coroner said Ormerod's death was being investigated by police and that a forensic post mortem examination had taken place.

An inquest was opened but adjourned while a police investigation is carried out.

The coroner said that the inquest would not be resumed if there was a criminal prosecution, however should there be a need for a conclusion, it would take place on 26 May 2027.

Philip Ormerod's son Robert previously said his father was a "pub character" and that he wanted justice for him.

Following Ormerod's death, Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said a criminal investigation is ongoing and urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.

The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 BST on the night of the incident to contact them.

News.title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
News.content:
Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.

More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than Â£30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.

After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.

The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.

Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".

In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

"In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.

"The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."

Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.

Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.

Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.

Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

News.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
News.content:
Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.

Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson .Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.

Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.

The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

The recordings will go out throughout October on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at midday on the pair's new show.

A performance from Stockport-formed band Blossoms on 5 October will kick off the run.

Rock band Nothing But Thieves, US rising star Stella Lefty, Brit-nominated singer Beabadoobee and London-based artist Odeal are also among the artists on the line-up.

Brighton duo Royal Blood will close out this year's sessions on 30 October, but a surprise artist, who will perform just before them, is still to be announced.

West Midlands superstar Jorja Smith will be performing following on from the release of her third album, What Are The Odds.

The Brit Award winner's latest album received largely positive reviews, with Rolling Stone UK describing it as her "best album yet". , external

Electronic heavyweights Chase & Status will also take to the studio after they headlined Reading and Leeds Festival last month.

And Oscar-winner Sam Smith will be rolling out their vocals following on from the release of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes, last month.

News.title: Exclusive: I unboxed the Sephora advent calendar before anyone else, here’s my review
News.content:
There’s plenty to like about Sephora’s beauty advent calendar for 2026, particularly the full-size Medik8 niacinamide peptides and Dr Sam’s flawless cleanser, the latter of which has a cult following among skincare fans.

Sol de Janeiro may have passed its viral peak (around 2023), but I’d still take a full-size body wash from the brand over yet another Rituals mini any day. Likewise, eyeshadow may have found itself on beauty’s unofficial blacklist, but Mario Dedivanovic has somehow made his Makeup by Mario ethereal eyes palette the exception.

Sephora always matches the number of products in its 25 drawers, but it has dropped the number of full-size items by three this year. This seems to be a recurring theme among retailers. For me, this is a good thing, as brands move their focus away from creating the biggest advent calendars and towards well-curated, high-performing beauty rosters.

Then again, the worth of Sephora’s calendar has been reduced by £19 since last year, while the retail price has increased by £10 – though, in the grand scheme of things, these figures are practically negligible. It also shouldn’t be overlooked that Sephora is the lowest-cost beauty advent calendar if you’re looking for one with a worth of more than £1,000 and a product count this high. For context, there’s a £10 price jump before the next calendar with a £1,000+ worth and that’s Cult Beauty at £245.

I got hands-on with all the products within (Lucy Smith/The Independent)

Speaking of well-curated product hauls, it’s worth mentioning that the selection here is more than just smoke and mirrors. Granted, brands like Summer Fridays and Gisou get ticks for aesthetics and Gen Z appeal, but the specific products Sephora has honed in on earned my expert approval in previous tests. Take the Summer Fridays’ blush butter balm, for instance; in my review, I described how the formulas were “oh-so-silky, diffusing onto my skin as if airbrushed into place.”

Likewise, K18’s leave-in conditioner – albeit featured in lots of calendars in 2025 – is a product I come back to time and again, so I won’t turn my nose up at the opportunity to top up my stash. In fact, in my guide to the best leave-in conditioners, I praised how “my hair was left hydrated, and the breakage I normally see around the mid to end of the hair shaft appeared smoothed.”

The calendar is available to shop now, so if you’re hoping to secure a Sephora advent in 2026, I’d get card details in, pronto.

News.title: Almost half of Brits think more should be spent on disability benefits
News.content:

Almost half of people think the government should spend more on disabled people, meaning proposals to cut disability benefits are likely to be “politically risky” for any major party, a new survey suggests.

While public attitudes to spending on welfare benefits have decreased overall, opinion on support for those who cannot work due to disability remains “remarkably strong”, according to the British Social Attitudes survey.

According to the findings of the BSA, carried out by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen), 49 per cent of respondents said there should be more spending on disability benefits, even if it would likely lead to higher taxes, compared to 7 per cent who said there should be less spending in this area.

The findings showed support for spending on disabled people was high even among right-leaning voters, with 40 per cent backing more spending on benefits for this group, while 10 per cent supported less.

The BSA survey is a long-standing survey that looks at social and political attitudes across a range of issues, including the NHS.

The survey also looked at public opinion on the NHS, comparing the results from when New Labour came to power in 1997 to the challenge facing Andy Burnham’s government.

The BSA found the scale of the NHS challenge facing the current Labour government is greater than that facing Sir Tony’s government.

The new analysis, including by experts from the King’s Fund and Nuffield Trust, showed that in 1996 people were most dissatisfied with NHS waiting times and hospital services.

This improved by 2010, but now dissatisfaction is much more widespread across all NHS services, with poorer ratings for GP services, A&E and hospitals.

‘Politically risky’

Reflecting on the findings about disability benefits, Dr Robert de Vries, senior lecturer in quantitative sociology at the University of Kent and BSA co-author, said: “Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong.

“Very few people favour cuts; disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum."

The news comes as the government awaits the final report of Sir Stephen Timms’s review into the personal independence payment (PIP) scheme, which was announced last year after ministers were forced to back down on proposals to tweak PIP assessment that effectively would’ve made it harder to claim

In an interim report earlier this year, Sir Stephen described the system for applying for the benefit as “dehumanising” and “degrading”.

Last month Reform UK announced welfare reform policies which would abolish personal independence payments (PIP) and the health element of Universal Credit for working-age adults.

In July the Conservative Party said it would “urgently reassess all mild PIP claims for anxiety, depression and ADHD.”

Comparing results by voters' political stance across all major parties, the BSA survey found Reform and Conservative voters are most likely to support spending less on benefits for disabled people who cannot work, as seven per cent of Tory voters and 11 per cent of Reform UK voters supported cutting disability benefits.

Public opinion on NHS

In the most recent BSA survey of 3,400 people in the UK last autumn, only 16 per cent were satisfied with the length of time it took to get a hospital appointment.

At the same time, only 14 per cent were satisfied with the length of time people spend waiting in A&E, while only 27 per cent said the same about a GP appointment.

The new report acknowledges shocks to the system such as the Covid-19 pandemic between when New Labour were in power and now, and argues the NHS is facing issues that “were largely absent” in 1997.

These include a more ageing population, with the share of the population aged 65 and over rising from 16 per cent in 1997 to 19 per cent in 2024, putting pressure on the NHS and social care.

Bea Taylor, co-author of the report and Fellow at the Nuffield Trust, said: “There is a striking similarity in the inheritance faced by the current Labour government and its New Labour predecessor when it comes to the NHS: low public satisfaction driven by concern over the speed at which patients can access care.

“But this time around the malaise felt by the public about the NHS is more widespread, affecting perceptions of all NHS services, not just hospital care. What’s more, the long tail of the Covid-19 pandemic has sent shockwaves through the NHS, making the road to recovery much more challenging for the current Government.”

In 1996, just before New Labour came into government, 36 per cent of the public were satisfied with the NHS, and this increased to a record 70 per cent by 2010 when Labour left office. In 2023, 24 per cent of the public reported being satisfied with the NHS, and in 2025 this figure increased to 2026.

The analysis also suggested that the public’s concerns have widened, with more people reporting problems with access to multiple services.

Figures showed that in 1996, 79 per cent felt the time it took to get an appointment with a consultant was in need of improvement, while 76 per cent said the same about getting a hospital operation. At the time, 43 per cent felt GP appointments needed improvement, and 77 per cent were satisfied with their GP service.

In 2023, 58 per cent were dissatisfied with the time it takes to get a GP appointment, and 63 per cent were dissatisfied with the time it takes to access hospital care. Now 35 per cent of the public report to be satisfied with their GP service, and 37 per cent are satisfied with their hospital service.

Danielle Jefferies, co-author of the report and senior analyst at The King’s Fund, added that it took the New Labour government 13 years to restore public confidence in the NHS, and that the challenge is now “broader and the money tighter.”

A Government spokesperson said: “We inherited a system of rising costs and poor outcomes for too many people which we are rectifying by extending award review periods, increasing face-to-face assessments, and helping sick or disabled people into jobs backed by £3.5bn by the end of the parliament.

“The final recommendations from the Timms and Milburn Reviews due this autumn will lay the foundation for sustainable long-term reform.”

The Conservative, Reform, Liberal Democrats and Green Parties were approached for comment.

News.title: From Trump to the Tardis and another new PM: Charles marks fourth year as king
News.content:

King Charles has maintained a prominent public profile throughout the fourth year of his reign, driven by an energetic diary of duties.

Over the last 12 months, Charles undertook official duties on 164 separate days. While this is a slight drop from 176 days the year before, it marks an increase on both his first year on the throne (161) and his second (133).

Alongside extensive nationwide travel, the King’s itinerary featured an audience with the Pope, two meetings with US President Donald Trump, and the arrival of a new UK prime minister Andy Burnham.

These commitments were fulfilled alongside ongoing cancer treatment, indicating that the 77-year-old monarch plans to maintain his workload.

Other key members of the royal family also increased their public appearances over the same period. Queen Camilla, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and the Duke of Edinburgh all recorded more working days than in the prior year, highlighting a joint push to expand royal engagements.

open image in gallery US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump bid farewell to King Charles III and Queen Camilla outside the White House in Washington DC in September ( PA )

The data was gathered by the Press Association from the Court Circular, which serves as the official published log of royal appointments.

September 8 marks the anniversary of the death in 2022 of Elizabeth II, aged 96, after reigning for 70 years.

It was the moment her son and heir Charles became King, and the date will remain a poignant occasion for the head of state.

The fourth year of Charles’s reign saw him visit places as far apart as the Eden Project in Cornwall, Grimsby Town Football Club in Lincolnshire and Ards Allotments in County Down.

In East Sussex he walked part of the renamed and expanded King Charles III England Coast Path; at Taff’s Well near Cardiff he took the controls of a tram-train; and at Jedburgh in the Scottish Borders he kicked off a game of the traditional street sport of hand ba’.

He even appeared to make a journey in the Doctor Who Tardis, stepping out of the time machine during the opening ceremony of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Charles did not undertake quite as many international engagements as in his third year, when he travelled to Australia, Canada, Italy, Poland and Samoa.

The main foreign trip of the King’s fourth year was a state visit to the United States, followed by a tour to Bermuda, in late April and early May 2026, when he delivered a well-received speech to the US Congress that celebrated Anglo-American relations.

It was only the second time in history that a reigning British monarch has addressed Congress, while Charles’s trip to Bermuda was his first royal visit as sovereign to a British Overseas Territory.

open image in gallery King Charles III and Queen Camilla walk out of the TARDIS during the opening ceremony ahead of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games ( Getty )

While in the US, the King was greeted by President Trump – an encounter that came just seven months after the two met at Windsor Castle in September.

Nearer to home, Charles made a two-day state visit to the Vatican in October 2025, during which he met Pope Leo XIV and attended a service in the Sistine Chapel.

The Press Association has classed a day with engagements as one where the monarch is recorded on the Court Circular as undertaking at least one visit, meeting or function in an official capacity.

Days where he carried out other, non-official events, such as attending church in a private capacity, have not been counted.

Using the same criteria, the Court Circular shows the Queen carried out engagements on 114 days during the fourth year of her husband’s reign, more than in each of the previous three years (104 in 2022-23, 107 in 2023-24 and 104 in 2024-25).

Camilla accompanied her husband on his overseas trips to the US and the Vatican as well many of his visits in the UK, besides travelling for solo engagements to places including the set of Disney’s TV drama Rivals in Bristol, the Pooh Sticks Bridge in Hartfield in East Sussex, and Spellow Library in Liverpool.

The last 12 months also saw the King greet the fourth prime minister of his reign in as many years, when Andy Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July.

Liz Truss was prime minister when Charles became King in September 2022, but was succeeded by Rishi Sunak the following month, who in turn gave way to Sir Keir in July 2024.

open image in gallery King Charles welcomes Andy Burnham, during an audience at Buckingham Palace, London ( PA )

Such a rapid turnover in premiers is unprecedented in modern times and last occurred more than 100 years ago, during the reign of Charles’s great-grandfather George V.

The King had 26 formal audiences with his prime minister during the past 12 months, 24 with Sir Keir Starmer and two with Andy Burnham.

This is broadly in line with previous years, which saw 26 audiences in his first year as head of state, 22 in his second and 23 in his third.

In addition, Charles held 12 meetings of the Privy Council.

This is the body of advisers that meets regularly with the monarch to oversee the issue of royal proclamations, charters and other ceremonial matters.

Privy Council members are mostly senior politicians past and present, though only a few serving ministers attend each session.

The council met slightly more frequently during Charles’s first year as King – 16 times – perhaps reflecting the increased amount of official business that accompanies the arrival of a new monarch, while there were 13 meetings in his second year and 11 in his third.

Besides public appearances and political meetings, the King has continued to hold many official one-to-one audiences with senior figures from UK charities and businesses, as well as greeting diplomats and leaders from around the world, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in both October 2025 and March 2026, and most recently French President Emmanuel Macron in September.

He has carried out these audiences throughout the past four years, even in the months of March and April 2024 when he was largely out of public view because of his illness.

open image in gallery The Princess Royal has also had a busy year - with 183 engagements listed for the past 12 months ( PA )

Buckingham Palace announced in February 2024 that the King had been diagnosed with a form of cancer, since when he has received regular treatment.

Among other senior royals, Press Association analysis shows the Princess Royal has maintained her reputation as the “hardest-working” member of her family, with engagements listed for 183 days in the past 12 months, close to the 190 in the previous year.

Edward is listed as carrying out engagements on 147 days, up from 130; William on 115 days, up from 108; and Kate on 63 days, up from 39.

All data is based on the Court Circular up to and including September 7 2026.

Gangs of criminals are “actively targeting” schools by creating deepfake sexualised images of children from pictures on their social media and websites and using them to blackmail schools for ransom, experts have warned.

Nearly half of headteachers have reported pupil images being used as part of harmful acts including extortion or blackmail threats, according to a new report published on Tuesday. More than half of them also reported being concerned images on their school website could be vulnerable to AI misuse.

It comes amid what child safety experts called a “pandemic” of deepfake child sexual image abuse being created online, with safeguarding experts warning schools are being “exploited”.

open image in gallery Criminal gangs are targeting school heads and trustees, experts said ( PA Wire )

The In Plain Sight report, commissioned by AI safeguarding tool Aidos, surveyed 500 primary and secondary school teachers in the UK. It found that 49 per cent of them had experienced an incident involving pupil image misuse, manipulation or an extortion attempt.

Additionally, 54 per cent said they have personal concerns that their school’s published images are vulnerable to AI misuse, and 45 per cent said their school has received a direct complaint from a parent about the misuse of a pupil’s image.

Speaking to The Independent, former national policing lead for child protection Simon Bailey said organised crime groups are “targeting school heads with a precise understanding of the pressure points”.

“They know that many school leaders will prioritise protecting their school's reputation above all else,” he said. “That instinct is entirely human and entirely understandable, but it is also a vulnerability, and it is being exploited.

“I strongly believe that many schools that have been targeted are, in many cases, not reporting it. They are managing it all behind closed doors, and the true picture continues to remain hidden.”

open image in gallery Schools have been told to be aware they could fall victim ( Getty/iStock )

Aidos founder Carole Osborne said as well as gangs of criminals extorting them, schools are also experiencing paedophiles using their images to generate their own child sexual abuse material (CSAM), and children creating deepfake images of other children and of teachers.

“I always knew that this was happening more and more, but I didn't realise how much it was happening, and how many schools it had happened to,” Ms Osborne told The Independent. “So to hear that those numbers were as high as they are was a real shock to me.”

Ms Osborne said she believes a lot of schools are still in the mindset that it won’t happen to them. “I would say stop hoping that it doesn't happen because it is happening and actually put some some real kind of practical resources in place to stop it happening to your school,” she added.

It comes after parents were advised not to post pictures of their children online in a stark warning by the National Crime Agency (NCA) and the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF).

Dan Sexton, the IWF’s chief technology officer, told the paper he was “very uncomfortable” about telling parents not to put pictures of children on public display but felt there was no other option.

“I don’t know what else to say to parents,” he said. “I would be very cautious [about putting pictures of children online] because there is no protection.”

Retailers suffered a disappointing August as looming household bill increases saw consumers reining in their spending, figures show.

Total UK retail sales increased by just 0.7% year on year, plunging from last August’s 3.1% and below the 12-month average growth of 1.6%, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC) and KPMG.

Food sales were up 2.6% on the year, but even this was below last August’s growth of 4.7% and below the 12-month average of 3.2%.

Non-food sales were down 0.8% on a year ago, against growth of 1.8% last August and below the 12-month average growth of 0.2%.

open image in gallery A shopper on Oxford Street, London (Jordan Pettitt/PA) ( PA Archive )

BRC lead economist Harvir Dhillon said: “August was a disappointing month for retail sales. Despite pockets of growth, particularly in some food categories, overall performance was below the average for the past year.

“With the cost of household bills rising, and set to rise further, many shoppers have clearly been tightening their belts.

“This was particularly true for discretionary spending, as big-ticket purchases like furniture and household appliances declined and consumers opted to instead treat themselves to smaller luxuries in health and beauty.”

Separate figures from Barclays show consumer card spending grew by 2.1% year on year in August, up from July’s 2% increase.

Consumers’ confidence in their household finances reached its highest level in six months, at 66% in August, up from 64% in July, a survey for the bank found.

Consumers also reported feeling more confident in their ability to live within their means at 71%, up from 69%.

Despite improving consumer confidence, 84% are concerned about rising prices.

Jack Meaning, chief UK economist at Barclays, said: “Consumer spending and confidence remained resilient in August, even as pressures from the Middle East began to filter into prices.

“This positive news suggests consumers should be able to weather the bout of narrowly focused, temporary inflation we think is coming down the track.

“However this week has shown risk remains.

“If the situation in the Middle East persists or intensifies in the coming months, squeezed households may need to be even more discerning with their spend.”

Seven in 10 (70%) parents avoid talking to teenagers about money, with some not wanting to worry their children, a survey indicates.

More than a quarter (28%) said they avoid money conversations because they do not want to worry their children, while 22% believe teenagers already have enough to focus on, according to the research commissioned by savings and investment firm M&G.

A fifth (20%) of parents feel financial conversations are not yet relevant, with nearly a third (31%) discussing money with their teenagers less than once a month.

The research surveyed parents of 16 to 18-year-olds and the teenagers themselves.

More than a third (35%) of teenagers said they believe their parents avoid financial discussions because they feel anxious about finances themselves.

Seven in 10 (70%) teenagers said they want to feel better prepared for their financial future, while only 21% believe they are too young to start learning about money.

More than seven in 10 (71%) said they would also like stronger financial education, particularly around investing and long-term planning.

The research also indicated that money conversations tended to focus on day-to-day spending rather than long-term financial planning, with parents being most comfortable discussing food shopping (47%) and holidays (36%).

Matthew Ings, a chartered financial planner at M&G said: “Teenagers are telling us they want to better understand money and feel confident about their future, yet many parents are holding back, often because they just don’t feel confident enough to have these conversations.

Politeness is putting some people at risk of scams, with more than half (53%) of adults having remained on an unexpected phone call in the past year for longer than they wanted to, according to an anti-fraud body.

The Take Five to Stop Fraud campaign, which commissioned a survey, found nearly a third (32%) of people said concerns about seeming rude would contribute to them feeling uncomfortable about halting a conversation.

Take Five’s campaign is warning people that fraudsters will try to exploit people’s politeness in order to keep conversations going, so they have a longer opportunity to build trust, apply pressure and influence people’s decisions.

Backed by Strictly Come Dancing judge Craig Revel Horwood, the campaign is encouraging people to resist the instinct to always be polite.

He said: “People know I’m not afraid to tell it like it is.

open image in gallery (Take Five/PA)

“Some would say I could do with a few more manners myself.

“But when it comes to fraud, being a bit rude is exactly the right thing to do.

“If someone unexpectedly asks for your money or personal information, don’t feel obliged to keep the conversation going.

“It’s perfectly acceptable to stop, take your time and check they’re really who they say they are.

“You don’t owe anyone your time just because they asked for it.”

More than nine in 10 (93%) people surveyed said they were brought up to be polite to people they do not know, according to the survey of 2,000 people across the UK carried out by Opinium Research in July.
