Sports.title: ‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea
Sports.content:
The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

View image in fullscreen Chief inspector Pete Dearden gives a briefing in the police room inside the stadium three hours before kick-off in the match between Arsenal and Chelsea. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Pete Dearden: ‘We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.’ Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”

Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal fans walk past live facial recognition cameras on their way to the ground. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen The Premier League has invested millions of pounds into the intelligence-led live facial recognition pilot. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.

Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”

The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

View image in fullscreen A constable high-fives a young Arsenal fan as he patrols the podium level at the Emirates. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen An officer acts as a spotter at the Emirates before kick-off. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

View image in fullscreen A Chelsea supporter is escorted out of the ground by Arsenal stewards. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Officers support a Chelsea content creator as he tries to record a piece after Arsenal’s 2-1 victory. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.

But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

Sports.title: Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start
Sports.content:
Unai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.

Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier Leagueand still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for the Champions League for the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.

It is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”

In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.

Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.

Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.

After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery is remaining calm despite Aston Villa’s slow start to the season. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Stewart Kendall/Apl/Sportsphoto

Another Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.

Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.

For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.

One of the most exciting of their 11 summer arrivals, the 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye, was an unused substitute for PSG in Salzburg. Another talent signed this summer, Johan Manzambi, continues to step up his fitness after a knee injury and could feature as early as Saturday against Nottingham Forest.

Only two of Villa’s new arrivals – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson – started at Hull last time out. Matteo Ruggeri, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho arrived from the bench. Taylor Harwood-Bellis, a £25m buy omitted from Villa’s Champions League squad, had a watching brief in Yorkshire. João Gomes was sent off on debut. Leon Goretzka, who joined on a free after leaving Bayern Munich, will not feature until at least October after a knee injury setback.

Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month.

“We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”

Sports.title: Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for Porto
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca believes Erling Haaland has become “complete” as his priorities have changed after the birth of the Manchester City No 9’s son two years ago.

Haaland has again started the campaign in prolific form, scoring three goals in City’s opening three Premier League victories. In three of the 26‑year‑old’s four previous seasons at City he has won the Premier League golden boot. Maresca pointed to how the birth of his son in 2024 changed the Norwegian’s motivation.

The manager said: “He’s a man now. He’s a dad. When he arrived here [in summer 2022] he was not a dad and now he’s a dad and life completely changes because the priority becomes his son. I’m happy for him because he was already top as a player and as a boy but now you can see that he is complete. He is a family man, he is still scoring goals so I’m very happy for him.”

City are at Porto in the opening league‑phase game of the Champions League on Tuesday. Haaland has played every competitive minute of the campaign so far, and Maresca said he will be rested at some point, particularly as as the striker was part of the Norway team that reached the World Cup quarter-finals.

The Italian said: “It’s not easy for Erling or for any of the players that play for club and international teams. I think it is normal that you [may] see these players start to be tired. So, it’s correct to give them some rest. It can be one game out or one week away.

“It depends on which moment we are in but the priority is to allow the players to be good and happy. When you see them tired the risk of injury increases, and we need players who are 100%.”

While Maresca’s options if Haaland is rested against Porto would be selecting Antoine Semenyo at centre-forward, or fielding Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki as a false 9, he pointed to the in-game control the two latter players can give City when required.

View image in fullscreen Nico O’Reilly pulled up with an injury before the Coventry match but will ‘probably’ be available to face Porto. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

“There is always a gameplan and Rayan can drop a little bit to manage the tempo and the game,” the 46-year-old said.

“We [also] need Rayan in the position to be dangerous – the last game against Coventry [a 1-0 win] we made contact with him five or six times between the lines and created chances.

“It depends on the game. Against Coventry, it was good for him to drop a little bit and manage the tempo and not always be a reference for the other team. We need him in the right position because he gives us the quality. Phil can also do that – and the last pass between the lines is very good so we are lucky that we have two very good players that can do this.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In his first campaign as head coach, Francesco Farioli led Porto to their 31st title, and they have a maximum 15 points from their opening five Primeira Liga games.

Maresca was asked if City will be favourites at the Estádio do Dragão. “We are here to do our best,” he said. “The game will dictate the favourite. This is a hard place to come. This season they started very good. In the last 14, 15 games in Europe they just lost one so we are going to try our best and try to win the game.

“I know that Porto is very good in set pieces. I think it has become part of the game now so we need to do our best, defend in the right way, score goals as much as we can from set pieces because it’s part of the game and you need to be perfect because all teams are prepared for that.”

Maresca said Nico O’Reilly would “probably” be available after missing the Coventry game with a late fitness problem, but the manager said he was “not sure” about Jérémy Doku’s availability after injury.

Sports.title: Chelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantage | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

View image in fullscreen Romeo Lavia and Cole Palmer (right) of Chelsea try to dispossess Myles Lewis-Skelly of Arsenal. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

Sports.title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down
Sports.content:
The former footballer Joey Barton will remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.

The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last week accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.

Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.

His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.

Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino wants the US to become ‘one of the most powerful countries in soccer’
Sports.content:
It’s been two months since the US men’s national team crashed out of the World Cup in disappointing fashion, and their head coach, Mauricio Pochettino, is back at work.

The former Tottenham and PSG manager was largely viewed as a short-term hire when he joined the US in 2024, brought on to help the team capitalize on their first home World Cup in more than three decades. Along the way, Pochettino and US Soccer warmed to the idea of a contract extension, one they finalized in August.



The US will play four friendlies in late September and early October against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada, but that stretch of games pales in comparison to the larger task at hand. Pochettino must guide the US to qualification for the 2030 World Cup, of course, but the Argentinian – and the federation – have more ambitious goals that involve reshaping the structure of soccer in the United States.

The US will also play at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, and it’s been widely reported they may feature in the Copa América that same summer. On Monday, Pochettino joined a small circle of reporters to talk about the task at hand. His quotes have been lightly edited for clarity and length.



Pochettino’s expanded role



Pochettino has said that choosing to remain with the US for another World Cup cycle is a chance for him to “have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly – and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field.” Indeed US Soccer’s announcement of Pochettino’s contract renewal came with an interesting wrinkle – the federation said the Argentinian would take a more prominent role steering the direction of youth development and coaching education, and would advise on professional league collaboration and a handful of other areas.



That sort of broad influence isn’t exactly an alien concept in international soccer, but no US coach has ever taken such a prominent role in steering the direction of the program as a whole. He will not have to wait long to make his mark, as US Soccer is undergoing a significant restructuring and is in the process of filling two new director roles for the men’s and women’s senior and youth programs. On Monday, Pochettino said he’s made it clear he’s happy to help with that process – “but it can’t [just] be my guy,” he said, laughing.

“This is the future of the USA,” said Pochettino. “We want to try to perform in the World Cup and to create something special with the fans. And now it’s about being a part of the legacy that the federation wants to create – becoming one of the most powerful countries in soccer. That is a dream, no? It’s amazing. If we can be part of that, we are so excited and so happy.”



On Folarin Balogun’s deadline day drama



This summer’s transfer window was a decidedly quiet one for the USMNT. Aside from a few notable moves – Gio Reyna to Strasbourg, Sebastian Berhalter to Middlesbrough and Zavier Gozo’s leap from MLS to Crystal Palace – many players stayed put.



The list includes Monaco forward Folarin Balogun, who seemed poised for a big-money move after a breakout World Cup. Instead, Balogun saw a move to Everton fall apart at the last moment, with the Premier League club citing a potential fitness issue, something Monaco (and Balogun) both contested.



Balogun is far from the first player to suffer a deadline day letdown, and Pochettino offered support for the 25-year-old on Monday.



“Yes, it’s difficult because you cannot influence that decision,” said Pochettino. “You need to support what they are doing with the people making the decisions. In some special cases, like Flo’s, I will call in the next few days. I wanted to give him a little bit of space after that situation in Everton. I want to know from him what happened. But we are always offering our support, and that’s it. I think he’s an important player for us, he was an important player in the World Cup and I hope that he can find being in Monaco, or in another place, his best place to perform in the best way.”



Dual nationals



Pochettino said little about the 26-man roster he’ll call into camp later this month. One player we know will not be there, though, is Augsburg center-back Noahkai Banks. The German-American remains undecided about his international future and will not feature for the US this window.



The 19-year-old has said he wants to make a decision by “the next international break, or at the latest by the international break after next.” German media has reported that newly appointed Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has gone so far as to scout Banks in person.

“We are in contact with all the potential dual nationals,” said Pochettino. “I think it’s important for us, of course, because that is the human connection that is so important. Even if they, like in that case, Noki, didn’t change his mind and is waiting still, no decision, and of course we cannot consider him for the next camp … But the organization is working with all the dual nationals and players with the possibility to make a decision. That human connection is important because if one day they feel that they can defend and they want to fight and to be part of our national team … Of course, if they deserve it, and we consider that they deserve to be involved, of course we are going to call [them up].”

Los Angeles 2028

Olympic soccer, as it always has, takes a backseat to any number of global and continental competitions. Still, the 2028 Games in Los Angeles present a massive opportunity to the USMNT, who will once again look to captivate a home audience after this summer’s World Cup.



The Games, Pochettino said on Monday, are a top priority to his staff, who are working in concert with U-23 head coach Steve Cherundolo. Curiously, Pochettino mentioned making use of this coming window to examine a handful of younger players who could feature at the 2028 Olympics.



“I think we have a core of young players that need to play the Olympic Games because I think an objective for our federation and for the country … is to try to be a contender for the gold medal. [The Games are] going to be in our country, and we are going to support that. And always the decision on the first team with the players that are in that process – we are going to take the best decision altogether, always, and to try to protect those players in the best condition, and to help them to arrive, not only being important for the first team, but important for [the] type of competition that is important for the country.”



On those young players



Pochettino has been a frequent critic of the mentality of some American players. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, he expressed frustration with players who he felt did not prioritize national team call-ups and sometimes seemed to struggle with soccer’s place in American culture.



On Monday, Pochettino seemed eager to change the mentality of coaches and young players who decline call-ups, sometimes citing fitness or load management concerns.



“[It’s important that young players] want to be involved,” said Pochettino. “[When a player in MLS or elsewhere] has the possibility to join the under-18 or under-19 national teams, or the Olympic Games, it’s so important to be part of them. That is another habit that we need to change. Sometimes the coaches say, you know, ‘I have a 17-year-old guy that plays in MLS,’ but when the under-19 national team calls they say: ‘No, they need to rest.’ If you’re 17 and need to rest? Ay, ay, ay. You have a big problem.



He added: “You cannot rest at 17. When I was 17, 16, or 15, all of my teammates, when we played in Newell’s Old Boys, sometimes you play two, three games in the same day. You cannot treat a 17- or 18-year-old player like a 30-year-old player. Sometimes we [treat younger players like older players], rather than settling the good principles and good habits. We make 18-year-old players like [28- or 30-year-olds]. That is amazing, no? Physically, when you are 18, the possibility to recover from one effort to another is different when you are 32. Sometimes [young] players come with the older mindset, and that is the evolution that we need to change in [American soccer.]”

Sports.title: Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started better | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

Sports.title: WSL talking points: Palace result in doubt after substitution nightmare, Arsenal signings shine
Sports.content:
Threat of punishment ruins Palace’s big day

Kirsty Howat’s 60-second cameo deep into injury time could ruin what was a memorable day for Crystal Palace on their return to the top flight. An impressive 1-0 victory over Everton was celebrated emphatically by Jo Potter and her players but that joy would have been replaced by concern and frustration not long after. On Sunday evening WSL Football revealed that there had been a breach of the rules – the Eagles used four different substitute windows rather than the regulated three – which had not been picked up by either the coaching staff or the match officials. An investigation has now been launched with punishment to be decided (there is a potential for the result to be overturned). The needless error has put a dampener on what should have been a positive afternoon thanks to England Under-23s forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s winner on her WSL debut. Sophie Downey

Chelsea must sharpen their claws

It was not the first time Chelsea have struggled to kill off games under Sonia Bompastor and, on the basis of Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villa after an almost excessively dominant performance, it seems the issues of last season have not been put to bed. “I think in a few games we had last season we were in the same scenarios,” said Bompastor. “So, yeah, if you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that it’s crazy we couldn’t win the game.” It felt all too familiar, with last season’s 1-0 defeat to Everton in December, which ended a 585-day unbeaten run in the WSL, particularly springing to mind. Then, Chelsea accrued 79% possession, had 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times but came away with a loss. The fear for Chelsea fans will be that, in the 10 months since that defeat, the issues that were becoming increasingly evident have not been resolved. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-1 Aston Villa

View image in fullscreen Sjoeke Nüsken (left) shields the ball in Chelsea’s game against Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge. Photograph: Jermaine Addo-Yeboah/SPP/Shutterstock

Signings shine on competitive debut for Arsenal

Much has been made of Arsenal’s recruitment over the summer with many believing that Renée Slegers now has a team primed to challenge for the title. Four of their new signings started in the 1-0 win over Brighton, with two standing out. Recognition of Lisa Baum’s potential came to the fore with a series of impressive showings in pre-season. The 19-year-old caught the eye on her WSL debut on Sunday not just for her well-taken goal but for her direct, positive style of play. Meanwhile, Georgia Stanway showed exactly why Slegers was so keen to bring her in. The England international has added balance to the midfield, allowing Mariona Caldentey to operate more creatively. Stanway controlled the middle of the park, ranking first for touches – at 131, she had 25 more than anyone else – joint top for accurate passes (86%), first for passes into the final third (23) and second for chances created (2). SD

Role model Hemp brings up double century

“Just give her the ball and then something happens!” Andrée Jeglertz said of Lauren Hemp after her 200th appearance for Manchester City. The England winger was on typically strong form during the 3-1 victory over Birmingham City and became only the fourth Manchester City player to reach that landmark of appearances. Jeglertz was full of praise for the 26-year-old and continued: “One thing that is fascinating with Lauren is, if you come and watch one of our training sessions, she has the same joy for playing football. It’s also shown in the games. Our job is to put her in situations where she can show how good she is. [She] shows young players what it’s about. They need to love to go to work and love to go to the football field. It’s not just a job. It’s also an identity.” Tom Garry

Maestre masters the melting pot

Many believe the biggest challenges faced by the London City Lionesses manager, Eder Maestre, is integrating a squad that has experienced a high turnover of players and balancing the demands of an expectant cast of superstars. There have been eight arrivals this summer and seven players have departed. Teams that have experienced a high turnover of players after a strong WSL season have previously struggled. On Friday night, however, Maestre’s team showed signs they could buck that trend with a 2-1 win over Manchester United. It wasn’t always the prettiest of performances but fledgling connections were forming in Bromley, with the individual quality of players helping to cut across any lack of cohesion. Gelling players is not easy though. “I think it’s one of the most challenging situations for any coach,” said Maestre. “We have talented players, but we have a clash of cultures. I’m trying to align everybody in the same place, trying to create something big where everybody can feel represented … I’m very happy with the performance.” SW

Match report: London City Lionesses 2-1 Manchester United

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Daniëlle Van De Donk (centre) peels away after scoring London City Lionesses’ winner against Manchester United. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Are Charlton strong enough to stay up?

It was a worrying start to the season for Charlton Athletic fans, as the newly promoted side were convincingly beaten on home turf by the club that finished second from bottom in the WSL last season. Not only that, Charlton failed to register a shot on target during Liverpool’s 4-0 victory and the hosts could only manage two efforts off target, as Gareth Taylor’s visitors’ enjoyed 76% of the possession. It had been a much closer-fought affair when the two sides met on the same ground on April in the Women’s FA Cup quarter-finals, when Liverpool eventually squeezed through after extra-time, but the Merseyside club appear to have strengthened significantly over the summer whereas Charlton clearly have significant work to do. TG

Hanson makes instant impact for Spurs with debut double

Kirsty Hanson wasted no time making her mark at Tottenham, scoring twice on her debut to secure a 3-1 victory over West Ham after joining from Aston Villa this summer. The forward opened her account with a first-time finish after an assist from Signe Gaupset and then produced a superb left-footed strike into the top corner. Hanson was the third-highest scorer in the WSL last season, behind Bunny Shaw and Alessia Russo, with 12 goals in 22 matches. She was one of several key transfers made during the window with the club believing she will add a new dimension to their attack. Speaking to Spurs Women social media about her performance, the manager, Martin Ho, said: “The movement for her first one was outstanding, and the second was a wonderful strike. When she’s in those positions with that quality and control, she’s really hard to play against. There’s lots more to come from Kirsty.” Réshma Rao

Sports.title: 'Man City have got away with b****y murder': Lord Sugar makes incendiary claim as he accuses the club of 'frightening' the Premier League with case over 115 charges still unresolved after £450MILLION summer spend
Sports.content:
'Man City have got away with b****y murder': Lord Sugar makes incendiary claim as he accuses the club of 'frightening' the Premier League with case over 115 charges still unresolved after £450MILLION summer spend

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Tottenham chairman Lord Alan Sugar has explosively claimed Manchester City have 'got away with b****y murder' due to their 115 charges case remaining unresolved.

City were charged with 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League's financial rules in February 2023 and a 12-week hearing concluded in December 2024 – but an independent commission is still yet to publish its ruling on the 'hugely complex case'.

The club strenuously deny the allegations. The verdict could see City exonerated or facing historic penalties.

Lord Sugar, who served as Tottenham chairman from 1991 to 2001, became the latest critic of the length of time required for the infamous financial charges case.

'I am waiting to see what is going to happen with Man City, the thing is Man City have got away with b****y murder,' Lord Sugar said in an appearance on Football Uncensored.

'For about three years now there has been talk of them infringing these rules, they have most probably paid about half a billion to lawyers so far to frighten the Premier League.

Lord Sugar explosively claimed Man City have 'got away with murder' due to their long-running 115 charges case remaining unresolved

City’s hearing – over allegations of repeated breaches of the top-flight’s financial controls – ended in December 2024 but a verdict remains outstanding. City deny all wrongdoing

'When are they going to get done or aren't they going to get done.'

Host Piers Morgan, a vocal Arsenal supporter, agreed stating: 'It is a very interesting question, City have just spent an absolute fortune in this transfer window and yet they have got 115 charges hanging over them.

'It seems to have been going on with an interminable amount of time but will have dramatic consequences.

'If they are found guilty, you could see them having Premier League titles stripped from them, maybe three, maybe four - hopefully coming Arsenal's way - you could see them relegated. This has enormous implications, how can they spend all this money with this hanging over them?'

Man City spent £440million in the transfer window and equalled the British transfer record signing £125million Enzo Fernandez.

It was a bumper summer for City after the exit of long-serving manager Pep Guardiola. They also signed Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£86m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Allan and Geronimo Rulli.

David Bernstein, who served as Man City chairman from 1998 until 2003 and served as Football Association chair 2011-13, on Sunday also attacked the lack of an outcome and questioned the Premier League's handling of the case.

Writing in the Sunday Times, Bernstein said: 'The fact they have done this (transfer spend) against the background of the 115 Premier League charges is extraordinary and makes a mockery of regulation in England's top division, supposedly the best-run league in the world.

'Why the league decided to prosecute all 115 alleged offences is a mystery to me. Surely common sense (often in short supply) would point to simplifying the process by taking a handful of the bigger, clearer issues and pursuing these as specimen cases.

David Bernstein was City chairman from 1998 until 2003 and served as FA chair 2011-13

Premier League boss Richard Masters has claimed that Manchester City’s ongoing 115 charges saga is ‘not necessarily top of the list’ when it comes to his conversations with clubs

'Justice delayed is justice denied, and the longer this process is drawn out, the more the resulting implications and challenges are compounded.'

This is the fourth season to begin under the cloud of the City 115 charges announcement.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters conceded last month that the case was taking 'longer than expected', but said the saga was 'not necessarily top of the list' when it comes to his conversations with clubs.

Four Premier League sides have reserved the right to seek compensation should City be found guilty and it would appear that much of football is desperate for an outcome.

However, Masters suggested that the noise in boardrooms up and down the country is not as loud as one might imagine.

'I obviously speak to clubs all the time,' he said last month. 'It's not necessarily a topic of conversation that is top of the list. (There are) Lots of other things to talk about and do. The Premier League moves on. It's starting (again) on Friday evening.'

Masters has previously admitted to being frustrated by the length of time the independent panel is taking to return its verdict.

'The process is the process,' he said. 'It will resolve itself. But as you know, I literally can't say a thing about it. There's only one available option, which is to allow the process to reach its natural conclusion. I can't talk about the substance of the case. I can't talk about the timing of the case. Our rules are very clear about that. I understand that people are frustrated but it will take as long as it takes.'

Man City are joint top of the Premier League, having taken maximum points from their first three matches under the guidance of Enzo Maresca – including a 1-0 victory over promoted Coventry City on Saturday.

Sports.title: Champions League supercomputer: PSG are FIFTH favourites for a third consecutive crown and Man United are given almost the same chance of winning as Real Madrid - but which of Arsenal and Man City top the list?
Sports.content:
Two-time defending champions Paris Saint-Germain have been deemed fifth favourites to win this year's tournament, with a supercomputer viewing Arsenal as the team to beat. PSG became just the second team after Real Madrid to go back-to-back in the tournament in the Champions League era when the French giants overcame Arsenal in May. Luis Enrique's side overcame the Gunners in a penalty shoot-out in Budapest following a 1-1 draw. Ahead of the league phase of this season's competition beginning on Tuesday, Opta's supercomputer has deemed PSG have just a 7.1 per cent chance of clinching a third successive title. It follows PSG having endured their worst start to a season in 19 years after losing to Lens in the French Super Cup, as well as drawing against Rennes and Lille in Ligue 1 before a 2-1 loss to Monaco on the weekend. PSG are ranked behind Arsenal, Bayern Munich, Man City and Barcelona in the supercomputers list of favourites. Two-time reigning champions PSG are deemed by Opta to be the fifth favourites to win this season's Champions League Arsenal are backed as favourites as they bid to bounce back from losing last season's final to win the tournament for the first time The favourites have been devised after the supercomputer ran 10,000 simulations of the Champions League season. Arsenal have come out on top following the simulations, with Mikel Arteta's side backed to win Europe's elite club competition for the first time. The reigning Premier League champions finished as runners-up in the Champions League for the second time last season, having also made the final back in 2006. Arsenal have been given a 20.9 per cent chance of glory. The Gunners are seen as having a 50 per cent chance of reaching the semi-finals and are 34.8 per cent to make the final. Bayern Munich are narrowly behind Arsenal, with the German champions given a 19.4 per cent chance to win the Champions League for the first time since 2020. Man City follow at 12.3 per cent in their first season under Enzo Maresca, while Barcelona are fourth at 8.2 per cent. The Spanish giants last reached the Champions League final back in 2015, when they were crowned winners for the fifth time. Michael Carrick's Man United side are given just a 3.8 per cent chance of glory this season Barcelona's best showings since have been two semi-finals, achieved in 2019 and 2025. Liverpool are ranked as sixth favourites at 6.1 per cent, with Andoni Iraola set to experience his first Champions League campaign in charge of the Reds. Record champions Real Madrid are ranked down in seventh place, with Jose Mourinho's side given just a 4.4 per cent chance. Their prospects are only marginally better off than Manchester United, who are given an outsiders chance at 3.8 per cent on their return to the competition. The top ten is completed by 2025 runners-up Inter Milan and Europa League winners Aston Villa.
