World.title: Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.content:
SHAANXI, Northwest China — “You have gone off route. Recalculating.” For the fourth time that day, Zhao Yushun and his wife, Yuan Zhenzhen, ignored the GPS. By then, jujube trees, signs advertising local specialties, and a view of distant mountains had already pulled them off course.

Now it was a farmer sorting pears beneath a black sunshade by the roadside in Dali County, northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.

“What kind of pear is this? I’ve never seen it before,” Zhao asks after they pull over. “How’s the harvest this year? Have people here been growing pears longer, or jujubes?”

“Jujubes,” the farmer says with a wry smile. His family has grown them since he was a child, but over the past decade more and more people have started planting them, and the returns are no longer what they once were. “Things are worth more when they’re scarce.”

As he speaks, Yuan raises her camera and starts recording, keeping it around waist height to make it less conspicuous.

The farmer soon moves beyond pears, telling Zhao about his years as a migrant worker in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen and his eventual return home to care for his children and aging parents. With jujube profits falling, he has also begun growing pears, hoping for a better return.

Thirty minutes later, Zhao and Yuan are back on the road. The encounter becomes the closing scene of the fifth episode of their “Yellow River” series.

Since 2021, Zhao and Yuan have traveled through more than 1,100 villages and towns, turning roadside conversations and unplanned stops into short documentaries about rural China. Their account, Yuzhenjishi, or “Encountering Reality,” has more than 530,000 followers on Bilibili, one of China’s largest video platforms.

Many of the people Zhao and Yuan film are farmers in their 60s or older who grew up working the land, spent years as migrant workers in cities, then returned home after being aged out of many urban jobs. They now farm through falling crop prices, increasing mechanization, extreme weather, and the departure of younger generations.

Since July, Zhao and Yuan have been traveling along the Yellow River, one of China’s longest and most historically important waterways, filming a six-episode series on the farms and pastures along its banks. Sixth Tone joined them for three days as they traveled through Henan, Shanxi, and Shaanxi provinces.

Down to earth

For Zhao and Yuan, leaving rural China had once seemed the obvious measure of success. Both grew up largely in the care of older relatives while their parents worked in cities, part of a rural generation known in China as “left-behind children.”

When Zhao did well in school growing up in a village in central China’s Hunan province, villagers would tell him: “Your hands aren’t meant to hold a hoe. They’re meant to hold a pen. You have to get out and go to the big city.”

He studied journalism; Yuan, who grew up in a small town in the southern Guangdong province, studied Chinese literature. Both made it to university, but neither found the stable urban life that education had seemed to promise.

As graduates of second-tier universities, they moved between media jobs in Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and other cities, rarely earning enough to feel settled.

“We moved so many times,” Zhao said. “Every time we moved, we wondered whether we should hire a medium-sized truck, only to find that our stuff filled barely half of a small one. After we left, there wouldn’t be any trace of us in the city.”

By 2021, Zhao and Yuan were both 27 and living in a rented apartment in Beijing. Zhao spent about three hours a day commuting by bus and subway. He came to recognize the passengers who got on and off at particular stops without ever knowing who they were.

The routine made him feel like “a cog in the machine.” Yuan described herself as “someone stuck in a corner.”

One night in 2021, they decided to start their own video account. They named it Yuzhenjishi, combining one character from each of their names with the slogan: “Let the overlooked be seen.”

Their first post was an edit of news footage about a herd of elephants that had wandered north from their habitat in the southwestern Yunnan province. At the end, they added a caption: “A herd of elephants drifting north, just like us leaving home to make a living.”

The couple soon moved to Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, where they continued working in media while filming in their spare time. At first, they focused largely on small cities around the province. But after making a video about left-behind children in a mountainous area, they found themselves increasingly drawn to villages and towns.

Within a year, Yuan proposed a more drastic move: quitting their jobs and making videos full time. After spending much of their childhoods trying to study their way out of rural China, Zhao and Yuan began returning to it with cameras.

For Zhao, the change brought a sense of connection he had rarely felt while covering new skyscrapers and suburban redevelopment in cities. The rural stories were “things I genuinely care about,” he said. “I finally felt grounded.”

As they began filming rural communities, viewers increasingly responded with stories of their own. Some left comments 400 or 500 words long.

One viewer from Hunan described growing up in a mountainous area where families had little land to farm and few ways to save money. “We all ended up taking the same path: leaving home to find work,” the viewer wrote. “It was all just to make a living.”

An agricultural university student wrote that after drought destroyed an experimental crop, they began searching for coverage of similar losses and were struck by how little they found. “Farmers and real rural communities barely have a voice of their own,” the student wrote.

The responses became important enough that Zhao and Yuan later printed a selection in a leaflet accompanying their first book, an anthology adapted from the written narratives of their videos. They came to see their videos as only half the story; viewers supplied the other half.

“We’re like a little public square,” Zhao said. “I pick up a loudspeaker and shout, ‘If anyone has something they want to say, come over.’ And then people really do come and tell their stories.”

On record

In practice, Zhao’s “loudspeaker” is usually just a question.

In a cornfield, he picked up an ear the harvester had missed and called to a farmer gleaning nearby: “Do you still want this?” Soon, the man was telling him about a nearby reservoir he had helped repair years earlier.

On the banks of the Yellow River, Zhao approached two men overseeing repairs to an embankment. “We’re from the south and have never seen this kind of embankment,” he said. “Could you explain it to us?”

Few turn him away. And once they begin talking, Yuan watches for the moment to start filming.

After filming a group of peach farmers packing nectarines for delivery to a foreign trade company, Zhao and Yuan were offered some fruit. When they asked how much they owed, one farmer waved them off.

“No need to pay,” he said. “Just put this in your video.”

Zhao remembered another farmer telling him much the same thing: “Little brother, there’s no money in farming these days. Look how hard life is for us farmers. Film this and put it on people’s phones. I’ll give you a like.”

“Farmers actually really want to talk,” Zhao said after returning to the car. “They just don’t have a channel to do so. So we bring the microphone to their doorstep.”

Zhao and Yuan describe these farmers as “standing at the crossroads of an era,” perhaps the last generation shaped primarily by traditional small-scale farming.

Their conversations often return to money and work, from falling crop prices and thin margins to years of physical labor and pensions that leave many older rural residents with little to live on.

Zhao argues that rural life is often viewed from outside in one of two ways. “People tend to imagine the countryside either as an idyllic retreat or as a place of poverty and hardship,” he said. “But both are ways of looking in from the outside.”

“We’re part of this world ourselves,” Zhao said. “What we do is document it from within and then communicate it outward.”

One of their most watched videos underscored the point more directly. Released in 2022 under the title “China’s 760 Million Farmers Don’t Need Praise,” it has nearly 5 million views.

“Since primary school, textbooks have taught us to praise farmers and applaud their hard work, but they never taught us to truly understand them,” the video said. “For farmers, mountains and rivers are not poetic, and rural life is no pastoral idyll. Farming is about survival.”

They have also tried posting on YouTube, with limited success. Zhao believes many of their stories require too much background knowledge for overseas audiences.

“After all, we are not Li Ziqi,” he said, referring to the hugely popular Chinese creator known internationally for idealized videos of rural life. “We are not making a pastoral fantasy.”

Still rolling

This spring, Zhao and Yuan hoped to film elderly porters who haul oranges out of the mountainous Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River.

But by the time they went looking for them, drones had taken over most of the work. Only a handful of porters still do it today, mainly on plots with too few orange trees to meet the minimum charge for drone transport.

“And of course, that’s a good thing. It’s a sign of progress that people no longer have to do such grueling work,” Zhao said. “But what that generation of porters went through, the lives they lived, and the labor they endured, was never recorded.”

They have encountered the same problem while trying to document people who built reservoirs, canals, and other water projects more than half a century ago.

Yuan’s grandmother had helped build an irrigation canal when she was young. Before she died, Zhao and Yuan took her back to see it. “Canal, reservoir — I’ve come to see you with my walking stick,” she said.

Children were playing nearby. Yuan’s grandmother tried to strike up a conversation with a gray-haired man in his 60s. “Did you help build the canal?” she asked. “It was such hard work back then.”

“How could I have?” he replied. “Anyone who worked on it would be at least 80 or 90 by now.”

Yuan’s grandmother smiled and said nothing more.

Many of the projects were built more than 60 years ago, and Zhao said it is increasingly hard to find surviving workers who can still tell their stories.

During the Yellow River trip, they met a man who had worked on one such project. Later, Zhao repeated a line the man had uttered in his local accent: “Once it was finished, it had nothing more to do with us.”

“If we don’t film these stories now, in another 10 years, there’ll be no one left who remembers them,” Yuan said.

The couple says they plan to spend 10 years documenting rural China. They are not worried about running out of stories, because many of the questions they pursue — about farming, migration, aging, and the changes reshaping villages — have no simple answer.

For Zhao, putting those questions on camera is a necessary first step. “First it has to be seen,” he said. “Once it is seen, people can start paying attention.”

Keeping that space open also costs money. After quitting their jobs in 2022, Zhao and Yuan burned through their savings and accumulated more than 250,000 yuan ($37,000) in debt.

They bought their camera, drone, and car on installments and took on outside commercial projects to support their documentary work. Even now, they sometimes sleep in the car while filming and get a hotel only when they need to do laundry.

It was not until 2025, the year they married, that they felt for the first time that they had actually made some money. After paying down debts and heading out to film again, much of it was soon gone.

“We were constantly moving money around just to keep things afloat,” Yuan said. “At the beginning of the year, we landed some other commercial deals, and it barely made us feel alive again. It’s like dying and coming back to life, then dying and coming back again.”

The two have nevertheless settled into a division of labor that requires little discussion. Zhao does most of the interviewing, appears on camera and narrates; Yuan films and edits. On the road, they often know without speaking when Zhao should deliver a piece to camera, when Yuan needs another shot, or when they should stop and try again.

But they differ over what they expect the work to achieve.

For years, Yuan wrote the same sentence on every résumé she sent to prospective employers: “Images have the power to change the world.” Zhao often repeated it too.

She is less certain now.

“I’m just going through a bit of a period of uncertainty,” Yuan said. “Change is difficult. Video may not necessarily change the world, but it can record the world.”

“I want to change things; he wants to record them,” she added. “I’m the more radical one.”

For Zhao, the record itself is reason enough to continue. “These are precious historical records,” he said. “A hundred years from now, someone may look through our videos to understand what this generation of farmers was thinking.”

Along the Yellow River, Zhao and Yuan collected water in plastic bottles at different points on their journey. At the river’s estuary in the eastern Shandong province, they opened the bottles one by one and poured the water back in.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Zhao Yushun (left) and Yuan Zhenzhen film a flooded field in Baise, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, October 2025. Courtesy of Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.title: Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.content:
Photographer He Xu first passed through the China-Nepal border at Gyirong Port in 2010. He remembers that it was just a row of rustic, clay-colored bungalows.

Over the past 16 years, he has revisited at least 100 times, witnessing the area’s steady growth, with those bungalows eventually replaced by a grand, imposing building.

Yet that progress came to a violent halt on the morning of Aug. 26, when a flash flood caused by a mountain glacier ripped through the port in Shigatse, in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. As of Sept. 2, the disaster had killed at least 1,204 in Nepal and 21 in China, according to Xinhua News Agency. Almost 5,000 people remain missing, including 546 in Gyirong.

He, who runs a photo studio in the regional capital, Lhasa, was in Beijing when he heard the news. Over the years, he had gotten to know more than 20 people working at the port, including customs and immigration officials, firefighters, and disease-control workers. He began hurriedly searching through his phone contacts.

“Are you safe? Please reply when you see this. I’m really worried,” he texted them. Most of his messages went unanswered.

Nestled in a deep, winding valley at the foot of the Himalayas, about 100 kilometers from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, China’s Gyirong County is referred to as “the back garden of Mount Qomolangma” — or Mount Everest, as it’s known in the West. The land port there is historically among the largest for trade between China and Nepal. After opening for bilateral customs clearance in 2014, the volume of goods passing through has increased rapidly.

“On one side of the port was a huge parking lot, where vehicles from both countries waited for inspection,” He recalls. “Next to the lot were several white buildings, four or five floors each, where the on-duty staff lived.”

Across from the lot was a police station and a row of small stores including a supermarket run by a middle-aged couple from the neighboring Sichuan province, a souvenir shop run by a Nepalese merchant, and three restaurants.

“Most visitors were tourists who took a quick photo at the border gate and left,” says the 50-year-old photographer. “There wasn’t much demand for a bustling commercial street. But the port staff stayed year-round, and these outlets were their only options for shopping and dining.”

Many of these border officials are among the missing.

With the flash flood destroying about three kilometers of the highway leading to Gyirong, it took two days for the first rescue teams from Xizang and Sichuan to reach the disaster zone. The highway was reportedly reopened on Sept. 2, allowing access to more rescuers, emergency supplies, and heavy machinery.

A warm welcome

The first reply that He received was from a Tibetan friend working at the port’s disease-control station. He had requested the day off on Aug. 26 and gone into town, narrowly escaping the massive torrent of rock, ice, and water that had wiped out his workplace.

The photographer offered to transfer some money so that his friend could purchase food and emergency supplies and bring them to the port, but he declined. “All the roads over there are blocked,” he replied. “The rescue teams are still using bulldozers and excavators to clear a path, moving forward inch by inch.”

After two sleepless nights, He set off from Beijing for Gyirong on the morning of Aug. 28. He had no idea how he would help — he just knew he had to go.

Since the disaster, the Gyirong Entry-Exit Border Inspection Station’s official channel on the WeChat messaging platform has been inundated with messages from well-wishers.

Many staff at the port are in their early 30s and hail from various parts of China. Far from their families, most live quiet, monotonous lives.

He Xu once wandered into the staff dormitories and noted the austerity of the rooms, with just two beds, a desk, and simple storage cabinets. The housing complex had a recreation room with table tennis and other sports facilities, but he’d never seen anyone using them. “The most typical thing I saw staff doing after work was calling their families,” he says.

The workers rarely ventured far, He says, leaving them little opportunity to appreciate the valley scenery — so he decided his lens would be their “eyes.” One person wanted to see a kiang, an indigenous wild ass; another, the splendor of Ngari prefecture, a 15-hour drive west; another, the view from a 4,500-meter platform in the Himalayas just an hour away. Each time, He would capture what they asked for and share the pictures on WeChat.

The customs staff rotated every three or four days. Off-duty workers are accommodated in the county seat, about 90 minutes away by bus, where they can enjoy more variety in terms of meals, shopping, and entertainment.

Those who have passed through Gyirong Port often speak of the “pleasant, helpful” nature of the customs and security personnel there.

Wen Lili from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province visited in early August. She remembers a young police officer who helped suggest the best places to take photos — the checkpoint, boundary marker, and the Friendship Bridge over the border — and where to exchange Chinese renminbi for Nepalese rupees. “It’s such a tiny place, and he told me everything there was to see,” she says.

He Xu says that, one time, his pickup truck was dangerously low on fuel, and a police officer drove more than 40 kilometers to the nearest gas station to bring him a full jerry can.

Two years ago, He joined a customs officer named Dorje and some of his friends for a meal in town. Dorje came from Maizhokunggar County, more than 800 kilometers from Gyirong, and was 10 years from retirement. With a beaming smile, he had talked of his three children, who had all gone to work in major cities.

With the savings he had accumulated, Dorje had planned to return to his hometown, buy some cattle and sheep, and spend his days tending them with his wife. It was his ideal life, he’d said.

Two-way street

Ma Baoxiang, who runs a general store in Gyirong, would often drive the 20 kilometers to the port to shoot videos for his social media channel.

Having made countless trips, he had become familiar with its rhythms: mornings were busiest, as tourists and truck drivers rushed to cross the border before lunch, although crowds could also swell in the afternoon, with vehicles sometimes lining the road. Most were trucks bearing Nepalese license plates, but Ma says that in recent years he has noticed an increase in travelers crossing the border in private cars.

The Bangxing Logistics Park, a 40-minute drive from the port, is the initial destination for most goods arriving from across the border. The facility gets so busy that drivers can be stuck waiting for up to two days to load or unload their cargo.

Nepalese residents near the border with exit-entry permits would also regularly pass through the port to stock up on clothes, daily necessities, and food from the stores in Gyirong.

“You often see Nepalese merchants buying wholesale goods in town,” says Ma, who every few months goes the other way to buy copperware, handicrafts, tea, and other specialty products, which he ships home to sell to tourists.

Trade at Gyirong Port once largely consisted of small businesses run by local residents. In April 2015, when an earthquake in Nepal damaged facilities at the larger Zhangmu Port, Gyirong became the primary China-Nepal border crossing. It was expanded into an international port in 2017.

By 2024, the value of imports and exports passing through Gyirong reached 4.24 billion yuan ($632 million), the highest among all the ports in Xizang.

Ma Qi, the local branch manager of Musa International Logistics, says his company had at least a dozen trucks en route to the port when the disaster struck on Aug. 26. He immediately told the drivers to pull over and wait, and then contacted nearby warehouses to arrange 6,000 square meters of emergency storage for their cargo.

“Gyirong is the best port,” says Ma Qi, who has worked in cross-border export logistics for 13 years. His company exports 400 to 500 cubic meters of goods a day, including clothing, hardware, small household appliances, construction machinery for bridge and tunnel projects, and electric vehicles. He describes the port as a “lifeline.”

The growth in tourists has also helped turn Gyirong into an economic hub, bringing many restaurants and hotels.

“After the mudslide, Gyirong suddenly emptied out,” says Lin Tian, who has owned a store in the county seat selling Nepalese specialty goods for the past five years. “The only people here are residents and the people working or running shops.”

Locals are no strangers to floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. It has become an inevitable part of life.

When a mudslide triggered flooding on both sides of the border in July last year, Gyirong Port was closed for nearly six months, forcing logistics companies to shift operations to smaller ports.

“These past few days, the government has been coordinating with us to register and report the cargo stranded at the port. They will arrange for it to be shipped out through the Zhangmu and Lizi ports instead,” says Ma Qi. In the meantime, he is mobilizing resources and coordinating with relief organizations in Lhasa and Shigatse to help transport emergency supplies to the disaster zone.

In late 2024, Gyirong was hit by landslides, leaving many port workers stranded in town with no power for more than a week. The mud in some places was shin-deep.

He Xu recalls asking several port staff whether they feared natural disasters. One simply smiled and replied, “I’m not worried. We’ve always made it through before.”

This time, He wasn’t so sure. In the early hours of Aug. 28, he finally received another message from a contact at the port, this time from a police officer. “I’m in downtown Shigatse. I’m fine,” it said.

Reading it, he felt his anxiety ease a little. Yet many others have remained silent.

(Due to privacy concerns, Wen Lili, Dorje, and Lin Tian are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan, Zhang Lingyun, and Wang Qian.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Search and rescue personnel look for survivors in Gyirong Port, Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.content:
Content creators are falling victim to scammers lodging mass fabricated reports of platform violations in China, some of whom boast making over 50,000 yuan ($7,400) per month from their services.

Sellers are offering “account-striking,” including “software-based mass reporting” and “precision strikes,” on domestic secondhand trading platforms, according to an investigation published Tuesday by domestic media outlet The Beijing News. One such service was priced at 25 yuan for 500 platform complaints or 60 yuan for 5,000 complaints.

Account striking, or dahao, became widespread this summer, according to the investigation. This may in part be because it can take advantage of social media platforms’ increasing use of AI to review account-violation complaints.

One 19-year-old creator who posts short videos of herself painting told The Beijing News that one of her accounts, boasting nearly 60,000 followers, had been banned, while a second featuring 260,000 followers saw numerous videos taken down. Both incidents occurred after the same striker reported the accounts to their respective platforms.

The striker then privately messaged her, demanding a ransom of 1,000 yuan to withdraw the complaints. After she transferred the money, the complaints were withdrawn, and her videos were restored.

Jia Bojun, a vlogger who posts videos debunking claims about sports supplements and diets, was also targeted. On Aug. 14, eight of his videos were taken down in under an hour for “portrait rights infringement,” despite the videos featuring no other people.

According to interviews with content creators affected by account strikes, The Beijing News found that teams of strikers often submit complaints simultaneously through a platform’s official reporting channel and by email, doubling success rates.

“To avoid liability, the platform will take down the video as long as there is even a slight possibility (of a violation), regardless of whether the complaint is real or not,” an anonymous account striker told The Beijing News.

Another long-time operator said that many of the attacks stem from brand-to-brand mutual reporting, a commonplace tactic in today’s e-commerce-driven marketplace.

Some strikers go on to recruit apprentices, teaching them step-by-step takedown tactics and providing complaint scripts tailored to each platform, all for an additional fee. The most enterprising even establish their own online account-striking “schools.”

Multiple short-video vloggers were quoted saying that appealing complaints requires significant time and effort, as well as submitting extensive personal information and evidence that they have not violated platform rules — and even then, a successful appeal is not guaranteed.

A cybersecurity expert who works with multiple short-video platforms said that although AI moderation offers platforms a “low-cost, high-efficiency solution” to complaints, it tends to take accounts and videos down first and review later. The cost then falls entirely on creators. “The right to report is a public governance tool provided to users by platforms,” the expert said. “It should not be turned into a priced commodity.”

The expert urged platforms to employ real people to review high-risk reports and flag suspicious accounts, as well as to protect creators’ rights. Platforms should also be required to share malicious-reporting data with police, they said.

Wang Hongmei, a lawyer at Hebei Sanhe Shidai Law Firm, called fabricating complaints and exploiting platform loopholes to maliciously take down videos or ban accounts for illicit gain a form of online “soft violence.” According to Wang, such behavior potentially violates China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law and is therefore punishable by fines or detention.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iStock Vectors/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.title: China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.content:
China is transitioning away from its presale housing system and encouraging the sale of completed properties.

On Friday, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the Ministry of Natural Resources jointly unveiled new guidelines promoting the sale of completed homes.

China introduced its presale system in the 1990s, allowing developers to fund rapid expansion by selling unfinished homes. The model remains a major source of funding for the sector today, with roughly two-thirds of new homes in 2025 sold while still under construction.

The model fueled both the housing market and the country’s urbanization, but came under scrutiny in 2021 as a downturn in the property market exposed stalled projects, quality disputes, and fund-management risks.

The new guidelines encourage the sale of completed new housing projects. The presale model will remain in place for existing projects; however, a building’s main structural framework — including the foundation, concrete flooring, and roof — must be completed before sales begin.

Domestic real estate consulting firm CRIC estimates that the new policy could delay presales of existing projects by about a year, in part because most cities previously allowed presales as soon as a project’s foundation was completed.

Under the new policy, housing authorities are encouraged to strengthen sales oversight by requiring all homebuyer payments, including down payments and mortgages, to be deposited into supervised project accounts. Payments may be transferred to developers only after homes pass final inspections, conducted by the developer under the supervision of local housing authorities.

The same day the new policy was announced, China also introduced accompanying credit and market measures to cushion the financial impact of the transition.

China’s central bank, for example, issued a regulation requiring housing project financing to be tied to a lead bank and extended the maximum term for personal mortgage loans from 30 to 40 years.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission also published a guideline calling for reform of developer financing, shifting from a funding model that relies on a developer’s credit toward an overall evaluation of a project’s conditions.

Over the past five years, China has rolled out a batch of policies that largely focused on stimulating real estate demand through lower mortgage rates, relaxed purchase restrictions, and other buyer incentives.

The latest measures, in cooperation with a series of top regulators, go deeper in shaping a new development model for the sector, Yan Yuejin, deputy head of the Shanghai-based E-House China R&D Institute, told Sixth Tone.

“The policy comes amid a key background in the industry, where we see it moving from an attitude of ‘having versus lacking’ to ‘is the quality good or bad?’” he said. “Every housing reform is closely linked to real market needs.”

Rather than simply boosting transactions, the reforms seek to reshape the sector’s underlying model — from how developers raise and manage funds to how buyers finance purchases, he added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A residential development under construction in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, April 25, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Medicine shortages, missed targets delay tuberculosis healthcare delivery
World.content:
Bid notices for TB medicine show two failed and four canceled biddings from 2023 to 2025, resulting in shortages

Second of two parts

Part 1 | IN NUMBERS: Decades of tuberculosis in the Philippines

Despite being highly curable, tuberculosis (TB) has persisted in the Philippines for over two decades, with the country ranking third globally in terms of TB burden in 2024.

As case counts continue to climb, experts point to medicine procurement failures in 2023-2024 that caused supply shortages and disrupted treatment for about 700,000 people with TB.

Bid notices for TB medicine under the main office of the Department of Health (DOH) showed two failed and four canceled biddings from 2023 to 2025.

The first failed bid, in October 2023, targeted medicine worth P966 million. It was rescheduled to January 2024, but was canceled. The office issued another P966-million bid in August 2024, which also failed.

The order for pediatrics medicine for TB and bedaquiline, a medicine for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) patients — with approved budgets of P117 million and P112 million, respectively — did not push through at all, according to the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS).

PhilGEPS is a centralized platform for government agencies to post public bidding opportunities, award notices, and procurement activities for registered suppliers.

No bidding happened because of either a failure of bids or a cancellation altogether. According to documents cited by PhilGEPS, a failure of bids is declared when there are no bid submissions, the prospective bidders are ineligible, they did not comply with the bid requirements, or there was no award of contract.

Meanwhile, an agency’s Bids and Awards Committee can cancel a bid if the project becomes unfeasible or unnecessary, if funding is cut or withheld, or if a calamity or quarantine is declared.

In the case of the TB medicines, no specific reasons were cited for the bid failures or the cancellations.

All failed and canceled procurements, despite rebiddings, cost over P2 billion.

Dr. Jan Llevado, DOH Disease Control and Prevention Bureau director, pointed out that suppliers find it challenging to procure the DOH’s bulk orders as they mostly rely on manufacturers’ supplies.

“So the question is how the DOH can do a more reliable [multi-year] forecast so that the industry is also informed,” Llevado said in a mix of English and Filipino.

She also confirmed that there are drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB) medicine shortages across multiple regions, raising the risk factor for increasing drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) cases.

Drug-susceptible TB treatment requires consistent, six-month medication regimens of two to four drugs. Those with drug resistance may require up to 18 months, depending on their condition, with more medicines to take.

Straying from the regimen for just a few days could complicate the disease. Those with drug-susceptible TB could potentially develop drug resistance, too.

While the treatment is free in government-run health facilities, patients facing low supply may resort to buying their own. A six-month regimen for a DS-TB patient could cost more than P2,000, while a DR-TB patient may spend up to P400,000.

Reported shortages in 2026

The TB Health Education and Livelihood Support Community, Inc. (TB HEALS), a non-profit organization, said that they received 30 reports of medicine shortages or stockouts in various regions from 2025 to August 2026.

Their data comes from TB HEALS’ KomuKonek, a community feedback platform for reporting local health center TB service concerns.

Their data currently show 20 DS-TB medicine stockout cases for the four-drug fixed-dose combinations (FDC), followed by the two-drug regimen.

Four in total complained of DR-TB drug stockouts, while one said they’re short on TB preventive treatment (TPT).

Eight complaints came from Western Visayas, then seven from Calabarzon.

Florita Dalida, TB HEALS president, stressed that shortages threaten not just the patient, but also the people around them.

“For a disease like TB, shouldn’t it be treated as an emergency? Because if you don’t get treated, you can infect up to 15 people within a year,” Dalida said.

PH’s status of TB service delivery

Besides shortages, experts also monitor how the Philippines, through its national TB control program, accomplishes yearly targets.

Following the first phase’s unmet goals during the pandemic, the DOH is implementing its Philippine Strategic TB Elimination Plan Phase 2, or PhilSTEP 2 (2025–2030), to address the nation’s enduring TB crisis.

PhilSTEP 2 is a roadmap that envisions reducing the country’s TB mortality rate, incidence rate, and catastrophic costs by 2030, by following set objectives.

The four objectives follow the cascade of care framework for TB — screening, testing, treatment, and prevention.

A presumptive patient is screened via chest X-ray (CXR) or artificial intelligence computer-aided detection (CAD) software for signs of TB.

If positive, they will be tested further and diagnosed. This process determines whether the patient has DS-TB, which responds to first-line medication, or DR-TB.

The confirmed TB patient is registered in the system and placed under Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course, or DOTS. Healthcare providers will determine which drugs to take and how much.

To prevent transmission, contact tracing is conducted. Those with higher risk, asymptomatic patients, or people exposed to active cases are given preventive treatment.

How is the Philippines faring in achieving these goals?

1 of 2 Turn to the next page to view tuberculosis screening status per region. Presumptive tuberculosis testing accomplishment in the Philippines (2025 – Q1/Q2 2026) This graph shows a comparison of regional performance on presumptive tuberculosis testing targets for 2025 and the first and second quarters of 2026. Hover over each region for more details. Select Year Jump to Region — All Regions — National Population — National Target — National Accomplished — National Avg Accomplishment — Highest Region — Lowest Region — Lower Higher

Although the country reached a national screening rate of 98% in 2025, regional progress remains uneven.

BARMM has the lowest rate at 8%, with Bicol coming up next at 15%. Six regions have not reached the 50-percent mark. Another six regions have reached more than a 100% screening rate, pulling up the national average.

The DOH, along with the World Health Organization (WHO), has set a target of 12 million Filipinos screened for TB by 2026, as part of the commitment to prevent the disease.

As of August 2026, the screening rate has reached only a quarter of the annual target, with the same regions lagging as last year.

Even then, not everyone screened for TB underwent testing. The annual presumptive testing target for 2025 of 1.8 million people was 75% accomplished. Testing for 2026 is at 26% as of August.

Llevado noted that cartridge procurement issues for GenExpert machines — used to diagnose TB and detect drug resistance — drove down 2026 testing rates compared to the same period in 2025.

Based on notification rates, the DOH recorded the following treatment success rates for new and relapse DS-TB and DR-TB cases.

Drug-susceptible TB treatment had an average success rate of 91.3% from 2018 to 2025, while drug-resistant TB stood at 70.8%.

The success rate for the latter dropped by 10% from 2024 to 2025, which mirrors the gaps the WHO mentioned in treating drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant cases.

The Philippines also has gaps in preventive treatment, which Llevado considers a low-hanging fruit. As an airborne disease, it is important to treat TB before it even becomes an active case to prevent transmission, she stressed.

She added that for the DOH, strengthening programs is crucial. “We should find TB earlier, we should test accurately, we should initiate treatment immediately,” Llevado said, adding that the DOH should ensure the continuity and completion of treatment.

The health department is currently evaluating bids from September 3 to 10 and promised that TB medicine supplies will be delivered by October or November this year. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte trial: Confi fund admission may violate anti-alias law
World.content:
The anti-alias law as amended states that persons wanting to use an alias must obtain judicial authority, and must still affix their real name in documents

For the first time, the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte made the claim that the recipients of her offices’ confidential funds used aliases.

It’s a plausible explanation that could justify the oddity of the names of the signatories on the acknowledgment receipts — from surnames of senators to a mix of brand names, such as the infamous Mary Grace Piattos.

This, however, raises another question: did Sara Duterte, as head of agency for the Office of the Vice President and previously the Department of Education, violate the anti-alias law?

The prosecution believes so.

“This does not fall under any of the exemptions to the Anti-Alias Law. This could be yet another case or violation against them,” public prosecutor Joel Chua said.

Play Video

What does the law actually say? The original law dates back to 1936, when the National Assembly of the Philippines passed Commonwealth Act No. 142. It was extensively amended by Republic Act 6085 in 1969.

The amended law prohibits a person from using any name other than the one he was registered with at birth, or the one he was baptized with, or the substitute name approved by a competent court.

The only exceptions are pseudonyms “solely for literary, cinema, television, radio or other entertainment purposes and in athletic events.”

If persons wants to use an alias, they need to obtain judicial authority to do so. They also cannot have more than one alias.

“The judicial authority for the use of alias the Christian name and the alien immigrant’s name shall be recorded in the proper local civil registry, and no person shall use any name or names other, than his original or real name unless the same is or are duly recorded in the proper local civil registry,” the law reads.

Play Video

RA 6085 also explicitly states that no person — even those who use a pseudonym or those who obtained judicial authority to use an alias — shall execute any public or private document without affixing his or her actual name.

Violation of the law entails jail time of up to five years and a fine of P5,000 up to P10,000.

“It is clear that the Vice President, when she took her oath of office, swore under the Constitution that she would uphold all of our laws. This is again a culpable violation of the Constitution,” Chua said.

“Regarding its application to the acknowledgment receipts of confidential funds, it’s something that the impeachment court should answer,” prosecutor Lordan Suan also added in a separate interview with Rappler.

Play Video

One Supreme Court ruling in 1996 may be relevant to this issue. Ursua vs Court of Appeals says that the use of a fictitious name in a single instance without indication that the person intends to be known by that name does not fall within the prohibition contained in C.A. No. 142 as amended.

Defense lawyer Justine Gular, who publicly offered this fresh theory of their case for the first time, said they will thresh out their arguments when they present their evidence.

Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia, however, objected to what she called an “eleventh hour” admission of their position, since the angle on aliases was not revealed during the pre-trial. – Rappler.com

World.title: BARMM polls: Over half of Tawi-Tawi bets have ties to political families
World.content:
Members of political clans, former local officials, civil society leaders and professionals are campaigning for seats in the 80-member Bangsamoro parliament. More than half of them have ties to local political families.

CEBU, Philippines – Political dynasties in Tawi-Tawi, an island province in the southwestern Philippines near Sabah, are seeking to extend their influence into the parliamentary government of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), bringing familiar names and political alliances into the first elections for the region’s parliament.

In the province’s four parliamentary districts, members of political clans, former local officials, civil society leaders and professionals are campaigning for seats in the 80-member Bangsamoro parliament. More than half of them have ties to local political families.

In the first district, one of three Que brothers from Bongao is seeking a parliamentary seat. The Matba, Amilbangsa, Matolo, Jamalul and Ahaja clans also have members in the races for the second, third and fourth districts.

Tawi-Tawi Governor Yshmael Sali’s sister-in-law, Rhosatina Sulayman Matolo-De Asis, is among those seeking a seat in the third district.

Commission on Elections (Comelec) data as of May 8 show that Tawi-Tawi’s 11 towns have 264,192 registered voters for the 2026 BARMM elections.

Here are the candidates running in each of Tawi-Tawi’s four parliamentary districts:

1st District: Que clan scion vs educator

TAWI-TAWI 1ST DISTRICT RACE. From left: Julbert Que and Shirmal Hajim Sabal. Photos from their Facebook.

The first parliamentary district covers Bongao, where the Que family has established a political base. Jasper Que is the mayor of Bongao, while his brother Jimuel is the vice mayor.

Their brother Julbert, a former vice mayor of Bongao, is seeking the parliamentary seat in the first district.

Julbert is the candidate of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), founded by BARMM Member of Parliament Tomanda Antok and led by regional interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.

He is running against educator Shirmal Hajim Sabal, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) candidate. The UBJP is the political party of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), led by former BARMM interim chief minister Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim.

Sabal previously served as a provincial director of the BARMM Ministry of Science and Technology.

2nd District: Ex-vice mayors and retired colonel

TAWI-TAWI 2ND DISTRICT RACE. From left: Abdelaziz Halun, Gamal Hayudini, and Hadjimar Matba. Photos from their Facebook.

The second district includes the municipalities of Languyan, South Ubian and Panglima Sugala.

Former South Ubian vice mayor Abdelaziz Halun is in the race under the UBJP. He is up against Gamal Hayudini and Hadjimar Matba.

Hayudini, a retired Philippine Air Force colonel and head of the civil society organization Ako Sama, is the candidate of the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC).

The BGC is an alliance of the Bangsamoro Peoples Party (BPP), Serbisyong Inklusibo-Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP), and Al-Ittihad-Ungaya sa Kawagib Nu Bangsamoro.

Matba, a former vice mayor of Languyan and former provincial administrator of Tawi-Tawi, is the candidate of BARMM Member of Parliament Don Mustapha Loong’s Progresibong Bangsamoro Party (PRO BM).

Matba is a relative of incumbent South Ubian Mayor Hadzri Matba.

3rd District: Governor’s sister-in-law vs 3 bets

TAWI-TAWI 3RD DISTRICT RACE. From left: Mali Albrinji, Dayang Amilbangsa, Alnahada Dalagan, and Rhosatina Sulayman Matolo-De Asis. Photos from their Facebook.

The third district comprises the towns of Tandubas, Sapa-Sapa and Simunul.

Mali Albrinji is campaigning under the BGC. He is a former deputy regional manager of the Bangsamoro Ports Management Authority and former regional director of the Maritime Industry Authority under the now-defunct Department of Transportation and Communications in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

Rajsidana Kimble Amilbangsa, a nurse and member of the Amilbangsa clan, is running under the UBJP.

The BFP has fielded Rhosatina Sulayman Matolo-De Asis, a pharmacist and former municipal administrator of Sapa-Sapa.

She is in a race where her political connections are difficult to separate from the contest itself. She is the daughter of former Sapa-Sapa mayor Putli Aisa Sulayman Matolo and sister of Sapa-Sapa Mayor Rhodesia Matolo, who is married to Tawi-Tawi Governor Yshmael Sali.

Meanwhile, the Bangsamoro Party (BAPA), led by BARMM Minister of Labor and Employment Muslimin Sema, has fielded former Tandubas municipal councilor Alnahada Dalagan.

Dalagan is the daughter of the late Roxas Salih, a former mayor of Tandubas and the first chairman of the Tawi-Tawi State Revolutionary Committee of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF).

4th District: Ahajas, Jamalul scion, and Mapun native

TAWI-TAWI 4TH DISTRICT RACE. From left: Michail Ahaja, Nur-Mahadil Ahaja, Sanya Jamalul, and Hamdan Kasim. Photos from their Facebook.

Tawi-Tawi Provincial Board Member Michail Ahaja is seeking the parliamentary seat in the fourth district, which comprises the towns of Mapun, Sitangkai, Sibutu and Turtle Islands. The former Tawi-Tawi vice governor and vice mayor of Sitangkai is running as an independent candidate.

Also from the Ahaja political clan is BFP candidate Nur-Mahadil Ahaja, who served as a member of the Bangsamoro parliament from 2019 to 2022.

Sanya Jamalul, daughter of Turtle Islands Mayor Jay Sayang Jamalul and Vice Mayor Mohammad Faisal Jamalul, is an independent candidate for the district seat.

Mapun native Hamdan Musa Kasim is also running under the UBJP in the fourth district. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tim Cone unfazed as Gilas Pilipinas heads to Asian Games off blowout losses
World.content:
Tim Cone shoulders the blame as Gilas Pilipinas falls to South Korea by an average of 26.5 points in their two tune-up games ahead of the Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – A pair of blowout losses do not bode well for Gilas Pilipinas’ title defense prospects in the Asian Games, but head coach Tim Cone played down growing fears.

Instead, Cone shouldered the blame after the Philippines fell to South Korea by an average of 26.5 points in their two tune-up games, which formed part of both teams’ preparations for the quadrennial showpiece to be hosted in Nagoya, Japan.

The visiting Filipinos first absorbed an 81-55 defeat to the Koreans on Friday, September 4, then suffered a 69-42 rout on Sunday, September 6.

“We obviously couldn’t approach their level of execution and knowledge of each other,” Cone said of Korea. “These losses weren’t on the players, [they were] on us as a coaching staff.”

Cohesion continues to be a work in progress as almost half of this national team features multiple Gilas Pilipinas first-timers, including Adrian Nocum, Sedrick Barefield, Jerrick Ahanmisi, Zavier Lucero, and Brandon Bates.

The limited preparation time is also a factor, as the Nationals have only been together for around two weeks.

Moreover, the squad remains without Justin Brownlee, the hero of the 2023 championship crew, as the naturalized star has yet to confirm his Asian Games participation owing to injuries that have kept him out of action for over a month.

“We haven’t figured out how to best use the skills of our guys…yet. But me and our staff will be better, and we’ll be better in helping our players prepare for what’s ahead,” said Cone.

For Cone, his wards will have their chance to answer back when it counts.

“No need to panic,” he said.

Bunched in Group C, the Philippines will open its title-retention bid against Bahrain on Friday, September 11, before it tangles with Kazakhstan and China on September 12 and 14, respectively.

The Filipinos need a top-two finish for a sure spot in the quarterfinals. – Rappler.com

World.title: PhilWeb’s multibillion bet on JKS gaming tech triggers PSE suspension
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Fresh off Lance Gokongwei's P2-billion capital injection and appointment as chairman, PhilWeb is betting big on a multibillion-peso gaming tech investment that could define its turnaround

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) will suspend trading in PhilWeb Corporation starting Tuesday, September 8, after the gaming technology firm disclosed a multibillion investment in JKS Tech Solutions Inc.

PhilWeb said on Monday, September 7, that it and wholly owned subsidiary PhilWeb Capital Corporation had signed subscription agreements covering a combined 10.73 million Common B shares of JKS at P394 apiece.

PhilWeb itself will subscribe to 3.41 million JKS shares worth about P1.34 billion, while PhilWeb Capital will take another 7.32 million shares.

The scale is what makes this investment significant. As of June 30, PhilWeb reported just P548.46 million in total assets against P741.95 million in liabilities. This left the company with negative stockholders’ equity of P193.48 million.

Those figures, however, came before the completion of JG Summit tycoon Lance Gokongwei’s P2-billion capital infusion into PhilWeb.

Even before the big boost of capital that Gokongwei provided, PhilWeb had already begun improving operationally, returning to profit in the first half with net income of P60.97 million, compared with a P41.77-million loss a year earlier.

The PSE said the JKS deal falls under its rules covering substantial acquisitions and reverse takeovers and will suspend PhilWeb shares beginning 9 am Tuesday while waiting for the company’s required comprehensive disclosure.

Under PSE rules, the substantial acquisition provision applies when a listed company or its subsidiary acquires a direct or indirect interest in an unlisted company equivalent to at least 10% of the listed firm’s total book value. PhilWeb’s P4.23-billion investment blows past that threshold: it is roughly 7.7 times the company’s entire P548.5-million asset base as of end-June, before the Gokongwei capital infusion was factored in.

PhilWeb told Rappler that it respected the PSE’s disclosure process and had submitted the relevant filing on its investment in JKS Tech Solutions, adding that it would continue to provide the market with information through the proper regulatory channels.

“The transaction is part of PhilWeb’s strategy to strengthen its position as a digital gaming solutions and technology platform provider serving licensed operators,” PhilWeb told Rappler in a statement on Monday evening. “We believe the investment will support the Company’s recurring revenue base, expand its operating footprint, and advance its broader technology and digital infrastructure roadmap.”

Who is JKS?

PhilWeb described JKS as a “Philippine B2B technology, platform and digital infrastructure company serving licensed mid-market operators in the digital entertainment sector.”

Beyond PhilWeb’s relatively dry description of JKS as a technology and digital infrastructure company, Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) records reveal more about what the company actually does.

JKS is the PAGCOR-accredited gaming system administrator behind Epic Game, a regulated online gaming platform. Its approved offerings span traditional and electronic bingo, electronic casino games, sports betting, specialty games, and numeric games.

A two-way investment

Money and shares are moving in both directions. In a separate disclosure on Monday, PhilWeb said JKS agreed to buy 81.38 million PhilWeb treasury shares for P16.50 each, paying a total of about P1.34 billion. The shares to be acquired represent around 4.85% of PhilWeb’s issued and outstanding shares, giving JKS a meaningful stake in the listed company once the transaction is completed.

The P1.34 billion that JKS will pay PhilWeb almost exactly matches PhilWeb’s own P1.34-billion direct subscription to JKS.

PhilWeb Capital Corporation, meanwhile, will subscribe to a much larger P2.88 billion worth of JKS shares. Monday’s disclosures did not specify how the PhilWeb subsidiary would fund that investment.

Nevertheless, PhilWeb has raised significant fresh capital in recent months, which could help fund its latest multibillion deal. In June, Gokongwei agreed to personally invest about P2.03 billion in the company through common and redeemable preferred shares priced at P8 apiece. PhilWeb said at the time that the money would strengthen its capital base and give it greater financial flexibility, including for “expansion opportunities and investments.”

Gokongwei acquired 159.53 million common shares on August 27 and was appointed PhilWeb chairman on the same day, replacing Crisanto Roy Alcid, who remained a director. – Rappler.com

World.title: DepEd seeks more funds as ARAL gets zero in proposed 2027 budget
World.content:
BUDGET BRIEFING. Education Secretary Sonny Angara presents the proposed P976-billion budget of the Department of Education and its attached agencies during a House appropriations committee hearing on September 7, 2026.

The Department of Education is requesting an additional P145 billion in 2027 to fund the ARAL Program, hire new teachers, build classrooms, and improve students' health, among others

MANILA, Philippines – The Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program has no allocation in the proposed 2027 budget, according to Education Secretary Sonny Angara, potentially hurting efforts of the Department of Education (DepEd) to address the learning crisis in the country.

“There’s a zero allotment for this under the 2027 budget,” Angara told the House appropriations committee on Monday, September 7, when asked regarding the proposed allocation for the national learning intervention program next year.

The ARAL Program, institutionalized through Republic Act (RA) No. 12028 in October 2024, seeks to help public school students who struggle in reading, mathematics, and science.

With the program’s funding scrapped in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), the DepEd presented its “wishlist” to lawmakers on Monday. Part of the department’s request is P15.98 billion to carry out the ARAL Program in 2027.

In the 2026 national budget, the program was allocated P8.9 billion.

“The program has good results because out of the 6.67 million students that entered the ARAL Program, we saw at the end of the [previous] school year (2025-2026) that there were 4.5 million fewer struggling readers, with 2.5 million students improving to grade-level reading,” Angara said in a mix of English and Filipino.

So far, the DepEd has only rolled out learning interventions for reading, according to Angara. He hopes they can include sessions for mathematics and science.

Ruby Bernardo, Alliance of Concerned Teachers national chairperson, expressed dismay over the possible zero budget for the ARAL Program. She also stressed that remediation and learning recovery efforts must already be removed from teachers’ load.

“Kung mananatili ‘yan sa teachers natin, malaki ang epekto niya sa learning recovery ng mga bata. Kung walang pondo, wala ring maha-hire na external tutors,” Bernardo said in a chance interview. (If the task would remain with the teachers, it would have a huge effect on the learning recovery of children. If there’s no funding, there would be no hiring of external tutors.)

Angara sought intervention from lawmakers as RA 12028 is specific that teachers are only entitled to overload pay if they exceed six hours of teaching.

This is amid the unresolved issue of whether teachers should be compensated for handling ARAL tutor work regardless of teaching load.

Angara said that for now, the DepEd is studying the possibility of giving food allowance in cash, if allowed by the Commission on Audit. The agency is also eyeing to include in the six-hour teaching load some teacher-related tasks, such as the time spent on peer-mentoring sessions or advising students.

In a message to Rappler, Karol Mark Yee, executive director of the Second Congressional Commission on Education, said he hopes that Congress will fund the ARAL Program as it is an “urgent need,” given that there are millions of struggling readers.

But Yee also noted that there must be a thorough review of the DepEd’s utilization of the nearly P9-billion ARAL Program funding this year.

Other budget requests

In the 2027 NEP, the DepEd, including its attached agencies, may get P976 billion. However, the education department received P1 trillion in the 2026 budget.

In total, the DepEd requested from the House appropriations committee P145.19 billion in additional funds, while its attached agencies are seeking P1.74 billion more.

The additional funds being sought include P33.53 billion for new personnel. According to Angara, the proposed 2027 budget does not have an allocation for the hiring of new teachers.

Angara also lamented the proposed P11-billion budget for the school-based feeding program, a significant decrease from the P25.7 billion in the 2026 budget.

He explained that the feeding cycle might have to be shortened from 180 days to 120 days, and the lower budget would prevent the DepEd from offering universal feeding to all Grade 1 pupils.

Measures to address school violence, such as strengthening school safety and expanding access to mental health services, are also covered by the budget requests.

When asked how the budget cuts could affect the DepEd’s reforms, Angara told reporters after the seven-hour budget hearing, “It would slow it down a little bit, but we are hoping for a restoration of some of the items.”

World.title: Rescued endangered hawk-eagle eaglet turned over to DENR in Zamboanga
World.content:
A ray of hope for an endangered species: A juvenile South Philippine Hawk-Eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri) was safely rescued in Gutalac, Zamboanga del Norte, and turned over to DENR-CENRO Liloy authorities on Sunday, September 6. Photo by CENRO-Liloy

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – A juvenile South Philippine Hawk-Eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri), an endangered raptor endemic to the country, was rescued and turned over to environmental authorities Sunday, September 6, offering a rare sign of hope for the survival of the threatened species.

The young bird was retrieved at Barangay Sas in Gutalac town, Zamboanga del Norte by a team from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) Liloy.

READ: PH eagle Lakpue rescued in Leyte after losing talon in dog encounter

Article continues after this 

Initial physical assessments revealed the eaglet is in good condition despite months away from its natural habitat. The juvenile raptor is currently housed at the CENRO Liloy Wildlife Holding Facility, where wildlife officers are conducting further evaluation and health monitoring to prepare the bird for eventual release back into the wild.

The bird’s journey to safety began three months ago when Justine Jay Sapalleda and his friends heard distress calls coming from a fallen nest in a nearby tree. Finding the crying eaglet vulnerable and abandoned, the children brought it home to protect it.

For three months, the Sapalleda family sheltered and fed the juvenile eagle a diet of fish and chicken meat. Unaware that keeping protected wildlife is illegal under Philippine law, the family raised the bird through its most delicate developmental stage before local resident Jessica Pagente learned of the situation and alerted CENRO Liloy.

“The timely report and the care extended by the Sapalleda family helped ensure the juvenile eagle’s safety and provided it with an opportunity to return to the wild,” CENRO Liloy chief Maribel Acama said, highlighting the vital role local communities play in conservation efforts.

Also known as Pinsker’s hawk-eagle, the species is classified as “endangered” under DENR Administrative Order No. 2019-09 due to severe habitat loss and poaching.

Following the turnover, CENRO Liloy reminded the public that holding or keeping wildlife is prohibited, urging citizens to immediately report displaced, injured, or threatened animals to the nearest DENR office for proper rescue and rehabilitation. INQ

MANILA, Philippines – The 22nd day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial focused on the identities of alleged recipients of confidential funds released by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd).

Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande testified for the prosecution and confirmed that several names listed as confidential fund payees could not be found in the agency’s civil registry records.

Grande’s testimony covered the unusual or unique names of individuals who signed acknowledgment receipts used by the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education to liquidate their P612.5 million in confidential funds.

World.title: Remains of missing man found near river in Benguet town
World.content:
Inquirer files

BAGUIO CITY — Search and rescue teams on Monday (September 7) have recovered the remains of a 29-year-old Kibungan town resident of Barangay Sagubo in Benguet province, who had been missing since September 3.

Raul Aludos Juan was found at around 2 p.m. in the Sagilic area of Kaliwaga, Barangay Gaswiling, along the Manahongkong River, according to the Kapangan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO).

READ: Search continues for missing Benguet resident

Article continues after this 

Juan’s remains were brought to his home in Barangay Sagubo, where his family will make arrangements for his funeral.

Juan was reported missing to the Kapangan MDRRMO on September 5, prompting an initial search by barangay officials and community volunteers. The municipal disaster office later activated its search and rescue team and coordinated with other responding agencies and the La Union towns of Bagulin and Naguilian.

Based on the initial reports, the individual might have been swept away by water current along the river between the boundary of Gaswiling and Sagubo. Authorities believe the individual went to the river to catch fish as fishing equipment were later found in the area. /jpv

World.title: Sara Duterte trial Day 23: Reserved witness to testify on SC receipts
World.content:
The Senate Impeachment Court. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel on Tuesday is set to present its first reserved witness to testify in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay is one of two reserved witnesses expected to testify for Article I, or Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds.

While the prosecution refused to detail what it intended to present through Magay, its lead counsel, Rep. Gerville Luistro, said Magay would testify on the acknowledgment receipts that the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) submitted to the Commission on Audit (COA) as proof of CF disbursement.

Article continues after this 

Previously, defense lead counsel Sheila Sison took issue with the lack of details the prosecution gave about Magay’s possible testimony, saying the defense panel would have no prior preparation without a description of the “surprise witness.”

In response, Luistro assured that the prosecution would present its offer of testimony before it begins examining Magay, clarifying that she is an “additional witness.”

READ: Duterte trial Day 22: PSA official to testify on CF payees’ identities

Though the defense was seemingly unsatisfied with this response, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said the court would give the defense ample time to prepare for its cross-examination of Magay.

After Magay, the prosecution is expected to call to the stand DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Fajarda, wife of former DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda.

Article continues after this 

The Fajarda couple supposedly had a close relationship with Duterte, which began in 2011 when Duterte was mayor of Davao City.

Edward Fajarda turned over DepEd confidential funds to Duterte’s security detail when she was still Education chief. He was supposed to be another witness for the prosecution but was withdrawn after suffering a stroke and requiring a month-long recovery.

The couple are also Duterte’s co-respondents in the Office of the Ombudsman proceedings for plunder, malversation of public funds, and related offenses.

Fajarda’s testimony will be followed by that of the prosecution’s second reserved witness, COA Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office Assistant Commissioner Bresilio Sabaldan.

World.title: NBI probes P1.9B Davao flood control projects given to just 1 contractor
World.content:
NBI Director Melvin Matibag —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has conducted an investigation into the P1.9 billion flood control projects in the district of Davao City Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte, which were found to have been awarded to only one contractor, Director Melvin Matibag said.

According to Matibag, the bureau discovered from the Department of Public Works and Highways’ records that P1.9 billion in projects from Duterte’s district were all awarded to Genesis88 Construction, Inc.

“Di ba, ang pinagsimulan nga diyan [flood control scandal], ’yung mga kontraktor na sila na lang ang nakakuha nang nakakuha ng kontrata sa buong Pilipinas. Pero this is a specific area, specific district, na ang nakakuha lang ng kontrata ay yung Genesis 88. Kaya kailangan nating tingnan,” Matibag said in an interview with reporters on Monday.

Article continues after this 

(What started it [flood control scandal], the contractors were the only ones who got contracts all over the Philippines. But this is a specific area, a specific district, where only Genesis 88 got the contracts. So we have to look at it.)

READ: Rep. Duterte may be probed if linked to illegal activities – Matibag

He mentioned that the NBI’s initial investigation established that the contractor is a “long-time friend” of the Dutertes.

The NBI director also said that records show projects in the district started in 2024 but are still incomplete.

“So, titingnan pa natin. Ebidensya yung tinitingnan natin at hindi ‘marites,’” Matibag said.

Article continues after this 

(So, we will still look at it. What we are looking at is evidence and not speculation.)

Investigation is still underway

Meanwhile, the NBI director clarified that he is not yet implying that the P1.9 billion flood control projects already have irregularities, noting that the investigation is still underway.

Article continues after this 

“Kung wala silang kasalanan, then we’re willing to make a statement na tiningnan namin ’yung mga sinasabi na may issue diyan sa flood control at kahit isa lang yung contractor, tapos maayos ang gawa,” Matibag said.

(If they are not guilty, then we’re willing to make a statement that we have looked into the allegations that there is an issue with flood control and even if it was just one contractor, the work was done properly.)

“’Yung investigation is to clear people and to indict people. Kung merong guilty, may ginawang masama, there is a whiff of corruption na naamoy natin, at meron na talaga nangyayaring corruption, kasuhan natin. Pero kung inaakusahan, binabalita, may minamarites, na meron daw mga corruption, at ’yun pa lang, ginawa at tapos naman pala, sabihin din natin,” he added.

(The investigation is to clear people and to indict people. If there is someone guilty, something bad has been done, there is a whiff of corruption that we smell, and there is really corruption going on, let us indict them. But if it is being accused or reported, and there are speculations of corruption, but it turns out the work was done properly, we will also say that.)

‘NBI subpoena vs Duterte, contractor if needed’

When asked if the NBI would issue subpoenas to Duterte and the contractor as its investigation proceeds, Matibag said, “if needed.”

“Kung saan po tayo dadalhin ng ebidensya,” Matibag emphasized.

(Depending on where the evidence will take us.)

“But in the meantime, we’re having a table analysis of the pieces of evidence, documentary evidence that is presented to us,” he said.

In a Facebook post earlier on Monday, Duterte said the NBI must investigate not those who repeatedly win the contracts, but “if there is overpricing, ghost projects, substandard construction, kickbacks, or any theft from the public treasury.”

READ: Ombudsman to probe into flood control ‘epicenter’ Davao City

“Kung may irregularidad man sa pag-award sa proyekto, dapat lang imbestigahan. Pero kung dumaan sa tamang proseso, legal ang award, natapos nang maayos ang proyekto, at walang nakurakot na pera ng bayan, di naman siguro illegal kung sa iilang tao lang na award,” Duterte said.

(If there are irregularities in the awarding of the project, it should be investigated, but if it went through the proper process, the award was legal, the project was completed properly, and no public money was embezzled, then it is probably not illegal if it was awarded to only a few people.)

“Kung may ebidensiya kayo ng krimen, ilabas ninyo at panagutin ang dapat managot. Pero kung wala, tigilan ang trial by publicity at ang pagpaparinig na parang may hatol na bago pa matapos ang imbestigasyon,” the congressman added.

World.title: ‘Habagat’ to bring rains over parts of Luzon, Visayas on Sept. 8
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or “habagat” will continue to bring rains over parts of Luzon and Visayas on Tuesday, Sept. 8, with more areas being affected by the weather system in the next few days, according to the state weather bureau.

In the 5 a.m. weather forecast of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), weather specialist Veronica Torres said that no tropical cyclone is being monitored inside and near the Philippine area of responsibility. However, she noted that the possibility of a low-pressure area formation is not being ruled out.

READ: WALANG PASOK: Class suspensions on Tuesday, Sept. 8

Article continues after this 

“Asahan natin yung monsoon rains sa Zambales at Bataan. Kapag monsoon rains, ito yung halos tuloy-tuloy na moderate to heavy rains,” Torres said.

(Expect monsoon rains over Zambales and Bataan. Monsoon rains are the continuous moderate to heavy rains.)

Based on the 24-hour rainfall forecast, Zambales and Bataan will experience 100 to 200 millimeters (mm) of rainfall, where numerous flooding events are likely, especially in areas that are urbanized, low-lying, or near rivers. Landslides are also possible in highly susceptible areas.

Occasional rains will prevail over Pampanga, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro. They will experience 50 to 100 mm of rainfall on Tuesday.

READ: Heavy rainfall forecast in parts of Luzon, Visayas until Thursday

Article continues after this 

On the other hand, Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon will see cloudy skies and scattered rain showers and thunderstorms.

“Sa susunod na araw, posibleng makaapekto yung habagat sa malaking bahagi ng Luzon. Malaking area yung uulanin, pero pagdating ng Sabado, posibleng mas kumonti yung areas affected by southwest monsoon na magpapaulan sa mga lugar na iyon,” Torres added.

Article continues after this 

(In the next few days, habagat may possibly affect a huge portion of Luzon. A huge portion will experience rains but less areas may be affected by habagat on Saturday.)

The weather specialist said that rains will continue to persist over Western Visayas while the rest of Visayas and Mindanao will see slightly cloudy to cloudy skies with chances of thunderstorms.

No gale warning is raised in any seaboard of the country.

World.title: S&P Sees Stronger Bank Oversight in Kazakhstan as Credit Growth Slows
World.content:
ASTANA – S&P Global Ratings improved its assessment of Kazakhstan’s banking industry risk and upgraded or raised the outlooks on several financial institutions, citing stronger supervision as credit growth and banking-sector profits slowed in the first seven months of 2026.

In its Sept. 4 release, S&P said stronger supervision, banks’ capital buffers and Kazakhstan’s sovereign strength should help preserve financial stability during economic downturns. The agency raised Bank CenterCredit’s long-term issuer credit rating to BB+ from BB and assigned positive outlooks to Halyk Bank, Nurbank, Freedom Holding Corp. and four of its core subsidiaries. It also raised national-scale ratings on Nurbank, Freedom Finance and Freedom Bank Kazakhstan.

S&P improved its assessment of Kazakhstan’s banking industry risk to 6 from 7 under its Banking Industry Country Risk Assessment, or BICRA, framework. The economic-risk score remained at 7, while the starting point S&P used to rate Kazakh banks remained unchanged at BB. Scores range from one to 10, with one representing the lowest risk.

The revision, according to the agency, reflects the “number of initiatives undertaken by the Kazakh regulator to enhance supervision of the financial institutions in Kazakhstan over recent years.”

Among the highlighted improvements are regular systemwide asset-quality reviews, the adoption of the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process, or SREP, and measures to curb banks’ risk appetite, particularly in the rapidly expanding retail lending segment.

The agency also said stronger oversight should help banks withstand periods of heightened uncertainty stemming from geopolitical risks and their potential effects on commodity prices, supply chains, economic activity and credit conditions.

S&P also revised the trend for Kazakhstan’s economic risk assessment to positive while leaving its score unchanged at 7. The change indicates that the score could improve if inflationary pressures ease and banks’ asset quality strengthens.

“This reflects our expectation of a resilient macroeconomic perspective with solid GDP growth over the next couple of years and reducing risks for the banking system,” S&P said.

The agency said an improvement would require evidence that economic imbalances, particularly elevated inflation, are putting less pressure on banks and nonbank financial institutions. Any improvement would also depend on stronger asset-quality indicators, which it considers a weakness of Kazakhstan’s banking sector, supported by more effective regulatory oversight.

S&P said Kazakhstan’s banks could benefit as inflation slows and the National Bank gradually cuts interest rates. Annual inflation declined from 10.2% in July to 9.8% in August, while the National Bank has lowered its base rate by a total of 1.25 percentage points since the beginning of the year.

The agency expects inflation to ease to 7-9% in 2027 and 2028, and slower price growth could leave households with more disposable income and make it easier for borrowers to repay their loans, reducing risks for banks.

S&P pointed to closer coordination between monetary, fiscal and macroprudential policies. However, it expects the tenge to weaken gradually in the second half of 2026, particularly if the central bank continues cutting rates.

Credit growth slows

The latest sector data present a mixed picture: banks accumulated more assets and deposits, but lending growth slowed. According to the Halyk Finance analytical center, banks’ assets, loan portfolios and deposits increased in July.
