World.title: Under pressure to explain super policy, Joyce says he is 'not Jesus Christ'
World.content:
One Nation Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the impact of the party's proposed early superannuation access scheme, saying he is "not Jesus Christ" while being questioned about the policy's financial and economic consequences.

Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or have a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.

The money would retain the favourable tax concession Australians already receive on super savings under the plan, which One Nation said would provide "breathing room" for people struggling with the cost of living.

There were warnings the proposal would create a sugar hit for Australians while pushing up inflation in the long-term.

Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight.

On Tuesday, Mr Joyce sidestepped questions about modelling of the inflationary impact of the proposal, instead focusing on Australians' right to access their savings.

"When people say you've got to model it, you're saying, so I have to model whether someone gets access to their own money," he said.

"The implications that I have to model you getting your own money, I find a little bit perverse. It is actually your money."

When pushed on the loss of people's retirement savings over time, Mr Joyce insisted he was across the detail of the policy.

"I'm the Treasury spokesman, not Jesus Christ. I mean, you have to actually give me the details of these things, if you got to put them forward to me," he told 7.30 on Monday.

"Well, folks, how on earth? I mean, this is ridiculous. This is like saying, 'Well, look, I'm now going to give you an incredibly complex question.'"

Australians 'not stupid', Joyce says

Mr Joyce argued the money in retirement savings was already circulating in the economy because it was being invested via superannuation companies.

Can you access your super savings before retirement? Should you tap into your super early? There is a trade-off between instant cash and future growth.

"It's actually going to your rent, which was the money you were paying before for it, or your house payment, which is a money you were paying before your house payment," he said.

"If there's extra money in the economy and you put it into your bank account and don't spend it, it has no inflationary aspect."

He said "anyone with a brain" would be able to effectively use the scheme, which would be open to any working Australian who pays rent or a mortgage, and would not include means testing.

"People are not stupid," he said.

"The presumption by the socialists is that everyone's a total moron and is going to take money from a good return and take it to a bad return if they don't need it."

World.title: Alice Springs art exhibition highlights buffel grass devastation
World.content:
For Western Arrernte artist Carita Coultard, painting bush tucker that has been found across the nation's central desert for millennia is a chance to celebrate the region's bounty, but it also comes with an alarming message.

Her watercolour work depicts different foods she remembers collecting as a child in Hermannsburg, about 130 kilometres west of Alice Springs, which she laments "we don't see around anymore".

As the artist describes each plant, offering their names in English and her first language — including "the bush onion (yalka), the bush potato (lutjia) and all these sultanas (kutjirra ntjirrka)" — she points the finger at the invasive weed, buffel grass, for wiping them from the landscape.

Carita Coultard says buffel grass has wiped out many of the plants that feature in her paintings. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"I think about in childhood we used to just go around, walk around and get all these bush foods, but we can't see it now," Coultard said.

"We don't see them anymore around, especially around in the Alice area; like maybe way, way from town area, way up bush you might find some.

"It's so sad we can't even see.

" It's just no good at all — buffel grass is everywhere growing. "

A wet winter in the Alice Springs region has created prime conditions for buffel grass to flourish.

The hardy, drought-resistant grass was declared a weed in the Northern Territory in 2024 and spreads easily, smothering native plants and fuelling fire.

Introduced to control erosion and feed cattle in the 1960s, buffel grass spread from Central Australia and is now found in all states and territories except Tasmania and the ACT.

Carita Coultard's paintings are on display at the Olive Pink Botanic Gardens from today. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

To highlight concern over the invasive weed, Coultard and a group of artists have created an exhibition that opened at the Olive Pink Botanic Gardens in Alice Springs today.

The works have been painted on buffel paper handmade in the Many Hands art centre studio.

"You can just cut it all down in pieces … just boil it all in a pot … we just leave it to soak down, get real fluffy … blend it and then put on the mesh and put it outside to let it dry," Coultard said.

The artworks are painted on material hand made from buffel grass. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"The first lot was so rough. It was testing, trying to bring it smooth.

"We don't have a proper machine. We can just do what we can do here."

Buffel busting ahead of fire season

In another part of Alice Springs, a group of volunteers are battling buffel along the Todd River.

Its rampant run has sparked concerns of a big fire season, where excess fuel loads and predictions of a hot El Nino summer have residents on high alert.

Landcare volunteer Steve Eldgridge says he has seen change over the past 20 years where "buffel grass has really started to take over and what we see now is almost a monoculture".

Ben McIntyre and Steve Eldgridge have joined a weekly "buffel bust" to clear an area of more than 100 square metres near the centre of town. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Our aim is really to protect these huge … lovely big old red gums that grow along the Todd River," he said.

"Obviously with so much grass growth underneath, they're at real risk of fire and we just want to stop that happening.

" I've seen so many of these 300, 400-year-old trees burn down and we're left with very few of them now. "

Since May, a weekly "buffel bust" has seen volunteers clock around 150 hours to clear an area of about 5 hectares near the centre of town.

Charles Darwin University professor Kamaljit Sangha co-authored an economic impact assessment commissioned by the NT government that looked at the cost and benefits of the spread of buffel using a model of the grass established in 1,000 hectares.

"We looked more from societal perspective thinking whole of the society, including the pastoral sector, the conservation, tourism, public and the Indigenous sectors," she said.

Declared a weed in the NT in 2024, the hardy, drought-resistant buffel grass spreads easily, smothers native plants and fuels fire. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"We know that buffel grass has spread into other landscapes where it's not wanted, so the costs are about 60 times higher than the benefits that accrue to the pastoral sector."

She said the results were conservative and a key recommendation included a coordinated approach to managing the weed.

"The costs are going to be huge because there is no natural barrier for buffel not to spread to other places," she said.

"It's not just the cost with the spread of buffel for biodiversity, the most important thing is the public costs for managing fire in the landscape."

Not yet a weed of national significance

In response, NT Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne has written to the federal government seeking funding to support buffel management.

But the federal government is in the final stages of assessing if buffel will be declared a weed of national significance.

In late July, the National Biosecurity Committee found the invasive grass met the criteria but cited "a need to undertake further work".

The federal government is considering declaring buffel a weed of national significance. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

A statement through Weeds Australia said consensus was not reached as: "Buffel grass presents a unique and complex case that requires further consideration. It is a highly valued pasture for the cattle industry. Conversely, buffel grass has significant negative impacts."

A committee working group has been holding stakeholder meetings in every affected state, but a meeting hasn't been scheduled in the NT.

The Department of Agriculture said the committee will refer to the Territory government's buffel grass strategy and plan as it makes a final decision, which is expected by the end of the year.

World.title: Decade-long experiment in outback NSW changing the landscape
World.content:
Bec West has been involved in the Wild Deserts project for a decade. ( )

It has been more than a century since bilbies, bandicoots and burrowing bettongs roamed freely across outback New South Wales.

Their local extinction here and throughout most of Australia's mainland was due to cats, foxes and rabbits.

But now they are back and breeding.

Beginning in 2016, the Wild Deserts project aimed to reintroduce seven locally extinct native species to an area in the north-west corner of NSW.

They included crest-tailed mulgaras, stick-nest rats, western quolls and Shark Bay bandicoots, formerly known as western barred bandicoots.

" The idea is to turn back the tide of extinction," says principal ecologist Bec West, "giving these species a chance to come back and turn our deserts back into a really healthy place. "

The project is based at Fort Grey, a former grazing property in Sturt National Park, nestled in the remote north-west corner of NSW. ( )

But before it could get off the ground, Wild Deserts, based in Sturt National Park, needed the right people running it.

That is where Bec and her husband, Reece Pedler, stepped in.

Bec West and Reece Pedler moved to Fort Grey in 2017. ( )

The couple had been working on threatened species and conservation in South Australia.

"We thought, 'Maybe we'll apply as a double act and see how it goes,'" Reece says.

They were exactly what Wild Deserts team leader Richard Kingsford was looking for.

Both were trained scientists, working in arid areas and had PhDs.

"It was a great opportunity, this young couple with amazing talents … able to love living where they are," he says.

For the species to survive, the team first needed to build two 2,000-hectare fenced-off exclosures to keep predators out.

And then remove any predators from inside the enclosures.

"Before the fence was even finished, we started mapping all the rabbit warrens, about 1,000 … on foot with a little conservation detector dog," Reece says.

With the exclosures declared feral-free in early 2019, the first crest-tailed mulgaras and bilbies were released the following year.

Bec West and Reece Pedler celebrated feral-free status with a cake. ( )

One of more than 400 bilbies living inside Sturt National Park. ( )

The team built about 50 kilometres of fences. ( )

The area is traditionally known for its cattle. ( )

Then came Shark Bay bandicoots, golden bandicoots, bettongs and western quolls.

As the top native predator, the quoll was a significant addition for Richard.

"They keep a cap on the sustainability of the herbivores," he says.

" If you just let these animals go for it within one of these safe havens, there's nothing to stop them building up their numbers and becoming unsustainable. "

They are surrounded by a 100-square-kilometre "wild training zone", which contains a low density of feral cats.

A formidable native-cat-sized carnivore, the western quoll preys on small animals up to the size of a rabbit. ( )

It is where the native animals are eventually released.

Most of the species are "ecosystem engineers". Not only are they repopulating the desert, but they are bringing it back to life.

"[They] are … really good at turning over soil to look for their food and build their burrows," Bec says.

" All that soil turnover helps with plant growth. "

One of Sturt National Park's resident wedge-tailed eagles. ( )

Only one species, the stick-nest rat, couldn't adapt to the environment.

"They just did not do well here," Richard says.

David Damschke and a UNSW student collect a golden bandicoot from a cage trap. ( )

David Damschke is the only other full-time staff member with Bec and Reece.

He spends most of his time tracking, trapping and checking the animals before preparing them for release outside the exclosures.

Six of the seven species, including crest-tailed mulgaras (pictured), have been successfully released. ( )

"We know that animals can live in a fence where there are no predators and nothing to worry them," he says.

"But getting them beyond the fence … where they can continue on their natural function and the ecological role, that would be the key part."

Killer cats

The biggest threat to introduced species is feral cats, which kill more than a billion Australian native animals a year.

"We've got the worst extinction record of any country in the world," Richard says.

"The combination of cats, foxes and too many rabbits basically obliterated many of these species from this landscape."

The 100-square-kilometre wild training zone has a low density of feral cats. ( )

David Damschke looks for a place to release a golden bandicoot inside an exclosure. ( )

This baby bandicoot was too young for the wild training zone. ( )

The team is hopeful the natives will develop better survival instincts to combat the threat of cats.

"They're going to be learning to listen when they're feeding [and] to look around them to make sure they've got really good safety," Bec says.

"All these skills sound like things they should innately know how to do, but they didn't evolve with cats and cats have different hunting strategies."

Each captured animal is equipped with a radio collar to help track them. ( )

" These animals have got to learn what this predator is and what it's capable of … to avoid it. "

It is what sets the project apart from native species sanctuaries.

"There's a whole range of feral-free safe havens across Australia, but there are only a few places where there's this work going on trying to expose native animals to feral predators and to train them," Reece says.

"Wild Deserts and Arid Recovery are the only two I'm aware of."

Bilbies and golden bandicoots (pictured) are in excess numbers behind the fences and need to be released beyond the exclosures. ( )

Professional shooters, camera traps, and Felixer grooming traps (pictured) are used to contain the cat population. ( )

Richard acknowledges they are still trying to find the right balance.

"We're still not sure that we've got the right formula … but we're getting better at it," he says.

The team is seeing positive signs following the release of dozens of bilbies, bettongs, golden bandicoots and quolls in the wild training zone.

"We're seeing survival, we're seeing breeding, we're seeing new individuals joining that population that's living beyond the fence," Bec says.

"All of those are really exciting indicators."

A sign warning motorists to watch out for bilbies, quolls, bettongs and bandicoots on the public road near Cameron Corner. ( )

Community connections

Throughout most of the past decade, Bec and Reece have been determined to engage the community in Wild Deserts.

It is one of the criticisms pastoralists across western New South Wales have levelled at the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service.

"We find it really important to have … all these kids and families in this region involved in this place," Reece says.

"Even though it's a remote place, there's a great little community here."

Local pastoral families were invited to Fort Grey in Sturt National Park to release animals. ( )

The couple see the community involvement as one of their greatest achievements.

"I'm constantly surprised at just how excited some of these people, who I didn't think would be so much into this, are wanting to be involved," Reece says.

"Successful conservation projects need to involve the local community," Bec says.

"[And to] make sure that they have the opportunity to engage with the project and understand why you're doing it but also get something from it."

The couple are raising three children, all born since the pair moved to Fort Grey, a former grazing property in Sturt National Park, in 2017.

"It was just the two of us, and that's nice, but it's a bit lonely," Bec says.

"So over the last few years we have built a workforce who are all mini ecologists … we hope."

Reece Pedler, Isla, 7, Zachary, 5, and Edwin, 3, playing with their horse. ( )

Isla, Reece, Bec and Zachary at nearby Lake Pineroo in 2022. ( )

Isla and Zachary get a picture together. ( )

Future guaranteed

Until recently, the funding for the next 10 years of Wild Deserts was not assured.

But in late June, NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe signed off on a new agreement.

"It's really important for the future that we take responsibility for what we do now, being able to restore these landscapes," Ms Sharpe says.

"Spending time with the people who are doing this work, seeing their dedication and seeing these animals being released and now breeding … [has been] one of the highlights of my time as the minister."

Over the past 10 years, Reece says climatic conditions have been in their favour.

A fence line is cleared for one of the Wild Desert exclosures in 2019 during a drought. ( )

In the project's early years, drought conditions made it easier to find and eliminate feral pests.

Above-average rainfall in recent years has provided food, cover, and protection for native species, helping their numbers grow inside and outside the exclosures.

The same stretch of the exclosure following heavy rainfall this year. ( )

"If we could've ordered the climatic conditions … we would've ordered it just like it's happened," Reece says.

"We're definitely in a boom in the desert at the moment … some of that is due to really good seasonal conditions but some of that is due to our restoration work," Bec says.

"For me, as a conservation biologist, it's incredibly rewarding to be able to watch this restoration process unfold in front of my eyes."

Recent heavy rainfall has highlighted the impact of these reintroduced species, with booming flora.

"Because every tiny digging pit … has collected seeds … has collected water … we're seeing really, really good plant growth," Bec says.

"There's quite a difference between where we have the animals and where we don't."

National Parks area manager Jaymie Norris's staff have noticed a significant difference too.

"Undoubtedly there have been changes in the environment," Jaymie says.

Working on the Wild Deserts project has been one of the highlights of Jaymie Norris's career. ( )

Sturt's desert peas have sprouted up across Sturt National Park. ( )

NSW National Parks and Wildife Service staff have noticed changes in the landscape. ( )

"You find a lot of plant species … that are rarer to come across in other parts of the park."

While the changes can be subtle, Jaymie says there is certainly a shift.

"Literally at a landscape scale you can start to see the difference," he says.

Further expansion

According to Bec, the project has surpassed initial expectations.

"We've got the largest rabbit-free area … 4,000 hectares … we've returned six native species … and we've also put four of those beyond the fence," she says.

Shark Bay bandicoots were released into the exclosures in May 2021. ( )

The next decade's goals are shaping up to be even more ambitious, according to Bec.

"We're going to be in a really fantastic position to provide a giant landscape experiment," she says, "where we can really understand how to do this restoration properly and how to do it at scale.

The team hopes the animals can survive predation and inevitable future droughts. ( )

"Especially beyond the fence and really inform future conservation strategies across Australia."

It could include neighbouring pastoral properties and other national parks.

"I would like to start seeing how we might be able to return bilbies to other places where people are interested in seeing that sort of ecosystem restoration process," Bec says.

The team hopes its work will help inform future conservation strategies. ( )

And while Reece acknowledges Australia will never be rid of feral predators, their goal is a landscape where natives can survive their threat.

"We need to try and breed smarter native species that can tolerate these animals and survive in a modern-day arid Australia," he says.

"How do we get these animals to take back the desert, to reinvade the places they used to be?" Richard says.

" We're still early days here … but it is a really tremendously exciting journey. "

The hope is this precious desert ecosystem will be restored for generations to come.

"I hope that we are leaving something that in future generations they'll be able to look back on and be like, 'Wow, those guys did a really epic job, thank God someone did something about it,'" Bec says.

"So that we're not just reading in history books about all the animals that once went extinct and are no longer here.

"If we can work out some of the recipes for how to do this in different places, we might be able to change the future of conservation for a lot of these species."

A golden bandicoot ready for the wild. ( )

Credits

World.title: Housing high-rise boost alongside $880m Parramatta Metro development
World.content:
Hundreds of new homes have been flagged for Western Sydney as part of the $880 million Parramatta Metro station and precinct development.

The proposal would see the construction of four buildings between 24 storeys and 43 storeys high, introducing 470 residential dwellings and 500 units for student accommodation in the heart of Parramatta.

In March 2025, the NSW government had outlined concept plans for 111 new homes to be built above the metro station, as part of the Sydney Metro West project — a 24-kilometre railway line connecting Sydney CBD to Parramatta CBD.

Now, new plans reveal that number has increased and will include a build-to-rent 43-storey residential tower, a 29-storey commercial tower, a 24-storey building dedicated to student housing and an eight-storey hotel.

The planned precinct includes four buildings. (Supplied: NSW government)

Design details are subject to further planning approvals, with the final proposals to go on public exhibition for community feedback at a later date.

Minister for Planning and Public Spaces Paul Scully told the ABC the state government's focus was building a "good, connected community".

"Sitting alongside the new metro station, surrounded by jobs, services and open space is exactly the sort of site we should be maximising our housing opportunities from," he said.

"It shows what's possible when you take a considered approach to planning around new infrastructure."

Parramatta Metro tunnelling completed

Construction continues for the Parramatta Metro. (Supplied: NSW government)

Mr Scully acknowledged the "big infrastructure investment" associated with the $880 million contract for the design and construction of the Parramatta Metro station, precinct and associated developments.

Parramatta is not the first precinct along the Sydney Metro West route to have housing plans announced.

The new Bays West precinct, which promises to deliver up to 8,500 new homes in Sydney's inner west, will also be served by the Sydney Metro West line via The Bays station.

Sydney Metro West is expected to open in 2032. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Procurement for integrated station developments at Sydney Olympic Park and Pyrmont remained underway, with contracts expected to be awarded by the end of 2026.

"We've got a number of transport oriented accelerated precincts … we'll have a look at opportunities to make sure we are connecting homes to transport, jobs, services and amenities into the future," Mr Scully said.

Minister for Transport John Graham said tunnelling had finished for Parramatta Metro, with construction of the station set to commence in mid-2027.

With Parramatta Metro expected to open in 2032, Mr Scully said the precinct around the metro would take "a number of years" to be completed.

World.title: Erin Phillips and Bruce McAvaney given SANFL's highest honour
World.content:
South Australia's Football Hall of Fame has inducted its first woman, former Port Adelaide and Adelaide Crows player Erin Phillips, at the SANFL's Magarey Medal count on Monday.

Phillips was one of four inductees recognised. Long-serving AFL commentator Bruce McAvaney, former Norwood player Neil Button and former Sturt player Tony Burgan were also granted South Australian Football's highest recognition.

Phillips was raised in Adelaide, where her father Greg was a multiple premiership player for Port Adelaide in the SANFL. She played junior football until her teenage years, but switched to basketball due to limited female football opportunities.

She played for the Adelaide Lightning in the WNBL and later made her mark on the world stage as a double WNBA championship player.

Bruce McAvaney called more than 1,000 AFL games. (Supplied: Channel Seven)

Returning to Australia, she joined the Adelaide Crows as captain for the first AFL Women's season in 2017. She played in three AFLW premierships, twice won the AFLW's best and fairest award and was named best-on-ground in the 2017 and 2019 AFLW Grand Finals.

She later joined Port Adelaide for the 2022 AFLW season as its inaugural captain.

"All I wanted to do was to play footy and be like Dad," Phillips said.

"I could've missed that opportunity, and I get so many women that come up to me that played or just wish they had the opportunity [and] that missed the boat.

" So, every game I felt that I was never going to take it for granted. "

McAvaney began calling SANFL matches in 1978 and went on to call more than 1,000 VFL/AFL games and 20 grand finals during his career.

"I felt like I'd reached Mount Everest by calling a South Australian league grand final in 1983," McAvaney said. "I had no idea what would happen afterwards."

The Norwood Football Club's Nik Rokahr won the Magarey Medal for the SANFL's best and fairest player on Monday night, after recording one of the highest vote tallies in the medal's history.

He was named best afield in 10 of Norwood's 18 games.

Nik Rokahr of Norwood Football Club won the 2026 Magarey Medal. (Supplied: Channel Seven)

His success makes him the first player to have won both a Magarey Medal and a WAFL Sandover Medal.

"[It's] a little bit harder to compare my year in the WAFL, but I feel it was my strongest season," Rokahr said.

Norwood last week won through to the SANFL Grand Final, when it will compete for its 32nd title against the winner of Sunday's preliminary final between Sturt and Woodville-West Torrens.

World.title: The grassroots queer clubs popping up in regional Queensland
World.content:
With no permanent LGBTQIA+ venue on the Sunshine Coast, queer residents are creating their own safe spaces.

For Alison Nolan, the lack of options meant travelling outside the region.

"Every queer person I've spoken to on the Sunshine Coast has the same comment," Ms Nolan said.

"There's nowhere to go, no events, no spaces specific to queer people."

Inspired by a club in Brisbane, Ms Nolan and co-founder Lucy Upston established a social club that runs events including trivia, picnics and games nights for queer women and gender-diverse people.

Attendance is increasing at the Lesbian Social Club. (Supplied: Alison Nolan)

Ms Nolan said the need was clear.

"Having a place where you can show up and be your true authentic self without hesitation and without having to explain is something that is so important," she said.

Grace Manning started an LGBTQIA+ run club after moving to the region about a year ago.

"I was really missing that queer community," Ms Manning said, adding that finding queer belonging locally had been "really special".

The LGBT Run Club engages in a range of active activities and "treats" afterwards. (Supplied: Grace Manning)

"If you don't see a particular box [you fit into] or you don't see yourself in your peers, you just feel lonely and isolated."

Community adapting

Queensland Council for LGBTI Health chief executive Rebecca Reynolds said queer spaces traditionally centred on bars and clubs, but that was changing with the growth of social and wellness-focused groups.

" Maybe what we're seeing isn't the disappearance of queer community spaces so much as a broadening of our imagination about what queer community space can be. "

Rebecca Reynolds says geographic isolation is one of many intersecting barriers that may impact LGBTQIA+ communities in regional towns. (Supplied: Rebecca Reynolds)

She said what was happening on the Sunshine Coast was "unique" and an example of the community "responding to its own needs".

"The more places of safety and belonging we can grow, the better off we will all be," she said.

Maroochydore had a dedicated queer cafe in recent years, but it closed its doors after less than two years due to "mounting financial challenges".

Aqualicious, a Queensland Masters swimming club for LGBTQIA+ people, expanded to the Sunshine Coast two years ago.

Aqualicious has been operating in Brisbane since 2003, but only started on the Sunshine Coast two years ago. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

President Isaac Goessling said the club deliberately avoided being "overly rainbow", catering to people at different stages of their queer journeys as well as allies.

"A lot of our members have perhaps only just come out about their sexuality and who they are," he said.

"Whereas some of our members go to every single Pride event."

Mr Goessling said sporting environments could be "jarring" and "not particularly safe" for queer people.

Homophobia in sports

In 2024, the Free to Exist report found LGBTQIA+ young people were 50 per cent less likely to participate in a sporting club than the broader community.

"For us … it's not even a question; it's just, 'Come and swim,'" Mr Goessling said.

" It doesn't matter who you are, but you're safe here and we value you for who you are. "

Aqualicious welcomes a range of people from 25 to 65, from working professionals to travellers, and LGBTQIA+ members to allies. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

Mr Goessling said the club was about more than swimming.

"It's about engaging in healthy lifestyles, getting coffee together, doing bits and pieces of our life together and just being who we are," he said.

Connection overcomes isolation

James Fowler, an affiliate research fellow at the University of Queensland's Schools of Psychology, said social connection was one of the "biggest predictors of mortality".

James Fowler's work involves research to address the mental health needs of communities, with a specialist focus on LGBTQIA+ issues. (Supplied: James Fowler)

"As you get older, a lack of social connection can have really devastating health impacts," Dr Fowler said, adding that fear could be a powerful driver of isolation, and connection could help to overcome it.

"Opportunities to connect are so important for people to see other people like them, to have role models who have faced similar things to them that maybe they won't get from traditional media outlets or family members."

Dr Fowler said the trend on the Sunshine Coast could point to an unmet need.

" There is queer joy happening in the Sunshine Coast and people are coming together to have that shared joy, potentially coming together because there aren't any other spaces where they feel safe to do so. "

A Sunshine Coast Council representative said it was "committed to fostering a community where everyone feels welcome, respected and connected, regardless of their background, identity or circumstance".

The representative said community facilities were designed to be inclusive for all members of the community, and that it had provided grant funding to LGBTQIA+ events such as the Pride Festival Fair Day and the Rangebow Festival.

Ms Nolan said she hoped to see places of safety for queer people continue to grow on the coast.

"You can't really put into words how important having a space where you can just be your true authentic self is," she said.

World.title: Growers forced to find off-farm incomes after fruit fly financial hit
World.content:
On a building site hundreds of kilometres away from his home, Jody Miltenoff works to make an income to offset the financial losses of Queensland fruit fly.

He has taken on a contract as project manager on a new hotel development in Port Adelaide, leaving his son to run his nursery business in Cambrai and orchards in Sunlands.

Mr Miltenoff said managing his jujube business from afar was challenging.

Jody Miltenoff says while he enjoys project management, he prefers farm life. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

But between extreme heatwaves last summer damaging most of his crop and the ongoing cost of fruit fly management, he was glad to have a safety net.

"I'm lucky that I've got the construction industry to fall back on and supplement our income," Mr Miltenoff said.

" I've heard of some apricot growers that are getting close to retirement and just walking away, just saying that it's too hard. "

Mr Miltenoff said sending some of his dried jujubes to Tokyo had been a boon but the loss of his fresh fruit market access had been tough.

Jujubes are a small, sweet fruit sometimes called a Chinese date or red date. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

Sending fruit to his main market of Adelaide requires costly cold treatment or fumigation, while shipping to the east coast means poor returns.

"Growers in the Riverland that have been affected by fruit fly have been sending to the eastern states, so they flood that market and … the prices dropped quite severely," he said.

Funding unused

The Riverland is one of two internationally recognised Pest Free Areas (PFA) in Australia, which provides growers with a trade advantage when exporting produce.

But since a Queensland fruit fly outbreak was declared in Renmark West in late December 2020, the region has been subject to rules which restrict produce movement and require approved treatments before it can be sold.

Queensland fruit fly is endemic to Australia. (Supplied: PIRSA)

State department of primary industries (PIRSA) budget data shows of the $43 million allocated for fruit fly management in the last financial year, $10 million was unspent due to fewer detections of the pest.

According to a department spokesperson, in 2024-25 there were 7,794 Queensland fruit fly detections in South Australia, while there were 4,030 detections in 2025-26.

With fruit fly deductions almost halved, Citrus SA chair Mark Doecke said it was a step in the right direction.

"Any money saving is good money saving, that's for sure," he said.

But Mr Miltenoff said it would have been worthwhile to use the funds to adopt new technology to boost eradication efforts.

A PIRSA spokesperson said in a statement that allocation of funds was subject to approval through normal state budget processes.

Pathway to pest-free

Grower industry bodies Citrus SA and Summerfruit SA organised meetings in Renmark and Waikerie last week for growers and packers to hear about a pathway to release towns in Riverland west from the fruit fly exclusion zone.

Some growers want to see more advanced fruit fly traps. (ABC Riverland: Anita Ward)

The area known as Zone Two includes the towns of Waikerie, Cadell, Holder, Sunlands and Taylorville, which have all had consistently low detections of the pest in the past 12 months.

It follows the release of Swan Reach, known as Zone One, which was officially declared fruit fly free by PIRSA last November.

Mr Doecke said PIRSA had "taken too long" to lift restrictions.

"We started talking about getting some of these areas out three years ago," he said.

Mark Doecke says fruit fly restrictions are costing the citrus industry about $20 million a year. (ABC News: Jackson Byrne)

" If we can get some of these areas out that will instil confidence back in the public and we can ask them to get behind us and keep that fight going. "

But the process to reinstate Pest Free Area status is complicated, and dependent on variables, such as the time of year because of the fruit fly life cycle.

A PIRSA spokesperson said it required "no further fruit fly detections for an agreed period of time and all protocol requirements are met".

World.title: Live: Building company collapse exposes private credit issues
World.content:
Rising oil prices, conflict in the Middle East and political uncertainty in Europe kept investors on edge overnight, leaving stocks to drift lower ahead of critical US inflation data later this week.

Tehran said it would announce a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, after US forces hit three Iranian tankers and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.

As a result, Brent crude futures rose 1.3% to $97.5 a barrel, the most in seven weeks. The oil price surged almost 8% last week and is now 35% above where it was in late February, before the war started.

Prices for diesel, which powers transport, shipping, farming and manufacturing, hit record highs last week and are about 90% higher than they were prior to the war.

With food and fuel prices rising everywhere, central banks are more likely than not to raise interest rates, making this week's reading of US consumer prices a key focus for investors.

The European Central Bank is expected to lift rates to 2.5% on Thursday. Futures imply traders also expect another hike to 2.75% by December.

Likewise, markets are pricing in a 75% chance the Bank of Japan will raise rates a quarter point at its meeting on September 18, with a 60% probability of another move by December.

Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan, put it this way:

"Central bank patience through the energy shock has been supportive of asset prices and the credit cycle. However, central banks are now on the move."

Rate hikes? Euro exits?

For the US Federal Reserve, last week's payrolls report, which blew past expectations with a rise of 162,000 in August, has left markets pricing a 58% chance of a hike when it meets on September 16, and 70% for a move in October.

With an ECB hike all but in the bag, the euro rose 0.14% to $1.1629. It has drifted lower since hitting three-month highs in August and, with political friction mounting on multiple fronts, may struggle to get much upward momentum, analysts said.

In Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, putting a far-right party within reach of power at state level for the first time since World War II. While short of a majority and a long way from gaining national power, the AfD has said one of its policies would be to ditch the euro.

"This development is dangerous for the longer-term stability of the single currency," XTB research director Kathleen Brooks said.

In France, recent polls show far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who in the past has favoured abandoning the euro, would likely win the first round of next year's presidential elections.

"The next few years could see waves of political change in Europe and a shift to the right in the two largest economies. This may not be a problem for FX traders today, but it is a problem for tomorrow, and it could explain why the euro is one of the weakest currencies compared to its peers so far in 2026," Brooks said.

The euro has fallen 1.1% this year, making it the weakest-performing major currency against the dollar, compared with a modest 0.7% gain in the Japanese yen, which has been partly boosted by official intervention, and a 0.4% rise in the pound.

The dollar retreated against the yen, falling 1.2% to 154.32, as a burst of buying propelled the Japanese currency to a seven-month high. The Japanese currency posted its strongest weekly performance in a month last week, as mounting expectations for the BOJ to hike rates, along with the ongoing threat of more official buying, triggered a short squeeze.

Meanwhile, European stocks struggled into positive territory, while on Wall Street, a US holiday kept turnover light, with S & P 500 futures down 0.2% and Nasdaq futures up 0.2%.

- With Reuters

World.title: Father and daughter identified as plane crash victims
World.content:
Dairy company founder Ian Campbell and his daughter Hannah have been identified as the victims of a light plane crash south of Brisbane. The bodies of the 56-year-old and 23-year-old, both from Ascot in Brisbane, were found in the burning wreckage on Monday. Ian Campbell and his daughter Hannah, who died in a plane crash south of Brisbane, had recently completed the Kododa Track to raise funds for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Instagram The Beech A36 Bonanza aircraft they were travelling in crashed into a paddock and erupted in flames, after taking off from Archerfield Airport shortly after 11am. It crashed about 10 minutes later along Musch Road in the Logan suburb of Stockleigh, sparking a large grass fire.



Campbell, the founder of Barambah Organics, and his daughter were the only occupants of the plane. The family recently featured in South Burnett media, where they were described as Goondiwindi farmers, pilots and ambassadors for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Campbell, a keen pilot, founded dairy company Barambah Organics. Facebook The Maranoa Today article also said Ian Campbell completed his pilot training in 1999. A resident who reported seeing the crash said it sounded like the plane was struggling before it hit the ground.



“It was flying directly over our house, quite low, and it was spluttering so it was clear that there was some engine issues,” Eldjie Cojocaru told Seven News. Related Article Updated

Aviation Man and woman killed in plane crash as witness reports ‘spluttering’ “I saw it bank and it went down, and then I heard a ... bang.” Firefighters took about an hour to gain control of the fire, but a tree stump continued smouldering for hours. Ian Campbell founded Barambah Organics with his wife Jane, and the family also ran Mañana Pastoral, which produced grassfed lamb and olives.



The Campbells were recently involved in a fundraiser for the Flying Doctors at Archerfield on August 22. They then completed the Kokoda Track to raise money for the service. Hannah Campbell, who died in the plane crash. Instagram Logan district officer Chief Superintendent Mel Adams appealed for anyone who saw the plane in the air or who witnessed the crash to come forward. “It was a very confronting scene, as you can imagine,” she said.



“What I would ask is for anybody who heard the aircraft, saw the aircraft in the air before it crashed in the Stockleigh area ... [or] for anybody that may have witnessed the aircraft hit the ground – it was close to a roadway, perhaps there is vehicle dashcam or something of that nature – please, as a matter of priority, contact police.” Firefighters extinguish the grass fire after the plane went down. Nine News The Australian Transport Safety Bureau deployed three investigators to the scene. It asked anyone with video footage of the plane or the crash to send it to investigators via its website: atsb.gov.au/witness. World.title: ‘We want to find out why’: Parents face men accused of killing Australian brothers as Mexico trial begins
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime ‘We want to find out why’: Parents face men accused of killing Australian brothers as Mexico trial begins Jack Gramenz September 8, 2026 — 9:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of two Australians killed on a surf trip in Mexico says her sons would want their parents to be there, as a replacement judge begins presiding over a trial of three men accused of murdering the brothers and their American friend. Jake, 30, and Callum Robinson, 33, were allegedly murdered, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, while on a surfing trip in the state of Baja California on Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024. Loading The Perth brothers had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found dumped in a clifftop shaft several days after they went missing. They had gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men – Jesus Gerardo, also known as El Kekas, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus – are on trial over their killings.



The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday (Mexico time). Debra Robinson told media outside the court that it was very important for the pair to attend. The parents of Callum and Jake Robinson want to know what happened to their sons and why. AFP “We’re doing this because we believe Callum and Jake would want us to be here,” she said. “We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” Martin Robinson said.



A total of 35 witnesses are expected to be called during the trial, and the Robinsons are expected to address the court. A judge appeared remotely on the first day of the trial, after a previous judge had to withdraw from the four-week trial due to an injury. Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson. Their replacement did not have enough time to travel to the location to attend in person, the ABC reported. Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their ute, which was found burned near their bodies.



The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery to steal the ute’s tyres. Ary Gisell Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had “good phones and good tyres”. The Robinsons head into court. AFP The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanised a major search on social media for their bodies. Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US, while Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.



Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. A burnt-out ute found during the search for the missing Perth brothers, left, and the ute they were travelling in that Callum posted to Instagram. Instagram Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor’s social media changes to go before the Senate; Joyce flounders under pressure to clarify One Nation’s superannuation proposal
World.content:
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie has demanded the government legislate an “opt-in” model for its social media reforms, as she railed against big tech firms and social media’s impact on young people.

“I’m not giving big tech any more control than what they already have. If you want to, you will opt in, but don’t give us the choice to opt out. Okay, make it very clear that we have to opt in, and that way, it is our choice,” Lambie told journalists at Parliament House.

“I want to see very clearly when we go to their platforms, right at the top there. If you want to opt out on the next day or any other day after that, you can opt out. That simple.”

Senator Jacqui Lambie. Alex Ellinghausen

Draft legislation for the government’s digital duty of care reforms will be announced today, with an expectation the government will force tech firms to offer an “opt-out” setting to disable addictive content algorithms. Many have advocated for a stronger “opt-in” model, which would more widely disable the algorithm.

Lambie rebuffed claims from some members of the Coalition and One Nation that the changes would amount to censorship, saying: “I’ve had a gut full of big tech, and it’s about time. I tell you what, it’s about time we put a leash around them. They’ve had way too much freedom up here, way too much, and it’s time to stop”.

The senator called for the government to appoint a minister responsible for AI, arguing that until this was done Labor could not be seen to be taking the new technology seriously.

World.title: Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch
World.content:
TechnologyGadgets Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch Mark Gurman September 8, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apple has spent much of the past 15 years refining existing product lines and launching services to generate more recurring revenue. There have been a few fresh device categories, like the Apple Watch and AirPods, but no steady stream of new concepts. That is all about to change, beginning this week at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday, US time (Thursday AEST). John Ternus recently took the reins as Apple’s chief executive. Getty Images New chief executive John Ternus will take the stage that day to unveil the latest iPhones and Apple Watches, but that will only be the beginning. The company is about to start the biggest run of device releases in its history, delivering a wave of fresh designs and whole new product areas in 2026, 2027 and beyond. Apple has been working on this pipeline for the past half decade, and Ternus has touted plans for a dawning era of innovation. “I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” he wrote to employees last week. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet.”



Though Tim Cook was Apple’s CEO when all these products were conceived and developed, they are largely the work of Ternus’ team within the company. When Cook made the decision to allow Ternus to introduce them, it underscored Apple’s next phase. That’s why the CEO transition was set for September 1, putting Ternus in command just days before the event where he would introduce work he has overseen. Here are the myriad products Apple is developing for the coming years. (Of course, the company’s plans and timelines will remain fluid in many cases, with some devices getting delayed or scrapped altogether.) A spokesperson for Cupertino, California-based Apple declined to comment. What to expect this week, as well as in late 2026 and early 2027: Foldable iPhone: The centrepiece of this year’s product rollout will be a foldable smartphone that many people inside Apple refer to as the iPhone Ultra. It will have a large interior screen with a small external display, and be about the size of a passport when folded. Major features include an A20 Pro chip, in-house C2 modem, dark and light colour options, regular and ultrawide-angle cameras (no telephoto), Touch ID support, split-view multitasking, an advanced hinge, and a crease that is far less apparent than on prior foldable devices. The price, meanwhile, is expected to be over $US2000 ($2770). A render of a folding iPhone based on rumours and speculation. YouTube / AppleTrack



iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: The Pro-level iPhones will look roughly the same as prior models, other than new light-blue and dark-red colour options. The big new features are mostly internal: A20 Pro processors, in-house C2 modems, better battery life and improved vapour chambers to prevent overheating. They’ll also come with camera upgrades, including a mechanical aperture for fine-tuning light adjustments and depth control, at least on the Pro Max. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: This year’s Apple Watch refresh will include new colours and ceramic cases on the Series 12, as well as fresh health and fitness features. Updated internal components will help power the AI version of the Siri assistant. One new offering in testing is a continuous heart-rate sensor that can run the whole day, regardless of whether a person is working out or not. AirPods 5: This model will represent a refresh to the low-end AirPods, complete with versions of the regular and noise-canceling earbuds. These are not the AirPods with built-in cameras for AI, which were delayed and are coming next year. Apple will unveil its latest AirPods this week. Apple TV set-top box: The new Apple TV looks mostly the same as the current model, but it includes a faster chip that smooths operating system navigation and enables Siri AI for the first time. There’s also a tweaked remote control.



HomePod mini: The HomePod mini story is the same as the Apple TV: There won’t be major aesthetic changes to the smart speaker, but a faster processor will help power Siri AI capabilities. The company has been testing a new full-sized HomePod with Siri AI support as well, but that doesn’t appear to be imminent. Related Article Updated

Phones Apple set to unveil foldable iPhone next month iPad mini with OLED screen: The new iPad mini will mark one of the biggest updates in that product’s history, giving it an OLED screen for the first time that should make watching video, playing games and doing various other tasks more enjoyable. OLED, short for organic light-emitting diode, offers more vibrant colours, sharper contrasts and true blacks because it doesn’t need a backlight. M6 iMac refresh: Apple is preparing an upgrade to the iMac with the M6 chip and potentially new case colours. It’ll mark the desktop’s first update in two years. M6 14-inch MacBook Pro refresh: The new MacBook Pro 14-inch will look like the current model but trade in the base-level M5 chip for the entry-level M6 chip.



First MacBooks with touch display and OLED: After finally deciding around 2022 that it would enter the touch-screen laptop space, Apple is preparing the biggest overhaul to the MacBook Pro in half a decade with a redesigned model that sports a multitouch screen, OLED technology and the Dynamic Island element found on the iPhone. It also will have a software interface more amenable to touch. This machine will come in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes and include the M5 Pro and M5 Max processors launched in March. Related Article Wall Street Apple’s value grew by $1b a day for 15 years under Tim Cook. But he had one big flaw First smart home hub with a screen: Apple’s other major new product category due in the next few months is a home hub with a square, roughly seven-inch screen. Siri AI and facial recognition abilities will serve up personalised content to the person looking at the device. It will come in versions that could sit on a bedside table or be affixed to the wall, run widgets, clock faces and apps, and allow for FaceTime and smart home control. The product will represent Apple’s biggest-ever push into the smart home market. Here’s what is in development for 2027: M6 MacBook Air: For the 2027 MacBook Air, don’t expect Apple to reinvent the wheel. Look for a move to the company’s latest chip, similar to the last several refreshes to its most popular computer offering.



A19 Pro MacBook Neo: With the success of the first MacBook Neo, Apple is looking to maintain momentum – even at the now-higher $US699 price. A new version with a faster chip and more memory is in the works, and the company has designs on refreshing the Neo’s colours every so often as well. Entry-level iPad refresh: After a long hiatus and a price bump, the company is readying a new entry-level iPad with a faster chip and support, finally, for the Apple Intelligence platform. iPad Air update: the big change to the iPad Air for 2027 is a move to an OLED screen, matching the underlying technology in the iPad Pros since 2024 and this year’s iPad mini. This week’s launch will include new iPads. iPad Pro refresh: The iPad Pro upgrade won’t be as significant as that of the iPad Air, but – in addition to adopting a new chip – the company has tested the idea of adding a vapour chamber. If included, that would help sustain performance over longer periods and reduce overheating. New Pencils: Apple is working on updates of the Pencil Pro and entry-level USB-C Pencil tied to the 2027 iPad refreshes.



iPhone 18 and 18e: The biggest change here is not the devices themselves, but the timing. In a first, the company is splitting the release of its Pro phones and entry-level phones into different parts of the year. In 2027, the regular iPhone 18 will join the lower-budget “e” models launching in the northern spring. iPhone Air 2: The updated iPhone Air is also set for the northern spring, and its major changes will include the addition of a second rear camera (this one for ultrawide-angle photography), a faster chip and battery life improvements. Editor's pick Analysis

Gadgets AirPods with cameras and smart specs. Big tech is keen, but are we? M7 14-inch MacBook Pro: Apple is preparing a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro with its first base-level M7 chip for next year. It will use some of the same design elements as the upcoming high-end touch-screen MacBooks. AirPods with cameras: The long-in-the-works AirPods update – with built-in camera sensors that work with Apple’s visual intelligence feature – is on the docket for next year. This device will provide reminders triggered by visual cues, allow users to analyse the surrounding environment and offer turn-by-turn directions with context. The cameras, however, won’t be able to record photos or video.



In-home security sensor and system: Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service. First smart glasses: Apple will take on Meta in glasses for the first time, rolling out a model without displays. The device will let users listen to music, handle phone calls, and take pictures and video. The cameras – coming in an oval shape – also will be able to support the same AI tasks as the camera-equipped AirPods. The frames themselves will be available in a few colours and shapes. Apple is taking on Meta in smart glasses. Bloomberg 20th anniversary iPhone overhaul: Other than the foldable iPhone, the most groundbreaking model in years will be a version that celebrates the product’s 20th birthday. Expect curved glass around all corners and edges, with thinner bezels. It will be the biggest overhaul to what is now the iPhone Pro line since the iPhone X. Second-generation foldable iPhone: A second-generation foldable iPhone with a new chip is already well into testing for release a year after the initial model. It shows Apple’s confidence in the category.



Redesigned watches: The company has gone back to the drawing board on its fitness wearables and is exploring several new directions for the Apple Watch. In the meantime, it’s working on a redesigned smartwatch with a plan to release it next year or the year after. M7 Pro and M7 Max high-end touch MacBooks: Apple is already working on second-generation versions of its high-end touch MacBooks with OLED displays. The big change is a shift to the upcoming M7 Pro and M7 Max processors. Here’s what is in development for 2028, 2029 and beyond: A tabletop robot version of the smart home hub: This will build on the smart home device launching this year, offering a roughly nine-inch screen as well as more advanced and communicative AI features. The biggest difference is the presence of a robotic arm that will move the display around, helping the machine interact with people and handle things like FaceTime calls. M7 Max and M7 Ultra Mac Studio: Apple’s M7 processor series will add a more powerful Ultra model. The company aims to release a new Mac Studio in 2028 that takes advantage of the latest high-end chips.



Potential Apple Vision Pro overhaul: The future of the Vision Pro headset is still in flux, especially since Ternus has been sceptical of the design. For now, though, a revamped, lighter version of the headset remains on Apple’s road map for the end of 2028 or early 2029. Related Article Analysis

Phones Like an iPad in your pocket: The best big folding phones of 2026 Potential pendant with camera for artificial intelligence: As part of its push into new AI wearables, Apple has been developing and testing a pendant that can be clipped onto clothes or worn as a necklace. The gadget has a camera and is designed to work with an iPhone and serve as the eyes for AI tasks, similar to what would be handled by glasses or AirPods. If it ultimately launches, the pendant could be an alternative for people who want the capabilities without wearing something on their face or in their ears. Larger foldable iPhone: Apple already has its sights set on a third-generation foldable iPhone for 2028, with the company discussing a version that has a slightly larger display on the front and inside (up from the 5.5-inch panel on the front and the 7.8-inch screen on the inside of the inaugural model). Potential foldable iPad: Even before it went full steam ahead on the foldable iPhone, Apple had been prototyping and testing a foldable iPad that opens up to a roughly 20-inch screen. Internally, the device was imagined as the future of the laptop. It was once destined for 2028 but has run into snags related to pricing, manufacturing and practicality. That led it to be postponed and then shelved. We’ve seen Apple bring products back into development before, so it’s possible this still arrives by the end of the decade.



Related Article Opinion

Privacy My smart glasses were brilliant. Now people think I’m a creep David Swan Technology editor Higher-end MacBook Air with OLED: The current MacBook Air design dates back to 2022, so this update will be a long time coming. Apple is preparing a major upgrade to the product for 2028 or 2029 that includes an OLED screen. Like the high-end OLED MacBooks launching soon, this will be a tier above the current MacBook Air line. By this point, much of Apple’s iPhone, iPad and Mac lines will have made the transition. Higher-end iMac with OLED: OLED displays get pricier as the screen gets larger, making it hard to offer the technology on bigger devices. But by 2028 or 2029, Apple’s supply chain may be ready to handle a long-desired OLED iMac. The last major iMac overhaul arrived in 2021. Augmented reality glasses: Apple’s long-term goal has always been to release true AR glasses — lightweight spectacles that can superimpose data on real-world views — and nothing has changed other than the timing. Look for these to arrive towards the end of this decade at the earliest. Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling as $400m flows to party seats
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGovernment grants Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling as $400m flows to party seats Rob Harris September 8, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than $400 million in taxpayer-funded community grants has flowed into Labor-held electorates under a $560 million Commonwealth infrastructure program, prompting questions over whether public money was allocated on merit or political advantage. A study by the Centre for Public Integrity found 73.2 per cent – $409.1 million – of funding under the “invite-only” grants program went to safe Labor seats and marginal seats. Coalition-held seats received $126.3 million, or 22.6 per cent, while the remainder went to other electorates. A golf course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate was a beneficiary of the grant. AP The centre said the disparity became even more pronounced when the political competitiveness of electorates was considered, in what has been compared to the Morrison government’s controversial $100 million sports grants program, dubbed “sports rorts”. The analysis found Labor-competitive marginal seats received $66.5 million more than a proportional distribution would have suggested, while seats where Labor was not competitive and safe or fairly safe non-Labor seats received $116.6 million less.



The Major and Local Community Infrastructure program was established to allocate grants heading into the 2025 election from Labor’s election campaign, including upgrades to sporting facilities, parks, playgrounds and swimming pools. But the program was invitation-only, meaning community groups first had to be selected by the Commonwealth before they could nominate a project. Professor Gabrielle Appleby, the research strategy director of the Centre for Public Integrity. The Centre for Public Integrity’s research strategy director, Professor Gabrielle Appleby, said the government had not adequately explained how those organisations were chosen, despite repeated questions in parliament. “When questions were raised about who was invited and why, they were never sufficiently answered by the government,” she said. “Now analysis shows us where the money went, and the pattern raises serious questions that need to be answered.”



Infrastructure Minister Catherine King told ABC’s 7.30, which first reported the story, the program was consistent with longstanding government practice and Commonwealth grants rules. She said ministers did not make funding decisions on applications in their own electorates, while successful projects were assessed against criteria including value for money, community amenity and economic benefits. But the closed nature of the program has become a central point of attack with allegations of blatant pork-barelling. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Independent MP Helen Haines, whose electorate of Indi was among 45 divisions not invited to participate, said community organisations had been denied the chance to compete for funding.

She said the issue was highlighted by the contrasting treatment of golf clubs.



Marrickville Golf Club, in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, received $6 million for upgrades, while the Rutherglen Golf Club in Indi was not given an opportunity to apply. Haines questioned why the Marrickville club was selected when sporting organisations across the country were seeking infrastructure funding. “This isn’t about whether these projects are worthwhile, it’s about whether every community gets a fair shot at funding for projects that matter locally,” she said. “Taxpayers shouldn’t have to wonder whether their local sporting club, community organisation or council misses out because their electorate wasn’t politically useful.” In 2020, the Australian National Audit Office found evidence of distribution bias in the scheme and that the then-sports minister, Bridget McKenzie, had departed from Sport Australia’s recommendations in some funding decisions. McKenzie ultimately resigned after failing to declare her honorary membership of a gun club that received a $36,000 grant.



Labor spent years attacking the Coalition over sports rorts and demanding greater transparency in the distribution of taxpayer-funded grants. Senator Bridget McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman. Alex Ellinghausen McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman, turned the comparison back on the Albanese government, arguing the current program was even more opaque because it was not subject to a competitive application process. She has questioned who selected the projects and whether adequate conflict-of-interest safeguards were applied, including in relation to the Marrickville grant. “Delivering on election promises is an important part of trust in a democracy. However, I think it is concerning that this is a closed program where there were no other invitees other than those who were selected by it seems the Labor Party,” she told the ABC.



Related Article Exclusive

World.title: ‘Don’t know why I’m there’: Even Nathan Fielder is baffled by his bizarre Elizabeth Holmes doco
World.content:
Colorado: Thirty-four days before Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of the medical testing company Theranos, reported to prison to begin her 11-year sentence for defrauding investors, she invited a camera crew into her rented home in Southern California in an effort to clear her name. Yet the two people she chose to chronicle her life were Nathan Fielder, the absurdist comedian behind Nathan for You, and documentary director Lance Oppenheim.

That decision turned into a three-year odyssey for the filmmakers and a three-hour documentary called You Can See Everything that may upend the documentary genre itself. The film had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in a secret screening on Sunday night (US time) that was not revealed until audience members took their seats. It will make its theatrical debut, courtesy of American independent production company A24, on October 16.

Elizabeth Holmes talks to Nathan Fielder in the trailer for You Can See Everything. YouTube

The movie features long, intense conversations between Fielder and Holmes with extreme close-ups. It also reveals that while Holmes serves her time at the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas, she and her partner, Billy Evans, are making plans “to launch a new and improved Theranos”, the company that collapsed after its deceptive claims about blood-testing technology were exposed in The Wall Street Journal in 2015.

What can’t be featured in on-camera interviews is depicted in innovative re-creations. Two weeks before she leaves for prison, Fielder moves into the home and is there for moments many would consider off limits. There’s also a surprise plot point that shouldn’t be spoiled.

Dairy company founder Ian Campbell and his daughter Hannah have been identified as the victims of a light plane crash south of Brisbane. The bodies of the 56-year-old and 23-year-old, both from Ascot in Brisbane, were found in the burning wreckage on Monday. Ian Campbell and his daughter Hannah, who died in a plane crash south of Brisbane, had recently completed the Kododa Track to raise funds for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Instagram The Beech A36 Bonanza aircraft they were travelling in crashed into a paddock and erupted in flames, after taking off from Archerfield Airport shortly after 11am. It crashed about 10 minutes later along Musch Road in the Logan suburb of Stockleigh, sparking a large grass fire.



Campbell, the founder of Barambah Organics, and his daughter were the only occupants of the plane. The family recently featured in South Burnett media, where they were described as Goondiwindi farmers, pilots and ambassadors for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Campbell, a keen pilot, founded dairy company Barambah Organics. Facebook The Maranoa Today article also said Ian Campbell completed his pilot training in 1999. A resident who reported seeing the crash said it sounded like the plane was struggling before it hit the ground.



“It was flying directly over our house, quite low, and it was spluttering so it was clear that there was some engine issues,” Eldjie Cojocaru told Seven News. Related Article Updated

Aviation Man and woman killed in plane crash as witness reports ‘spluttering’ “I saw it bank and it went down, and then I heard a ... bang.” Firefighters took about an hour to gain control of the fire, but a tree stump continued smouldering for hours. The Campbells were recently involved in a fundraiser for the Flying Doctors at Archerfield on August 22. They then completed the Kokoda Track to raise money for the service. “What I would ask is for anybody who heard the aircraft, saw the aircraft in the air before it crashed in the Stockleigh area ... [or] for anybody that may have witnessed the aircraft hit the ground – it was close to a roadway, perhaps there is vehicle dashcam or something of that nature – please, as a matter of priority, contact police.” Firefighters extinguish the grass fire after the plane went down. World.title: ‘We want to find out why’: Parents face men accused of killing Australian brothers as Mexico trial begins
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime ‘We want to find out why’: Parents face men accused of killing Australian brothers as Mexico trial begins Jack Gramenz September 8, 2026 — 9:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of two Australians killed on a surf trip in Mexico says her sons would want their parents to be there, as a replacement judge begins presiding over a trial of three men accused of murdering the brothers and their American friend. Jake, 30, and Callum Robinson, 33, were allegedly murdered, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, while on a surfing trip in the state of Baja California on Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024. Loading The Perth brothers had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found dumped in a clifftop shaft several days after they went missing. They had gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men – Jesus Gerardo, also known as El Kekas, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus – are on trial over their killings.



The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday (Mexico time). Debra Robinson told media outside the court that it was very important for the pair to attend. The parents of Callum and Jake Robinson want to know what happened to their sons and why. AFP “We’re doing this because we believe Callum and Jake would want us to be here,” she said. “We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” Martin Robinson said.



A total of 35 witnesses are expected to be called during the trial, and the Robinsons are expected to address the court. A judge appeared remotely on the first day of the trial, after a previous judge had to withdraw from the four-week trial due to an injury. Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson. Their replacement did not have enough time to travel to the location to attend in person, the ABC reported. Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their ute, which was found burned near their bodies.



The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery to steal the ute’s tyres. Ary Gisell Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had “good phones and good tyres”. The Robinsons head into court. AFP The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanised a major search on social media for their bodies. Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US, while Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.



Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. A burnt-out ute found during the search for the missing Perth brothers, left, and the ute they were travelling in that Callum posted to Instagram. Instagram Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.
