World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor’s social media changes to go before the Senate; Joyce flounders under pressure to clarify One Nation’s superannuation proposal
World.content:
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie has demanded the government legislate an “opt-in” model for its social media reforms, as she railed against big tech firms and social media’s impact on young people.

“I’m not giving big tech any more control than what they already have. If you want to, you will opt in, but don’t give us the choice to opt out. Okay, make it very clear that we have to opt in, and that way, it is our choice,” Lambie told journalists at Parliament House.

“I want to see very clearly when we go to their platforms, right at the top there. If you want to opt out on the next day or any other day after that, you can opt out. That simple.”

Senator Jacqui Lambie. Alex Ellinghausen

Draft legislation for the government’s digital duty of care reforms will be announced today, with an expectation the government will force tech firms to offer an “opt-out” setting to disable addictive content algorithms. Many have advocated for a stronger “opt-in” model, which would more widely disable the algorithm.

Lambie rebuffed claims from some members of the Coalition and One Nation that the changes would amount to censorship, saying: “I’ve had a gut full of big tech, and it’s about time. I tell you what, it’s about time we put a leash around them. They’ve had way too much freedom up here, way too much, and it’s time to stop”.

The senator called for the government to appoint a minister responsible for AI, arguing that until this was done Labor could not be seen to be taking the new technology seriously.

World.title: Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch
World.content:
TechnologyGadgets Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch Mark Gurman September 8, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apple has spent much of the past 15 years refining existing product lines and launching services to generate more recurring revenue. There have been a few fresh device categories, like the Apple Watch and AirPods, but no steady stream of new concepts. That is all about to change, beginning this week at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday, US time (Thursday AEST). John Ternus recently took the reins as Apple’s chief executive. Getty Images New chief executive John Ternus will take the stage that day to unveil the latest iPhones and Apple Watches, but that will only be the beginning. The company is about to start the biggest run of device releases in its history, delivering a wave of fresh designs and whole new product areas in 2026, 2027 and beyond. Apple has been working on this pipeline for the past half decade, and Ternus has touted plans for a dawning era of innovation. “I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” he wrote to employees last week. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet.”



Though Tim Cook was Apple’s CEO when all these products were conceived and developed, they are largely the work of Ternus’ team within the company. When Cook made the decision to allow Ternus to introduce them, it underscored Apple’s next phase. That’s why the CEO transition was set for September 1, putting Ternus in command just days before the event where he would introduce work he has overseen. Here are the myriad products Apple is developing for the coming years. (Of course, the company’s plans and timelines will remain fluid in many cases, with some devices getting delayed or scrapped altogether.) A spokesperson for Cupertino, California-based Apple declined to comment. What to expect this week, as well as in late 2026 and early 2027: Foldable iPhone: The centrepiece of this year’s product rollout will be a foldable smartphone that many people inside Apple refer to as the iPhone Ultra. It will have a large interior screen with a small external display, and be about the size of a passport when folded. Major features include an A20 Pro chip, in-house C2 modem, dark and light colour options, regular and ultrawide-angle cameras (no telephoto), Touch ID support, split-view multitasking, an advanced hinge, and a crease that is far less apparent than on prior foldable devices. The price, meanwhile, is expected to be over $US2000 ($2770). A render of a folding iPhone based on rumours and speculation. YouTube / AppleTrack



iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: The Pro-level iPhones will look roughly the same as prior models, other than new light-blue and dark-red colour options. The big new features are mostly internal: A20 Pro processors, in-house C2 modems, better battery life and improved vapour chambers to prevent overheating. They’ll also come with camera upgrades, including a mechanical aperture for fine-tuning light adjustments and depth control, at least on the Pro Max. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: This year’s Apple Watch refresh will include new colours and ceramic cases on the Series 12, as well as fresh health and fitness features. Updated internal components will help power the AI version of the Siri assistant. One new offering in testing is a continuous heart-rate sensor that can run the whole day, regardless of whether a person is working out or not. AirPods 5: This model will represent a refresh to the low-end AirPods, complete with versions of the regular and noise-canceling earbuds. These are not the AirPods with built-in cameras for AI, which were delayed and are coming next year. Apple will unveil its latest AirPods this week. Apple TV set-top box: The new Apple TV looks mostly the same as the current model, but it includes a faster chip that smooths operating system navigation and enables Siri AI for the first time. There’s also a tweaked remote control.



HomePod mini: The HomePod mini story is the same as the Apple TV: There won’t be major aesthetic changes to the smart speaker, but a faster processor will help power Siri AI capabilities. The company has been testing a new full-sized HomePod with Siri AI support as well, but that doesn’t appear to be imminent. Related Article Updated

Phones Apple set to unveil foldable iPhone next month iPad mini with OLED screen: The new iPad mini will mark one of the biggest updates in that product’s history, giving it an OLED screen for the first time that should make watching video, playing games and doing various other tasks more enjoyable. OLED, short for organic light-emitting diode, offers more vibrant colours, sharper contrasts and true blacks because it doesn’t need a backlight. M6 iMac refresh: Apple is preparing an upgrade to the iMac with the M6 chip and potentially new case colours. It’ll mark the desktop’s first update in two years. M6 14-inch MacBook Pro refresh: The new MacBook Pro 14-inch will look like the current model but trade in the base-level M5 chip for the entry-level M6 chip.



First MacBooks with touch display and OLED: After finally deciding around 2022 that it would enter the touch-screen laptop space, Apple is preparing the biggest overhaul to the MacBook Pro in half a decade with a redesigned model that sports a multitouch screen, OLED technology and the Dynamic Island element found on the iPhone. It also will have a software interface more amenable to touch. This machine will come in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes and include the M5 Pro and M5 Max processors launched in March. Related Article Wall Street Apple’s value grew by $1b a day for 15 years under Tim Cook. But he had one big flaw First smart home hub with a screen: Apple’s other major new product category due in the next few months is a home hub with a square, roughly seven-inch screen. Siri AI and facial recognition abilities will serve up personalised content to the person looking at the device. It will come in versions that could sit on a bedside table or be affixed to the wall, run widgets, clock faces and apps, and allow for FaceTime and smart home control. The product will represent Apple’s biggest-ever push into the smart home market. Here’s what is in development for 2027: M6 MacBook Air: For the 2027 MacBook Air, don’t expect Apple to reinvent the wheel. Look for a move to the company’s latest chip, similar to the last several refreshes to its most popular computer offering.



A19 Pro MacBook Neo: With the success of the first MacBook Neo, Apple is looking to maintain momentum – even at the now-higher $US699 price. A new version with a faster chip and more memory is in the works, and the company has designs on refreshing the Neo’s colours every so often as well. Entry-level iPad refresh: After a long hiatus and a price bump, the company is readying a new entry-level iPad with a faster chip and support, finally, for the Apple Intelligence platform. iPad Air update: the big change to the iPad Air for 2027 is a move to an OLED screen, matching the underlying technology in the iPad Pros since 2024 and this year’s iPad mini. This week’s launch will include new iPads. iPad Pro refresh: The iPad Pro upgrade won’t be as significant as that of the iPad Air, but – in addition to adopting a new chip – the company has tested the idea of adding a vapour chamber. If included, that would help sustain performance over longer periods and reduce overheating. New Pencils: Apple is working on updates of the Pencil Pro and entry-level USB-C Pencil tied to the 2027 iPad refreshes.



iPhone 18 and 18e: The biggest change here is not the devices themselves, but the timing. In a first, the company is splitting the release of its Pro phones and entry-level phones into different parts of the year. In 2027, the regular iPhone 18 will join the lower-budget “e” models launching in the northern spring. iPhone Air 2: The updated iPhone Air is also set for the northern spring, and its major changes will include the addition of a second rear camera (this one for ultrawide-angle photography), a faster chip and battery life improvements. Editor's pick Analysis

Gadgets AirPods with cameras and smart specs. Big tech is keen, but are we? M7 14-inch MacBook Pro: Apple is preparing a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro with its first base-level M7 chip for next year. It will use some of the same design elements as the upcoming high-end touch-screen MacBooks. AirPods with cameras: The long-in-the-works AirPods update – with built-in camera sensors that work with Apple’s visual intelligence feature – is on the docket for next year. This device will provide reminders triggered by visual cues, allow users to analyse the surrounding environment and offer turn-by-turn directions with context. The cameras, however, won’t be able to record photos or video.



In-home security sensor and system: Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service. First smart glasses: Apple will take on Meta in glasses for the first time, rolling out a model without displays. The device will let users listen to music, handle phone calls, and take pictures and video. The cameras – coming in an oval shape – also will be able to support the same AI tasks as the camera-equipped AirPods. The frames themselves will be available in a few colours and shapes. Apple is taking on Meta in smart glasses. Bloomberg 20th anniversary iPhone overhaul: Other than the foldable iPhone, the most groundbreaking model in years will be a version that celebrates the product’s 20th birthday. Expect curved glass around all corners and edges, with thinner bezels. It will be the biggest overhaul to what is now the iPhone Pro line since the iPhone X. Second-generation foldable iPhone: A second-generation foldable iPhone with a new chip is already well into testing for release a year after the initial model. It shows Apple’s confidence in the category.



Redesigned watches: The company has gone back to the drawing board on its fitness wearables and is exploring several new directions for the Apple Watch. In the meantime, it’s working on a redesigned smartwatch with a plan to release it next year or the year after. M7 Pro and M7 Max high-end touch MacBooks: Apple is already working on second-generation versions of its high-end touch MacBooks with OLED displays. The big change is a shift to the upcoming M7 Pro and M7 Max processors. Here’s what is in development for 2028, 2029 and beyond: A tabletop robot version of the smart home hub: This will build on the smart home device launching this year, offering a roughly nine-inch screen as well as more advanced and communicative AI features. The biggest difference is the presence of a robotic arm that will move the display around, helping the machine interact with people and handle things like FaceTime calls. M7 Max and M7 Ultra Mac Studio: Apple’s M7 processor series will add a more powerful Ultra model. The company aims to release a new Mac Studio in 2028 that takes advantage of the latest high-end chips.



Potential Apple Vision Pro overhaul: The future of the Vision Pro headset is still in flux, especially since Ternus has been sceptical of the design. For now, though, a revamped, lighter version of the headset remains on Apple’s road map for the end of 2028 or early 2029. Related Article Analysis

Phones Like an iPad in your pocket: The best big folding phones of 2026 Potential pendant with camera for artificial intelligence: As part of its push into new AI wearables, Apple has been developing and testing a pendant that can be clipped onto clothes or worn as a necklace. The gadget has a camera and is designed to work with an iPhone and serve as the eyes for AI tasks, similar to what would be handled by glasses or AirPods. If it ultimately launches, the pendant could be an alternative for people who want the capabilities without wearing something on their face or in their ears. Larger foldable iPhone: Apple already has its sights set on a third-generation foldable iPhone for 2028, with the company discussing a version that has a slightly larger display on the front and inside (up from the 5.5-inch panel on the front and the 7.8-inch screen on the inside of the inaugural model). Potential foldable iPad: Even before it went full steam ahead on the foldable iPhone, Apple had been prototyping and testing a foldable iPad that opens up to a roughly 20-inch screen. Internally, the device was imagined as the future of the laptop. It was once destined for 2028 but has run into snags related to pricing, manufacturing and practicality. That led it to be postponed and then shelved. We’ve seen Apple bring products back into development before, so it’s possible this still arrives by the end of the decade.



Related Article Opinion

Privacy My smart glasses were brilliant. Now people think I’m a creep David Swan Technology editor Higher-end MacBook Air with OLED: The current MacBook Air design dates back to 2022, so this update will be a long time coming. Apple is preparing a major upgrade to the product for 2028 or 2029 that includes an OLED screen. Like the high-end OLED MacBooks launching soon, this will be a tier above the current MacBook Air line. By this point, much of Apple’s iPhone, iPad and Mac lines will have made the transition. Higher-end iMac with OLED: OLED displays get pricier as the screen gets larger, making it hard to offer the technology on bigger devices. But by 2028 or 2029, Apple’s supply chain may be ready to handle a long-desired OLED iMac. The last major iMac overhaul arrived in 2021. Augmented reality glasses: Apple’s long-term goal has always been to release true AR glasses — lightweight spectacles that can superimpose data on real-world views — and nothing has changed other than the timing. Look for these to arrive towards the end of this decade at the earliest. Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling as $400m flows to party seats
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGovernment grants Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling as $400m flows to party seats Rob Harris September 8, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than $400 million in taxpayer-funded community grants has flowed into Labor-held electorates under a $560 million Commonwealth infrastructure program, prompting questions over whether public money was allocated on merit or political advantage. A study by the Centre for Public Integrity found 73.2 per cent – $409.1 million – of funding under the “invite-only” grants program went to safe Labor seats and marginal seats. Coalition-held seats received $126.3 million, or 22.6 per cent, while the remainder went to other electorates. A golf course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate was a beneficiary of the grant. AP The centre said the disparity became even more pronounced when the political competitiveness of electorates was considered, in what has been compared to the Morrison government’s controversial $100 million sports grants program, dubbed “sports rorts”. The analysis found Labor-competitive marginal seats received $66.5 million more than a proportional distribution would have suggested, while seats where Labor was not competitive and safe or fairly safe non-Labor seats received $116.6 million less.



The Major and Local Community Infrastructure program was established to allocate grants heading into the 2025 election from Labor’s election campaign, including upgrades to sporting facilities, parks, playgrounds and swimming pools. But the program was invitation-only, meaning community groups first had to be selected by the Commonwealth before they could nominate a project. Professor Gabrielle Appleby, the research strategy director of the Centre for Public Integrity. The Centre for Public Integrity’s research strategy director, Professor Gabrielle Appleby, said the government had not adequately explained how those organisations were chosen, despite repeated questions in parliament. “When questions were raised about who was invited and why, they were never sufficiently answered by the government,” she said. “Now analysis shows us where the money went, and the pattern raises serious questions that need to be answered.”



Infrastructure Minister Catherine King told ABC’s 7.30, which first reported the story, the program was consistent with longstanding government practice and Commonwealth grants rules. She said ministers did not make funding decisions on applications in their own electorates, while successful projects were assessed against criteria including value for money, community amenity and economic benefits. But the closed nature of the program has become a central point of attack with allegations of blatant pork-barelling. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Independent MP Helen Haines, whose electorate of Indi was among 45 divisions not invited to participate, said community organisations had been denied the chance to compete for funding.

She said the issue was highlighted by the contrasting treatment of golf clubs.



Marrickville Golf Club, in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, received $6 million for upgrades, while the Rutherglen Golf Club in Indi was not given an opportunity to apply. Haines questioned why the Marrickville club was selected when sporting organisations across the country were seeking infrastructure funding. “This isn’t about whether these projects are worthwhile, it’s about whether every community gets a fair shot at funding for projects that matter locally,” she said. “Taxpayers shouldn’t have to wonder whether their local sporting club, community organisation or council misses out because their electorate wasn’t politically useful.” In 2020, the Australian National Audit Office found evidence of distribution bias in the scheme and that the then-sports minister, Bridget McKenzie, had departed from Sport Australia’s recommendations in some funding decisions. McKenzie ultimately resigned after failing to declare her honorary membership of a gun club that received a $36,000 grant.



Labor spent years attacking the Coalition over sports rorts and demanding greater transparency in the distribution of taxpayer-funded grants. Senator Bridget McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman. Alex Ellinghausen McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman, turned the comparison back on the Albanese government, arguing the current program was even more opaque because it was not subject to a competitive application process. She has questioned who selected the projects and whether adequate conflict-of-interest safeguards were applied, including in relation to the Marrickville grant. “Delivering on election promises is an important part of trust in a democracy. However, I think it is concerning that this is a closed program where there were no other invitees other than those who were selected by it seems the Labor Party,” she told the ABC.



Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Last month this masthead reported that the Coalition also accused the government of exploiting a $171 million multicultural fund to bankroll its own seats and entrench “ghettoisation” of migrant communities. The $170 million Supporting Multicultural Communities program flowed at about 85 per cent to Labor seats. Appleby said the flow of grants was “bigger than one program or one government”. “Public money should be allocated through a system Australians can trust – with decisions made transparently, on merit, and subject to meaningful scrutiny,” she said. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino repeatedly insisted on ABC radio on Tuesday morning that the grant allocation was a “longstanding practice” but did not explain why the money was concentrated in Labor electorates.



“It is a specific kind of grants program which is designed to deliver election commitments and that’s something which is specifically set up after an election in order to allow governments to basically follow through on what they’ve promised to do,” he said. World.title: Woman and two children killed in Rotorua home
World.content:
A woman and two children have been killed at a house in Rotorua.

Police said they arrived at the property on High Street in Glenholme shortly before 10.30pm on Monday, where they found two dead children and a woman with life-threatening injuries.

"Despite extensive efforts by police and ambulance crews, the woman died at the scene," Bay of Plenty acting district commander Inspector Logan Marsh said.

A man at the address was assisting police with enquiries, and no-one else was being sought at this time.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"This was an incredibly traumatic incident for all those involved. Our focus now is on supporting the family, our first responders and getting answers to what occurred last night," Marsh said.

"We know this event will be felt widely in the community and people will want answers. We are methodically working through the scene, including a detailed forensic examination."

He said this could take several days and there would be a police presence in the area.

"We know people will be understandably shaken following this incident and police will be carrying out additional reassurance patrols over the coming days and nights in Glenholme and the wider community.

World.title: Chris Hipkins attacks coalition on Paris Agreement
World.content:
Labour's leader Chris Hipkins is lumping National in with ACT and New Zealand First's promises to exit the Paris Agreement, after weeks of National doing the same with Labour and tax.

Hipkins on Tuesday morning announced a new policy alongside his climate spokesperson Deborah Russell: an urgent review to fix the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS).

Hipkins said the carbon price was too low to drive meaningful emissions reductions, and make it cheaper to plant exotic trees than grow food.

He said the review would identify changes, reconsider the role of forestry, and develop rules to prevent whole-farm conversions.

New ETS forestry registrations would be paused while the review was being done.

ACT and NZ First have both promised to exit the Paris agreement, but National's leader Christopher Luxon ruled that out last week.

ACT has also proposed abolishing the Climate Commission.

Hipkins said Labour was fully committed to the Paris agreement and would put New Zealand on course to meet its targets.

"The National Party and their mates want to pull us out of the Paris Agreement. They want to abolish the Climate Commission. They want to wind back all action on climate change," he said.

"There are ministers in this government that don't even believe that climate change is real. We cannot afford three more years of this government."

National and its MPs have been running advertising and social media promos for weeks accusing Labour "and their mates" of wanting to bring in at least nine new taxes - despite Hipkins having ruled out taxes other than the narrow capital gains tax the party is campaigning on.

Hipkins has repeatedly called the adverts lies, but his coalition partners have maintained that Labour cannot simply rule out their ideas ahead of negotiations to form a government.

National's Christopher Luxon has said remaining in the Paris climate agreement would be a bottom line in coalition negotiations. RNZ / Nick Monro

Now, he appears to be turning that same argument on National and Luxon's climate promises.

"The National Party basically works in government with NZ First and ACT, both of whom have been clear they want to pull New Zealand out of the Paris Agreement. That means the National Party can't say that [they won't]," he said.

He could not remember which ministers did not believe in climate change, but said he could find examples.

"You've seen them on the other side, you know, talking about that. I mean, I can find you the various quotes. I haven't got them off the top of my head.

"They want to abandon action on climate change in New Zealand. Winston Peters has been very clear on that. David Seymour has been very clear on that."

Successive governments have ignored Climate Commission recommendations about how to improve the scheme across multiple reviews.

Hipkins said a review was needed because changes to the ETS needed to be worked through carefully, "recognising that there are billions of dollars invested through the ETS at the moment, so the responsible thing to do is to commit to a rapid review".

"The Climate Commission's evidence base that they and the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment's evidence base will certainly inform that review."

The NZ Herald on Sunday reported Hipkins had not committed to agricultural emissions pricing - despite Labour having pledged to do so at every election since 2008 - after National wound down the policy.

Hipkins took that a step further on Tuesday, saying Labour was "not going to be pricing agriculture by default".

"We want to reduce agricultural emissions. We think that we can work with farmers to do that without putting a price on methane emissions."

Major exporters like Fonterra and Silver Fern Farms were driving some change on emissions reductions themselves, he said, and new technology could make the on-farm economics work.

"I've visited farms where they're reducing their irrigation and they're reducing their use of synthetic fertiliser because it's good economics for them. New technology allows them to do that more precisely, and that means that they're reducing their emissions in a way that actually helps them with their farm balance sheet.

"It's going to be a good cost of living policy as well. Renewable energy is cheaper than fossil fuel energy. Good climate policy, good economic policy."

He said farmers knew that if they did not meet climate commitments including under the EU free trade agreement their access to international markets would be compromised.

Asked how Labour would meet the expected cost of falling short on climate targets, he said accelerating emissions reductions by fixing the ETS would help with increasing renewable energy and EV uptake.

Reducing emissions in that way would in turn would bring the cost down.

"There is a lot of work underway that's been sitting dormant for three years that we can get underway again," he said, and would aim to do so by 2030 when the next target is due.

"We'd certainly give it a very good go".

National's Climate spokesperson Simon Watts RNZ/Marika Khabazi

National's Climate spokesperson Simon Watts soon pushed back, saying Labour's policy could end up costing New Zealand households more than $400 extra a year.

"Aiming to drive up the carbon price will add costs to households, through higher electricity bills, more expensive petrol, and higher costs to get food from farms to your home," he said.

He pointed to an official information release from the Ministry for the Environment which indicated an increase of $10 for New Zealand Units under the ETS would add about $87 for the average household.

"Labour is already campaigning on a Capital Gains Tax, a $5 billion tax on businesses and a Bed Tax. Their mates want an Inheritance Tax, a higher top tax rate, a tax on rentals, a Gift Tax, and a tax on land right across the country - and now they want to whack Kiwi households by increasing the price of carbon.

"National has a sensible plan to reduce emissions while still growing the economy, creating jobs and lift incomes - working with businesses and using new technology to reduce carbon without pulling a massive economic handbrake."

Speaking at the 18th Climate Change and Business Conference in Auckland where Hipkins announced Labour's new policy, Watts said ETS units were "private property rights" owned by foresters and farmers and other major sector players.

"So I'm not going to sit up here sort of throwing around ideas which are going to, in effect, devalue that market, or on the flip side, have implications around massive increase in supply of that market," he said.

"We are very clear that we need the ETS to do the heavy lifting in regards to emissions reduction. We need credible policy in regards to that. We have introduced limits on exotic forestry into the ETS. No government before us have done that."

He said he was continuing to speak to the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment about other changes that were needed, but "there's no policy decisions in regards to that at this point".

World.title: One year on, we still don't know how Tom Phillips hid his children in the bush for four years
World.content:
One year on and it's still not known how Tom Phillips hid his children in the bush of Waikato's west coast for four years.

Phillips died following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September, 2025.

He had spent 1358 days in the bush with his children by that point and shot a police officer several times during the confrontation.

Child Matters CEO Megan West said the question on everyone's lips a year ago today was how this could have happened, and people were still waiting for answers.

In November, former attorney-general Judith Collins announced a public inquiry would look at whether all practicable steps were taken by government agencies to ensure the welfare and safety of Phillips' children.

It was received by the government in July, with the expectation it would be released in mid-August. A week later, the deadline was extended by a month "to clarify a matter".

"Without the answers to these questions, we cannot start putting the necessary safeguards in place to prevent a situation from getting to this point in the future," West said on Tuesday.

"While every situation involving children is unique, and this one even more so, many of the risks and warning signs are the same."

Police at the location of one of the campsites near Waitomo where Tom Phillips and his children had been hiding. Dean Purcell/New Zealand Herald via Getty Images

She said it needed to be asked at what points the child protection system, consisting of multiple agencies, failed in this case, and how the system could be improved.

"Those working at the frontline of child protection are constantly balancing risk, unknown factors, parental rights, and children's needs.

"This inquiry shouldn't be an attack on individual workers, rather a robust critique of a wider multi-agency system that isn't providing the right training, funding, or support to enable sound decision-making."

West said the Phillips case reinforced that children could be known to the system, but not safe.

"More needs to be done to enable agencies to work collaboratively and close the gaps that are allowing children to fall through the cracks.

"Despite being known to the system, ultimately the Phillips children's needs became invisible to health, education, justice, and child protection agencies, the error only being realised once it was too late."

She said releasing inquiry findings was the crucial step needed to identify specific failings and start building a safer, more robust network around vulnerable children, including immediate and extended family, community, and government.

"Without this, more children will become invisible to the system that is meant to help them."

West said the Phillips case wasn't alone in highlighting the need for systemic change, referring to a review into the killing of baby Mustafa Ali by his father Mukzameel Ali.

An Oranga Tamariki office, whose handling of the baby's death was the subject of the scathing internal review, also managed the Tom Phillips case.

"The internal baby Mustafa review identified several failings, including minimal analysis of risk, insufficient monitoring, and a lack of basic knowledge of practice and legislation among some workers. Again, multiple agencies were involved and questions remain on how this case unfolded.

"This is undeniable proof that we need an integrated, information-sharing system that goes beyond words on paper and genuinely implements legislative and child-centric frameworks."

World.title: Christopher Luxon announces National's alternative to introducing bed tax
World.content:
Christopher Luxon will be answering questions about the policy shortly. Watch the livestream below.

The National Party has announced its alternative to introducing the bed tax.

It would instead distribute money to all councils by resetting how the International Visitor Levy is allocated.

Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis announced the campaign pledge in Auckland - the country's biggest city where its mayor Wayne Brown has been highly critical of the bed tax backtrack.

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis says from July next year it would put $100 million into the Department of Conservation, $50m into supporting tourism growth and resilience, and the rest would go to councils based on the share of tourists they have.

In the first year it's estimated Auckland would receive $19.1m and Queenstown Lakes would be eligible for $17.1m.

Other councils would receive funding according to their share of international visitor guest nights.

"Under National's policy, every territorial authority that hosts international visitors will receive a share of IVL funding, so they can support responsible growth in tourism in their community.

"Funding would begin flowing to councils from 1 July 2027, around two years earlier than it would with a bed tax," Willis said.

National is also making clear it wouldn't increase the visitor levy for at least the next three years, which it says provides certainty to the tourism industry, she said.

In 2018 when the levy was first proposed under a Labour-led government, National campaigned strongly against it with then-leader Simon Bridges claiming it was "entirely unnecessary" and "just another tax".

After winning power in 2023, the following year the coalition government nearly tripled the $35 fee to $100.

Tourism spokesperson Louise Upston said a bed tax would "disproportionately impact New Zealanders booking a weekend away, whether that's for a sports event, a family funeral or to visit friends."

"This is a clear, practical alternative to that," she said.

World.title: What Methanex's departure will do to gas prices
World.content:
Methanex closure unlocks large gas supply Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

With New Zealand's single biggest gas consumer Methanex announcing a decision to close from next year and sell off its gas contracts, what impact will it have on households and small businesses?

Methanex was at times using close to half of the country's total natural gas supply.

The Canadian multinational's departure releases a huge amount of gas supply into a market that has struggled in recent years.

Electricity generator-retailer Genesis Energy has announced it has picked up major gas contracts that run from March next year through to December 2029.

Ben Gerritsen is general manager of customer and regulation at Clarus - the company that runs the gas transmission network in the North Island. He told Nine to Noon on Tuesday it was a "big shift" and "big deal" for the local Taranaki economy, which Methanex was a part of for more than four decades - but not a surprise.

"Thinking about Methanex's decision in the context of the overall gas market, it's not surprising and it is part of a transition in the New Zealand gas industry that started a few years ago when supply constraints started to emerge and gas has kind of been redirected, if you like, to its highest value use.

"Methanex's business model globally is to operate in countries with plentiful gas and export that in the form of methanol. So with the decline in gas production in New Zealand, it's not surprising."

But will it translate into cheaper prices for other users, be they industrial or household? Gerritsen said he had to be "careful" predicting future prices, but expected an easing in the near-term for both.

And it might even help some companies stay afloat, rather than shut up shop due to high costs.

"Ultimately that is in the hands of the gas retailers in terms of competition between the likes of Genesis Energy, Contact, Nova, others. But certainly having availability of more gas, that's been the key constraint in recent years.

"So when you've heard industrial consumers being concerned that they can't get a contract on terms that they used to, I think this extra supply in the short term will help that challenge. "

But the challenge remained in the long-term, he said, because New Zealand's known gas fields were "in a pattern of decline" with some expected to close soon.

Big energy companies, such as Genesis, had limited capacity to store gas, Gerritsen said - and may use what it has to produce electricity when needed.

"I think what Genesis may well look to do is, the sort of flexibility that Methanex has provided in recent years where it will essentially turn off during winter and redirect the gas to electricity generation - we may see Genesis look to other industrial customers to operate in a similar mode.

"So the industrial consumer will get the gas on relatively favourable price terms. It can use it during summer, it can use it during wet years. But when the electricity generator is needed, the gas can be redirected to generate electricity."

Households should not expect a price drop, particularly in the North Island where there are fixed costs involved in the pipeline supply network.

"The costs of the pipeline network and delivering gas throughout the North Island are essentially fixed. They're the infrastructure costs. of transporting the gas."

Further into the future, Methanex's absence could drive up prices, Gerritsen said, as local sources become scarce.

World.title: How Facebook is shaping public debate on sorcery violence in PNG
World.content:
A new discussion paper examines how Facebook can blur the line between feelings and conversations around sorcery accusation-related violence (SARV), or locally known as sanguma, in communities in Papua New Guinea.

The study, conducted by the Australian think tank Development Policy Centre (Devpolicy), analyses how Facebook influences the debate around SARV in PNG through the people involved, the messages they share, and the broader role the platform plays.

An estimated 200 people are killed due to SARV in PNG every year, with thousands more severely injured, tortured, mutilated and exiled. Sanguma violence in the era of social media has spread the belief and the violence to eyes beyond the communities the violence originates from.

Last month, the Melanesian Institute released the results of the first nationwide survey into the views on SARV, showing nearly three quarters of respondents use social media as their main source of SARV news.

Autralian National University's Professor Miranda Forsyth, the lead researcher of study, told RNZ Pacific why they chose Facebook as the social media platform to conduct their research.

"Facebook is Papua New Guinea's dominant digital public sphere, and so it made sense for me to look into that.

"Also, as a researcher who's been working in this space for a long time, I've constantly been sent Facebook posts about SARV, so I knew that was a place where these narratives were circulating."

The research found that 87 percent of posts opposing SARV came from government, non-governmental organisations (NGO) and advocacy pages, and when using strong human rights language disconnected with the intended audience.

Professor Forsyth said the PNG government adopted a hardline approach communicating distain to SARV for nearly a decade, which is slowly working. However, she added different approaches needed to be used.

"I'm not saying that messaging should be displaced. I'm saying it should be supplemented by conversations at other levels where people are able to talk in vernacular languages about their concerns," she said.

"And really be able to be brought into understanding how to interrogate claims that people are making that misfortune has occurred because of sorcery, [and] encourage to understand that there might be other explanations for what's gone wrong."

She said after analysing over a decade worth of Facebook posts (from 2013-2024), she was hopeful for the future as an anti-SARV ecosystem was starting to advocate for change.

"There are the beginnings of this sort of institutional coordination where survivor services and the criminal justice system are starting to be joined together, as well as a lot of demands for political accountability against leaders.

"And some leaders are really stepping up and calling out against this practice, which is fantastic."

In February, PNG's opposition leader James Nomane attended a SARV workshop and later raised its findings with Prime Minister James Marape and government.

Professor Forsyth said companies that own social media networks, like Meta which owns Facebook, also need to be held into account regarding the spreading of these videos.

"These videos are contagious. They're spreading this violence, and the platforms that are enabling that need to think about how they can stop doing that, 100 percent."

World.title: World Squash Championships to be held in New Zealand ahead of sport's Olympic debut
World.content:
New Zealand will host the World Squash Championships in 2028.

The World Championships will be the biggest squash event ever held in New Zealand, and will take place just four months before the sport makes its Olympic debut at the LA 2028 Games.

The event will be staged at the New Zealand International Convention Centre in central Auckland in February 2028.

The tournament will run concurrently with the inaugural World Club Championships, a new competition which will allow club players from around the world to compete in their own tournament, alongside the World Championships.

Together the two events are expected to be the largest squash event ever held. Nearly 40 courts across Auckland clubs will be in use.

"We are a small country with a deep squash history. To bring the world championships here, in the year squash finally reaches the Olympics, is going to be extremely special," said Martin Dowson, Squash New Zealand chief executive.

Squash makes its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028 with 16 men and 16 women in each singles draw.

Eight of those places will be decided on rankings, so the Auckland tournament will play a significant part in the makeup of the Olympic field.

Having played the majority of his games overseas, New Zealand's world number two Paul Coll is thrilled to have the opportunity to play at home.

World.title: PM Christopher Luxon's targets: Jobseeker numbers climbing, almost 80,000 over target
World.content:
Three of the Government's nine key targets risk not being met, the latest update shows.

The 218,500 people receiving Jobseeker benefits remains significantly higher than the 140,000 target, and education targets remain elusive.

In health, shorter wait times in emergency departments is considered "feasible", but still a way off. Shorter wait times to access elective treatments has improved from "feasible" to "probable".

A target to reduce the number of households in emergency accommodation has been met well ahead of schedule, as has a goal to reduce the number of victims of assault or robbery.

RNZ is tracking progress towards each of the Government's nine targets, which were announced by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon in April 2024. The targets were chosen to focus the public sector on priorities, and progress is updated each quarter.

Each responsible agency assigns a status to progress, ranging from "on track" to "unachievable". Progress toward reaching a target can still be classed as "feasible", even if there are major risks or issues in meeting it, as long as the agency in charge believes these can be resolved.

The nine targets are set to be delivered by 2030, beyond the current political term.

Health

Achieving the goal for 95 percent of patients to be admitted, discharged or transferred from an emergency department within six hours remains far adrift.

The latest update shows 74.4 percent of patients are seen within that timeframe - an increase from 74.2 percent in the last quarter.

When setting this target, officials warned there was a risk it would not be achievable in the short-term.

"Most ED (emergency departments) nationwide are over capacity most of the time," a briefing to ministers read.

This update noted improvements across the whole care system are needed to reduce emergency department wait times.

In March, $25 million was announced to tackle winter demand. This includes up to 378 additional staff across the country and 71 extra winter hospital beds. As of June, 82 percent of the staff had been recruited and 84 beds were made available. Eighty-one patients were discharged from hospital to short stays in aged residential care.

Reaching the 95 percent goal by 2030 is considered feasible, meaning there are major risks to achievement.

The second health target for 95 percent of people to receive elective treatment within four months is now considered probable, a change from the last quarterly update when it was considered feasible.

At the moment, 64.9 percent of people needing elective treatments, such as hip or cataract surgeries, are seen within four months. This is 0.4 percentage points higher than the 64.5 percent reported in the last quarter.

A Health New Zealand spokesperson says the change from "feasible" to "probable" wasn't just related to the latest quarter reported on.

"It refers to the ongoing and sustained improvement in delivery targets across the year, which includes the last quarter, as well as forward planning to maintain delivery against the next annual milestone. While improvements for the last quarter have increased.4 percent, year-on-year there has been an improvement of 7.6 percent, representing a total of 51,089 patients who've been treated."

The private sector is being used to tackle the waitlist, with 21,000 procedures to be funded through an Elective Boost programme to June 2026.

Weekend and twilight surgeries are also occurring in-house in districts under pressure to reduce the number of people who have had lengthy waits for surgeries.

Crime

The number of serious and persistent youth offenders has decreased from 829 in the last update to 814, and has now reached the target of 900 or fewer well ahead of 2030.

For a youth offender to be classed as a serious or persistent offender they must have committed three or more offences in the past 12 months, with at least one of them having a maximum penalty of seven years' imprisonment or more.

Bootcamps, improving response teams and locally-led initiatives, and increased school attendance are listed as areas the Government is focused on to reach the target.

A goal to reduce the number of victims of assault, robbery or sexual assault to 165,000 is classed as on track and has been reached ahead of the 2030 deadline. In this update the total is up by 8782 from the previous quarter's results, but remains below the target of 165,000.

The goal is based on data from the New Zealand Crime and Victims' Survey. Officials warned the survey data had a high margin of error and was more suitable for showing long-term trends, with quarterly data described as volatile and likely to fluctuate.

The survey asks respondents about their experience of reported and unreported crime over the past 12 months.

Initiatives to reach the target include the Three Strikes sentencing reform, gang harm legislation, and security installed at stores where there have been ram raids and/or aggravated robbery.

Employment

The number of people receiving Jobseeker support has risen to 218,500 since the March report, up by 3300.

This target remains classified as "at risk" and is still a considerable way from the goal of 140,000 or fewer people receiving support by 2030.

The Government's update suggested the flow of people receiving the Jobseeker benefit will decrease as economic conditions improve. Measures the update mentioned that will be used to decrease the number include a traffic light system, shifting people into work and increased case management work.

A test for Jobseeker eligibility for 18- and 19-year-olds was announced in October 2025, which will mean applicants whose parents have a combined income above $65,529 will be ineligible for the benefit. It's estimated 4300 young people will be affected by this. It will come into effect in November.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Nick Monro

Education

At 64.3 percent, Term 2's attendance rate is well below the target of 80 percent of students present for more than 90 percent of the term. This means students should take no more than five days off a term.

Absence is classed as either "justified" or "unjustified". Justified absences include illnesses, and other reasons which fall under school policy, such as suspensions. Unjustified absences include truancy, or taking holidays in term time. The Government target of 80 percent makes no distinction between the two.

Attendance management plans have been implemented from 2026, these are now mandatory. They include attendance targets for schools, and a process to identify and manage absences.

Public information campaigns for 2026 aiming to improve attendance include a focus on illness and taking holidays in term time.

Reaching the attendance target is deemed "probable".

Results for reading, writing and mathematics are well below the 80 percent target.

The update says the Government is focusing on a clearer curriculum, a better approach to numeracy and literacy and better reporting.

It says there are "some encouraging signs" for year 6 achievement.

This target is considered to be "at risk" of not being met.

Housing

Driving down the number of households in emergency housing is one target where progress leapt ahead of estimates.

From a baseline of 3141 households, the goal was to reduce the number by 75 percent, to 800 or fewer.

The current number is 459, well below 800, the 2030 goal.

Part of the plan to reach the target includes improving access to other forms of housing for emergency housing residents. As of June 2026, 1128 households (with 2403 children), have been housed in a social housing tenancy.

Climate

Ministry for the Environment / MfE projections corrected in January 2026

There are two targets New Zealand has committed to meeting as part of its net zero climate change goal.

The first target is for total greenhouse gas emissions between 2022 and 2025 to be no more than 290 megatonnes. The second target is for total emissions to be no more than 305 megatonnes between 2026 and 2030.

World.title: Mixed emotions as Andreeva embraces injured idol after US Open win
World.content:
US Open fans have witnessed a display of sportsmanship as Mirra Andreeva tended to and consoled an injured Anastasia Potapova as the fifth seed won their fourth-round match.

Potapova jarred her knee as she lost the first point of what turned out to be their final game on Louis Armstrong Stadium, prompting Andreeva to rush to the other end of the court to check on her.

She helped the 24th seed up and Potapova was able to limp to her bench, where Andreeva asked if someone could bring her ice.

The French Open champion finished off the next three points for a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory that sent her to the quarterfinals in Flushing Meadows for the first time, jogging around the net again for a warm embrace.

"It's not the perfect end to the match," 19-year-old Andreeva said.

Potapova appeared to be tearing up as Andreeva came around the net for a long embrace after the final point.

Potapova represents Austria but was born in Russia and still played under that flag when she won the junior Wimbledon championship in 2016.

"For me, Nastya, she was always like a prodigy," Andreeva said of her 25-year-old opponent.

"She came on tour early. She also had a lot of wins. I also remember we were all watching and cheering for her when she won juniors Wimbledon title. I remember watching that match.

"For me, she was always, like, a little star that I was kind of always looking at."

Potapova (right) appeared to be tearing up as the pair embraced after match point. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

Potapova won their first meeting on tour in 2022 but Andreeva has won the past four, preventing Potapova from reaching her first grand slam quarterfinal.

"First, she just beat me. So after, I just kind of knew that she's a tough player to play, but at the same time, she was so nice," Andreeva said.

"Then since then we would practice together, and just like that, the more you see each other, the more you spend time together, then you just talk about everything, discuss everything. Then, just like that, I feel like we have a good connection off the court."

Elsewhere, Qinwen Zheng mounted another extraordinary fightback to upset six-time major winner Iga Świątek and reach the quarterfinals.

Qinwen Zheng is the first qualifier since 2021 to make it this far in the women's draw. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng has become Flushing ‌Meadows' most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys.

She let the first five games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against 2022 champion Świątek before digging in, and she collapsed to the court with her hands ⁠in her face after sealing the win on the fourth match ‌point.

China's Olympic champion is the first qualifier ​since Emma Raducanu in 2021 ‌to reach the quarterfinals of the women's draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her career.

Two-time winner Naomi Osaka was summarily swept aside by second seed Elena Rybakina, who won 6-1, 6-4 in just over an hour.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 champion, plays Iva Jovic in an ​all-American clash to decide the final women's quarterfinalist.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of NFL Melbourne
World.content:
American Football will roll into the MCG for a regular-season NFL match for the first time on Friday.

The San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams, who are the nominal home team for the game.

This will be the first regular-season NFL game ever hosted in Australia, although American Football matches have taken place in the country before.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the game?

Davante Adams (left) will look to continue his excellent form into the new year. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The game takes place on Friday morning AEST, with kick-off at 10:35am.

That is what time kick-off will be in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, that is a 10:05am kick-off. In Western Australia, kick-off will be 8:35am.

This is to cater for the Thursday night television audience in the United States, with a New York kick-off time of 8:35pm, while in LA the game will get underway at 5:35pm.

If you are going to the game, the gates open at 7am local time, with access to the Yarra Park precinct, which the NFL has dubbed the NFL Stadium Campus.

There will be food, entertainment, sponsor activations and fan activities to keep punters busy once they get inside.

Who is playing?

The 49ers and the Rams will meet in their season opener. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers are the two teams who are set to play in this historic clash.

The Rams are the home team and come into the season as one of the favourites for this year's Super Bowl, with a stacked offence and miserly defence.

If you think the Rams sound familiar but the LA bit is confusing you, that's because the team has moved around a bit.

The team was formed in 1936 as the Cleveland Rams, moved to LA in 1946, but then shifted to St Louis in 1995, where they stayed for 20 years.

In 2015, the Rams moved back to Los Angeles.

You don't need a hat like this, but I'm sure it will help. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Keith Birmingham)

They are two-time Super Bowl Champions, winning their most recent in 2021. They play at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

The 49ers have always expected to reach the play-offs at an absolute minimum and will think they can do so again, despite a season beset by injuries last year.

Formed in 1944, the 49ers have always been based in the Bay area, although they currently play outside San Francisco at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

They have won five Super Bowls, but have not won one since 1994, despite appearing in three Super Bowls since then, most recently in 2023.

How can I watch?

The game will be available to watch in Australia on Fox Sports/Kayo or on free-to-air on Channel Seven or 7Plus.

Coverage starts from 10am AEST.

Are tickets still available?

Want to join the Rams fans? There's still time. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

If you'd rather watch the game live, as of Monday, there are still tickets available, both standing and seated, for the game at the MCG.

You can purchase the tickets via Ticketmaster.

Why is the NFL playing in Australia?

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

Starting in 2005 with Mexico City, the NFL has gradually expanded its global reach, with games in nine different cities so far, with two more added in 2026.

Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro join London, Mexico City, Toronto, Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, São Paulo and Madrid in hosting regular-season matches.

The idea is to spread the gospel and increase the global presence of a league that has no international competition outside of America.

MCG joins illustrious list

The MCG adds itself to an exclusive list of stadiums. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Morgan Hancock)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you — the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join it on that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946-1979 and 2016-2019.

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that will be used by the league this season.

Players to watch: Rams

Matthew Stafford had a career-best year in 2025. (Getty Images: Kevin Sabitus)

Quarterback Matt Stafford led the league with 4,707 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns last season, with just eight interceptions.

That was one reason why the Rams' offence was the best in the entire league, averaging 30.5 points per game last season.

He has two elite wide receivers in his armory in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, who was rated as the fourth-best player in the entire league by the NFL cohort.

The potential issue is that Stafford is now 38 years old and has historically struggled to back up productive passing seasons in the past.

Defensively, Myles Garrett was recently polled as the number one player in the NFL by his peers, and it's easy to see why.

According to the NFL players, Myles Garrett is the best player around. (Getty Images: Ric Tapia)

The 30-year-old defensive end led the league in sacks (23) and tackles for loss (33) last season for the Browns and his acquisition fills a gaping hole that was ruthlessly exposed as the Rams struggled down the stretch in 2025.

It's not just Garrett who has come in, though. The Rams have recruited two elite cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.

They will also welcome back Super Bowl-winning defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who has come out of retirement to lead the defensive line one last time.

Players to watch: 49ers

Two of the 49ers best players either side of the ball; defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they front up when they suit back up this year.

Brock Purdy will want to iron out his interceptions this season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game from defensive tackle

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Last year the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, the Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey got through a mountain of work in 2025. (Getty Images: Ezra Shaw)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions — the sixth most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes for 10 touchdowns, the eighth most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him as to whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

World.title: V'landys accuses NRL players of 'not telling truth' on rule confusion
World.content:
Peter V'landys has accused players of "not telling the truth" about set-restart confusion, as a survey of finals captains revealed ongoing uncertainty around the ruck.

The topic of set restarts is set to dominate the NRL finals, after Melbourne star Harry Grant claimed widespread frustration from players at the weekend.

The Melbourne captain declared most no longer knew what constituted a fast or slow play-the-ball, and the NRL needed to decide between being rugby league or touch football.

An AAP survey of captains and representatives at Monday's finals launch backed up Grant's claims, with six of the sides indicating they were still not entirely clear on what ruck speed referees wanted.

According to V'landys, Storm skipper Harry Grant (pictured) has 'got it wrong' when it comes to set-restarts. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Also raised by players was the fact there is no chance to ask for clarification, given the game rolls on quickly with a set restart.

But V'landys disagreed, pointing to the fact there are only two reasons for set restarts and players had become more compliant for offside ones.

"I don't buy that," ARL Commission chairman V'landys said.

"The wrestling's got to go. The fans did not like the wrestling, they didn't like people slowing down the ruck speed. And we've accommodated that.

"The players know when they're trying to control the ruck speed.

" I think that they're not telling the truth if they believe when they're giving a six again, they didn't know what it was for. I mean, I think it's pretty obvious. "

Set restarts increased dramatically over the first half of the season, before dropping off through the State of Origin period and rising again in recent weeks.

The rise at the start of the year coincided with the NRL expanding the area in which they can be awarded to from 60 metres of the field to 80.

V'landys indicated they would not be repealed next season, rejecting Grant's claims there was confusion this year.

"I have the ultimate respect for Harry, and Harry's an absolute ornament of the game, but he's got this one wrong," V'landys said.

"When you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. It's around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way.

Sharks co-captain Cameron McInnes (pictured) backed up Grant's viewpoint over the players' confusion. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down … we make no apology that we're going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams.

"The raw numbers don't back up what Harry is saying."

The majority of club representatives surveyed on Monday did not blame referees, but suggested there was still some grey area around ruck interpretation.

"With some of the six agains, who knows what they are for," Cronulla co-captain Cameron McInnes said.

"I just think about a fan watching at home … you just see them and think 'what was that for? It was like the tackle before'.

"That's a problem."

Warriors captain Roger Tuivasa-Sheck (pictured) is concerned that a faster game will lead to more injuries for the players. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if he shared the same confusion, McInnes suggested he did.

"I get the clear as day ones where guys are taking the piss … but then there are flops and re-grips that don't get called as well," he said.

"I don't know what their mindset is, but there will be some at the start of the game that is given a six again, and others that are not."

Some players at the NRL finals launch also raised concerns around whether a faster game had prompted an increased injury toll.

"I feel like it's not a clear understanding [of the interpretation]," injured Warriors veteran Roger Tuivasa-Sheck said.

"As players we understand they want a faster and more entertaining game, but they're risking that with the number of injuries every team has.

"That's what they have to weigh up.

"Yes we're building a very entertaining game and people love the product. But at the same time you lose all these big players out."

AAP

World.title: Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
World.content:
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.

The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.

Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.

Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.

Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.

It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.

Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.

This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.

The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Mills was seen on crutches as his Swans teammates celebrated their win over the Lions on Saturday. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.

Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

AAP

World.title: AFL acts to reduce head trauma at training for men and women
World.content:
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.

All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.

The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.

Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.

AFL hits Geelong with monster fine over concussion waiver scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.

Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.

Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.

Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.

Shane Tuck died in 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with CTE. (AAP: Mal Fairclough)

These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.

The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

AAP

World.title: 'Not value for money': Plans for Tuggeranong ice sports facility scrapped
World.content:
The ACT government has announced a proposed ice sports facility intended for Tuggeranong will not go ahead.

Plans for the facility featured two international-standard ice sheets for figure skating, ice hockey, broom-ball and speed skating.

But the government said today that despite extensive discussions with advocates of the project, it has been unable to reach an agreement on a way forward at the Tuggeranong site.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said an evaluation of an updated proposal to build and manage the facility found the project "did not represent value for money for the territory".

Canberra Brave players have been calling for an upgraded training facility. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

Updated proposal presented 'unacceptable risks'

The multi-purpose ice sports facility, dubbed Canberra Arena, was promised by ACT Labor during its 2016 election campaign, and at one stage of the project's planning, the completion date was even listed as 2025.

In addition to the government investment of $16.265 million, the remaining funds needed to build the estimated arena — estimated at $70 million at one stage — were to come from developers Cruachan Investments and Pelligra Holdings, who would "build, own, operate and maintain it".

"Unfortunately, we haven't been able to find a way forward with the partners Cruachan and Pelligra to build, maintain and operate this facility in Tuggeranong," Mr Steel said.

"The tender evaluation found that unfortunately there were a range of unacceptable risks and the updated proposal that was provided to the ACT government in January did not represent value for money for the ACT government."

Chris Steel says he's disappointed the project will not progress. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Steel said the proponents "were asking for more than double the territory's contribution to the project" in their latest updated proposal.

"That was one of the factors that led to the proposal being deemed not to be value for money," he said.

Cruachan chief executive Stephen Campbell said he supported the government's decision as additional costs associated with developing the site had become "prohibitive".

"We look forward to presenting a new proposal to the government in the coming months that will be more cost-effective, better meet community needs, and create improved access opportunities for all Canberrans," he said.

He said the Tuggeranong site was "too challenging" and the new proposal would include options for different locations.

Money to be spent on other sports facilities
