Tech.title: Two of the Universe's Great Mysteries May Have Their Own Dimension
Tech.content:
According to the standard model of cosmology, that expansion rate should be the same no matter how you measure it. But in recent years, scientists have found that the expansion rate of the early universe and that of the more recent universe vary by approximately 9 percent.

That discrepancy, or tension, “has provoked heated debates in the cosmology community about whether this difference could be due to systematic errors or whether it is a signal of new physics,” Teixeira and her co-authors wrote. Their model posits that in a world where dark energy and dark matter interact, what seemed to be a crisis caused by disparate expansion rates instead becomes something to be expected.

A Dark Dimension

If dark energy and dark matter do interact, it could mean that they have a common origin, Khoury said.

Ongoing work in string theory—the idea that our universe, at its smallest, most fundamental level, is made up of vibrating strings—suggests a way these concepts might be connected. In 2019, building on the idea in string theory that dark energy is naturally varying, Vafa and two collaborators concluded that the mass of dark matter particles may also vary over time. This led them to propose in 2022 that dark matter and dark energy could share a link with a so-called dark dimension.

String theory posits the existence of six or seven extra dimensions in addition to our familiar three dimensions of space and one of time. All of these dimensions are thought to be as small as physically possible—close to the Planck scale (10-35 meters)—but the researchers proposed that the dark dimension could be significantly bigger than the others—on the order of a micron (10-6 meters).

Gravitons, theoretical particles that impart the force of gravity, could leak into this enlarged dark dimension. If they did, they would pick up mass and become what are called dark gravitons. These massive gravitons would reside in the dark dimension, but their gravitational effects could be felt in other dimensions, allowing them to fulfill the role that is normally ascribed to dark matter.

Cumrun Vafa, a physicist at Harvard University, thinks the mass of dark matter may vary over time. Courtesy of Quanta

In this scenario, “there is a very natural coupling between dark energy and dark matter,” said Georges Obied, a physicist at the University of Chicago. Changes in the size of the dark dimension would affect both dark energy and dark matter.

In a July 2025 paper, Obied and Vafa, along with Alek Bedroya of Princeton and David Wu of Harvard, found that the scenario proposed in 2019 was consistent with the DESI data. Their model predicts that the strength of dark energy and the mass of dark matter will decrease over time and that the rate at which dark energy changes will be proportional to its energy density. Because astrophysical measurements tell us that the energy density of dark energy is extraordinarily small, “it won’t change fast,” Vafa said.

“It’s not surprising that we didn’t see it until now,” he said, because the rate of change is so tiny. “We had to wait the entire age of the universe to detect something that small.”

Tech.title: Astronomers Have Completed the Largest Map of Space. Yes, You Can Play With It.
Tech.content:
Though this particular survey lasted five years, it built on another 13 years of groundwork. More than 160 scientists were involved in data collection, and over the course of the project, researchers have already published upwards of 1,800 scientific papers referencing the data.

“It’s part of the fabric of astronomy research now,” David Schlegel, a researcher at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and co-lead of the Legacy Surveys, said in a press release. “When you're working with astronomical objects today, you often start by pulling up the Legacy Imaging Viewer to see what you’re looking at.”

Earlier this year, DESI researchers released another map, which projected the distances of 47 million galaxies and quasars. This reconstructed 11 billion years of cosmic history, bringing the effects of dark energy into focus. Dark energy is thought to be responsible for the expansion of our universe, and while the force itself remains ellusive, astronomers can track it by analyzing the rates at which other celestial objects appear to be moving away from us.

Data from the first three years of DESI’s survey—combined with observations of supernovae and the pervasive radiation leftover from the Big Bang—have hinted that dark energy may not be a constant force but is gradually weakening over time. An analysis of the full five years of data is scheduled to be released in 2027, which will scientists believe will paint a picture of the past and present of the universe more vividly than ever before.

Going forward, DESI’s observations will also serve as a reference and comparison point for other cosmic projects, such as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Researchers also plan to train artificial intelligence tools to accelerate analysis of the petabyte-scale astronomical data—within which much remains to be discovered.

“Explorations of our universe always start with images of the night sky,” said Arjun Day, co-director of Legacy Surveys and an astronomer with the National Science Foundation. “These data are fundamental to the investigation of the expansion history of the universe and the formation of our galaxy. But the skies belong to everyone, and this survey gives everyone the chance to marvel at their wonders.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

Tech.title: Every Samsung Galaxy Phone Comes With This Unique Add-On
Tech.content:
If you opt for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.

Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.

With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.

If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.

How the Edge Panel Works

You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.

When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).

There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).

Tech.title: Whispering Complaints Into Your Phone May Be the Future of Customer Feedback
Tech.content:
Some of the hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.

Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.

I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.

“In the last two years, we hit a tipping point,” says Karan Gupta, CEO of Voicebox, a startup designed to collect feedback via voice. “That voice could now be accurate. It could be fast.” His previous startup also relied on voice technology—an app called Alice designed for secure transcription.

Giving feedback through Voicebox is simple. Shoppers can scan a QR code or tap their phone to an NFC chip posted in a store and then say whatever they want. The feedback is automatically transcribed and sent to the company’s dashboard, with a sentiment analysis. Companies can also follow up over email, if needed. Voicebox has partnered with airport terminals so that travelers can give their two bits about bathroom messiness or gate directions.

Tech.title: I Actually Really Like Xiaomi’s Folding iPhone Ultra Rival
Tech.content:
Xiaomi took the wraps off its new foldable phone at IFA in Berlin and while I could only see it on a stand behind glass at first, I later managed to actually get my hands on the thing and have a brief play. It’s a nice-feeling foldable with a passport-style foldable that I absolutely love. Problem is, it’s got some stiff competition from both Samsung and Apple.

According to most rumors, Apple will be unveiling its first folding iPhone, likely named the iPhone Ultra, at its event on Sept. 9. Those same rumors suggest that Apple’s foldable will also have a passport-style design that’s short and squat when closed but opens out into a wider format that’s great for watching videos.

Xiaomi’s foldable next to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Xiaomi’s is a little smaller. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Neither are the first to the game; Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 launched earlier in the summer sporting a passport-style design that CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti liked enough to give a CNET Editors’ Choice award to. Xiaomi’s phone is in a similar vein to Samsung’s. It’s squat, with a 5.38-inch outer display that unfolds to reveal a 7.58-inch inner display. I agree totally with Abrar when she said that this form factor is “refreshing” and “fun.”

The inner display looked bright and vibrant (at least, under the dim overhead office lights of my demo room) and the crease was barely noticeable. I recently reviewed Samsung’s book-style folding Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and I prefer the more passport style for its wider aspect ratio inner display. It just feels more natural.

You can prop it open like this. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Xiaomi says its custom hinge uses a “three-link” design for added strength and durability. I honestly can’t speak to that in my brief hands on time but it did feel satisfying to open, with it also being able to hold its position so you can half open it and prop it open.

It’s the first phone the company has released using its own in-house XRing 03 processor, which Xiaomi claims is as powerful as any other flagship chip right now — presumably including the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 Elite found in Samsung’s Galaxy phones. It’s an interesting move to see the company build its own silicon from scratch. Both Apple and Google have done similar things and clearly Xiaomi agrees this is the way to have better control of all aspects of the product. How it performs on benchmarks remains to be seen.

I love that red color. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Other specs include a 200 megapixel main camera along with a 50 megapixel telephoto camera and a 6,000mAh silicon carbon battery. Solid specs, for sure, but I’ll have to reserve judgement on how these perform for when I get a model in my hands for some real testing.

But I’m impressed by the Xiaomi 18 Fold. It feels like one of the most sophisticated foldables the company has produced and I find that passport format much more intriguing than the more typical book- or flip-style of its previous foldables.

The wider format when open gives more space for videos. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Xiaomi has yet to say whether the phone will go on sale outside of mainland China, but I really hope it does. Xiaomi doesn’t officially sell any of its phones in the US, so don’t expect it there at any point, but I’ll keep my tea-stained British fingers crossed that I get a model at some point.

Editors’ note: Andrew Lanxon’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Hypershell’s Halo Full-Leg Exoskeleton Made Me Dream Big About the Hikes I Hope to One Day Attempt
Tech.content:
Do you consider yourself fit and healthy? I strength train, run, hike, climb and swim — albeit not according to any kind of training plan or schedule — and yet there are so many ways my body struggles on a daily basis.

Even people who consider themselves to have a high level of cardiovascular fitness might lack strength, balance or flexibility. It’s almost impossible for one person to adhere to a truly holistic training plan. We all have weaknesses. We all know what it’s like to feel fatigued.

What if technology could pick up the slack? That’s the premise behind the Hypershell Halo, a full-leg exoskeleton unveiled at IFA in Berlin last week. This is far from the first Hypershell exoskeleton, but unlike previous models, the Halo extends further down the leg to provide support through the knee and calf, as well as through the thigh and hip.

The Hypershell Halo is flexible enough to allow a full range of movement. Katie Collins/CNET

The Hypershell unified architecture is one carbon-fiber, load-bearing structure with what the company is calling a “fish-spine adaptive joint” to allow for flexibility through the hip and into the leg. Its four-motor system is designed to power you through a whole range of movements while reducing knee-muscle fatigue by up to 40% across all types of terrain.

As someone with chronically creaky knees, I was excited to try the Hypershell Halo over the weekend at IFA. The target audience for an exoskeleton may be older adults and people with limited mobility, but Hypershell seems to be hoping the Halo will have broader appeal. Someone like me, who is active and enthusiastic about exploring the outdoors, but who sometimes reaches their physical limits earlier than they’d like, is also a contender.

I quickly discovered that putting the Hypershell Halo on is all part of the adventure. One belt attaches around the waist, and two flexible straps feed around the thighs. It takes a good few minutes and help from two people to adjust the exoskeleton to fit my proportions, but once the settings are right, it’s very quick to take on and off. (In an on-stage demonstration during the Halo launch event, I watched as the presenter put the exoskeleton on in just 16 seconds.)

My first impression is that I feel a little stiff and restricted, but that sensation immediately evaporates once I start moving. The kit weighs 2.6kg in total, with the majority of that distributed around my waist. I thought the Halo would take some getting used to and might disrupt my natural gait, but it doesn’t at all. Instead, I instantly feel lighter in my natural movements. Squatting and standing from a low seated position without using my hands for support and thrust is totally effortless.

Most of the weight is distributed around your waist. Katie Collins/CNET

As I trample cheerfully all over Hypershell’s multistory booth, I find that that the only pressure anywhere in my legs is in my ankle joints. Going downstairs, I feel none of the usual pressure in my knees, thanks to the cushioning effect. The exoskeleton isn’t doing the work of walking for me, but it feels as though I could keep going for much longer.

This is one of the main use cases Hypershell is putting forward. Avid runners and hikers could potentially do far more than they’re used to without tiring. The Halo supports speeds of up to 17km per hour, which is a 2.5-hour marathon pace. Given that that’s the same as my half-marathon pace, I’d be interested to see what I could achieve while running in the Halo.

As I descend the stairs, thinking about how difficult it usually is walking down the side of a mountain — just one long exercise in trying not to fall — I wonder whether the Halo could allow me to attempt some of the more challenging and vertiginous hikes I’m drawn to, but currently find too intimidating. I have my eye on a multiday Iceland trek, some steep summits in Lofoten and a whole bunch of routes in Patagonia. It also occurs to me that the Halo could be useful for groups with uneven levels of fitness or walking speeds. Could it be responsible for helping couples dodge the infamous alpine divorce? Or is that just delaying the inevitable?

For longer hikes, the battery supports up to 20 hours of use and can be easily swapped out. It only 370g, meaning it shouldn’t be too much of a burden to carry a spare or two.

I briefly switch the Halo to fitness mode, which increases the resistance for people who enjoy the feeling of physically working harder. I get the logic behind it, but I’m not one of these people I ask for it to be turned off again almost immediately. I guess it’s good that it exists for those who want it, but it’s not what I need after multiple days at a trade show.

One of the most interesting aspects of the Halo is how it uses AI. Over 30 sensors continuously capture lower-body movement, feeding data into the on-board AI chip, which can predict how you’re going to move 200ms before you actually do. This predictive technology means the Halo is adapting in real time to your activity, supporting your every move as you make it.

It can’t tell that this is happening while I’m wearing the exoskeleton, but I also suspect that that means it’s working as it should. After all, AI is the kind of technology that’s largely invisible when it’s at its most effective.

Perhaps the only drawback of wearing the Hypershell Halo is that it’s not subtle, and exoskeletons are still rare enough that it will likely attract attention if you wear one in public. If that doesn’t deter you and you’re ready to embrace life as cyborg in the here and now, the Hypershell Halo is available for preorder immediately, priced at $2,299.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: JMGO’s New Projectors Go Big on Brightness and Refresh Rate. I Had a Look at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
At the IFA show in Berlin, projector manufacturer JMGO launched its new Iris line. While externally similar to the N3 Ultimate and other models of its gimbal projectors, inside is a new light engine with even greater brightness and the new headline-grabbing feature at the show: a 120Hz refresh rate while running at full 4K resolution.

A 120Hz refresh rate isn’t exactly new in projectors, and definitely not with TVs, but with projectors, that refresh has been historically limited to 1080p. Is this a big deal? Sort of. It’s an interesting technical feat for sure, and shows where projectors can grow. For most people, it’s not likely a huge deal. Yet, a new DLP chip and design like what’s in JMGO’s new projectors is definitely worth having a look at. So I did.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

All the refreshes fit to refresh

I got a brief look at the new Iris projectors at IFA, and there are two models. The Iris Ultra Max has a stated 6,500 lumens, a fully motorized gimbal and a higher native contrast ratio compared to its sibling. The less expensive Iris Ultra has “just” 4,500 lumens and only manual adjustments for the gimbal. Both models have a 0.9-1.7:1 optical zoom as well as horizontal and vertical image shift (separate from the gimbal). They also have a dual iris system to help dial in brightness and improve the dynamic contrast ratio.

I didn’t have any of my test gear with me, and no trade show is an ideal place to judge a product anyway, but the projectors certainly looked bright. JMGO had a side-by-side demo set up running fast-moving and fast-panning 60-frames-per-second content. One projector was running at a refresh rate of 60Hz, the other at 120Hz. The latter did have less blur on some aspects of the image. However, if you’re not watching 60fps content like sports or video games, I’d expect some severe motion-smoothing issues, aka the soap opera effect (this will be the case with any of these higher-refresh projectors). Then again, 120Hz is an even multiple of 24, so theoretically they could dejudder without interpolating frames. We’ll see.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

DLP has never had a significant issue with motion blur, so a faster refresh isn’t as big an improvement as it would be with, say, LCD. Reducing LCD motion blur is actually why we have faster refresh rates in TVs to begin with. JMGO says the faster refresh rate can also further minimize DLP’s infamous rainbow effect, where some people notice rainbow trails to certain objects on screen (or when they move their eyes). That could be very helpful for those susceptible to that issue.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

I really liked the N3 Ultimate when I reviewed it. It was, at that point anyway, the best gimbal projector. I’m not fully convinced of the need for a fully gimbaled projector for most people. But, with image shift and optical zoom, the N3 can fit in a lot of rooms regardless of how much or little you interact with the gimbal mechanism. And regardless of all that, its performance was excellent. If JMGO can keep the image quality just as high with these new projectors while increasing the already impressive brightness, that will be a very interesting projector. I’ll be getting one to test soon, especially to see if this whole 120Hz thing is worth the hype.

JMGO is expecting the MSRP of the Ultimate Max to be $3,699 and $2,299 for the Ultimate. Both start shipping in mid-October.

Tech.title: I Went Eyes-On With the Aurzen Zip Pro Foldable, Portable Projector. It’s Ready to Shine Your Entertainment Anywhere
Tech.content:
Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

A few months ago, I reviewed the Zip Cyber, a cyberpunk-themed pocket projector from Aurzen. It wasn’t very bright, but the trifold design made it extremely pocketable, and the overall appearance was great.

At IFA, Aurzen debuted the Zip Pro, an updated and upgraded projector with 1080p resolution and twice the brightness. The exterior design is similar, keeping some aspects of the cyberpunk aesthetic (wise, in my opinion) and adding a small touchscreen on the top to aid setup.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

While still sporting what Aurzen calls “trifold” (there are two hinges), the Zip Pro is actually slightly larger than the Zip and Zip Cyber at 4.5 by 3.8 by 1.7 inches versus 3.3 by 3.1 by 1 inches. So, it’s nearly three times the total volume and about twice the weight. This is still a remarkably small projector, just less pocketable than the original. It would get swallowed by any backpack.

Inside, there’s the aforementioned bump up to 1080p, as well as a slightly larger battery. Aurzen says it has 2.5 hours of playtime compared to the Zip’s 1.5 hours. Since it recharges via USB-C, though, you can extend playtime with any decent portable battery pack. So, with the improved performance, the larger size seems a reasonable trade-off.

The Zip Cyber (top) and the Zip Pro were on display at IFA. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

I got a quick look at the Zip Pro at IFA, and it did seem brighter, as evidenced by far larger image sizes to demo the projector compared to how I’ve seen it demo the Zip. The 200-lumen range makes the Pro far more usable in a wider variety of situations. It competes specs-wise,with the Anker Capsule 3, which was pricey but good. The Zip Pro is more expensive, but most tech is now compared to when the Capsule 3 was launched.

Connectivity

The biggest issue with the Zip Cyber was that it was a challenge to get anything onto it to watch. There’s still no HDMI, but it does have AirLink, Miracast, AirPlay P2P, DLNA and, especially notable since it was missing in the original Zip, Google Cast. You can also connect via USB-C to watch content from your phone.

You can preorder the Zip Pro now, and the MSRP is $630. I’ll be testing out the Zip Pro in my lab soon.

Tech.title: Xgimi’s New Aura 3 UST Projectors Get Bright and Look Classy
Tech.content:
At IFA in Berlin, Xgimi unveiled a pair of new ultrashort-throw projectors. Called the Aura 3 Max and Aura 3 Pro, they slot in above the Aura 2 in Xgimi’s range. Like several new projectors, notably from AWOL and JMGO, the Aura 3 models have high brightness and 120Hz refresh rates.

The classy, wood-paneled design holds a light engine capable of a stated 5,700 lumens in the Max and 4,100 in the Pro. Xgimi also says the Aura 3s have the world’s first dual iris system, giving greater control over the amount of light hitting the screen.

This dynamic contrast ratio isn’t quite as eye-catching as a high native contrast ratio, but I won’t be able to judge that until I get one in my lab for testing. Xgimi says it’s the same light engine as what’s in the Titan Noir, so I’d expect solid performance.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The designs are similar to the Aura 3. Xgimi had them set up on the floor, which would certainly work if you don’t have kids, clumsy adults or curious pets. UST projectors are typically designed to be the central hub of a home cinema, and as such the internal speakers play an important role. For the Aura 3 series, Xgimi has again partnered with Harman Kardon for assistance with the audio. Both models have 80 watts total, though the company hasn’t announced how many drivers those watts power.

Also shown with the Aura 3 at Xgimi’s IFA booth was the (maybe) production version of the Ascend screen I first saw at CES 2025. It’s a stylish, motorized ambient-light-rejecting screen.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Xgimi announced preorder pricing via Kickstarter. I’m not a fan of preorders in general and definitely not big companies using Kickstarter. It said a $50 deposit will get you $200 off, with the preorder price being $2,399 for the Max and $2,199 for the Pro. That’s a little higher than the Aura 2, which itself performs quite well for the price. The actual MSRP will likely be higher at launch.

Tech.title: Over Half of US Adults Want Better Battery Life, but Can Apple Deliver with its New iPhone Lineup?
Tech.content:
What’s motivating smartphone owners to consider upgrading hasn’t changed much over the years. Zain Awais/CNET

Charging your phone in the middle of the day can be annoying and inconvenient, especially when you’re on the go. Instead of fumbling with chargers, how about more battery life for your smartphone?

That’s what’s driving 52% of US adults to consider upgrading their phone according to a CNET survey. Besides that, 55% say a better price would convince them to get a new phone. With Apple’s Surprise and Shine event planned for Wednesday, Sept. 9, we’re expecting Apple’s first foldable phone and two phones from the iPhone 18 series. Analysts say the iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could have better battery life than older models. But don’t expect lower prices thanks to RAMageddon.

With Apple’s event just days away, here’s what US adults are looking for in a smartphone and how it may be able to deliver.

Key findings The top three motivations for US adult smartphone owners to consider upgrading their devices are price (55%), longer battery life (52%) and more storage (38%). That’s the same top three as last year: In 2025, price was the top motivator (62%), followed by longer battery life (54%) and storage capacity (39%). Despite AI’s growing presence, only 12% of smartphone owners say AI integrations would motivate them to consider upgrading. Only 13% of smartphone owners would be motivated to consider upgrading to a new phone concept, such as a foldable or flip phone. Over half of smartphone owners (58%) experience frustration with their phone’s battery life, and 31% say their phone’s battery doesn’t hold a charge as well as it did when it was new.

Most US adults aren’t motivated by new smartphone features and designs

Smartphone brands, like Samsung and Apple, are building in convenient features, such as a tool to remove unwanted objects from pictures, AI call screening and the ability to draft a message from a prompt. However, CNET found that US adults would consider upgrading for more practical reasons. Over half (55%) of US smartphone users are motivated by price, including 53% of Apple users and 56% of Samsung users.

Yet brands are still exploring new concepts and features, like Apple Intelligence, a built-in AI feature and even Siri AI which will debut with iOS 27. Analysts expect Apple to unveil a book-style foldable iPhone, which could be named the iPhone Ultra or iPhone Fold. But that’s not what most smartphone owners are after.

Smartphone owners are more convinced by other design and feature factors when deciding on a new phone, such as camera features (27%) and the phone’s display or screen size (22%). Here are the top motivators to consider upgrading for all smartphone users.

Zain Awais / CNET

You’ve probably noticed the price of a basic smartphone has increased drastically over the years and now there’s a rumor that the price for the iPhone 18 series could be higher at Wednesday’s event. A TrendForce analyst predicts that the iPhone 18 Pro could start between $1,199 and $1,299, and $1,299 to $1,399 for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Meanwhile, the iPhone Ultra could start between $2,099 and $2,299.

Higher prices may be a good reason to buy the iPhone 17 now if you see a good deal, especially if Apple doesn’t release the base model of the iPhone 18 next week.

The top upgrading motivators haven’t changed much over the years

Looking back at CNET’s survey data from 2024 and 2025, and now, people’s motivators for upgrading their phones haven’t changed much. Price, longer battery life and more storage have been top drivers in the past, and despite small dips this year, they’re still key upgrading factors.

Despite design upgrades and new features, smartphone owners are still focused on how much they’re paying and how long they can use their devices without needing a charger. Consumer sentiment about AI integrations dropped hard from 2024 to 2025, but it has edged up slightly in 2026. And smartphone owners aren’t as easily persuaded by phone color or the phone being thinner, either.

Even with these nice-to-have capabilities, smartphone owners are looking at the basics. That includes practical features like battery life and more storage to hold their many important files, photos and apps.

Most smartphone owners want better battery life

Taking a closer look at smartphone users’ hope for longer battery life in a new phone, over half (58%) are frustrated with their current phone’s battery life. Roughly 1 in 3 (31%) say their phone doesn’t hold a charge.

The reality is, battery life will decline the longer you have your phone, so you may find your phone’s battery charge doesn’t last as long as it used to. Even though you can replace your phone’s battery, most phone batteries have a lifespan of two to three years before they start degrading.

CNET Director of Editorial Content Patrick Holland examined battery life tests on over 35 current smartphones. And it’s not just iPhones that pack impressive batteries.



Based on CNET’s lab testing, the $1,200 iPhone 17 Pro Max had the best overall battery life, with a 5,088-mAh capacity. Another top performer was the $900 OnePlus 15, with a 7,300-mAh battery. There’s a rumor that if Apple releases a foldable phone in the future, it will be even better than the iPhone 17 Pro Max, but we’ll have to wait and see.

If you’re looking for a phone with better battery life, consider one with a silicon-carbon battery to increase capacity without requiring a larger phone. The OnePlus 15, Poco F7 Ultra, OnePlus 13R and OnePlus 15R all feature silicon-carbon batteries with large capacities and all performed well in Holland’s testing. Keep in mind that other factors can impact your battery life, like your carrier’s signal, software efficiency and processor.

Methodology

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample comprised 2,486 adults, of whom 2,407 owned a smartphone. Fieldwork was undertaken from April 29 to May 1, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

Tech.title: Sony Surprises With New 1000XM4C 2nd Gen Headphones With Updated Sound, Bluetooth 6.0
Tech.content:
When Sony’s WH-1000XM4 headphones hit the market back in August 2020, I awarded them a CNET Editors’ Choice Award, calling them nearly flawless. Despite their age and the release of two successors — the WH-1000XM5 and WH-1000XM6 headphones — the 1000XM4s remain quite popular.

Now, Sony is leaning into that legacy model’s popularity with the new WH-1000XM4C (M4 2nd Gen), which comes in new color options and has “updated sound tuning designed for today’s listening preferences,” according to Sony. The WH-1000XM4C headphones list for $300 and are being launched alongside the new WH-CH730N ($180) and WH-CH530 ($80).



WH-1000XM4C’s small differences

Aside from some tiny cosmetic changes, the M4 2nd Gen headphones look identical to their predecessor. The XM4C’s most notable feature upgrade is Bluetooth 6.0 instead of Bluetooth 5.1, and the headphones now support a new 10-band equalizer (and gaming EQ) for “greater sound personalization,” instead of the older five-band equalizer.

The WH-1000XM4C comes in three color options, including a new lavender color that will only be available online at Sony and Amazon. Sony says the XM4 has been popular among younger female users, and the new color is targeted at them. David Carnoy/CNET

The 1000XM4C (M4 2nd Gen) are still equipped with Sony’s QN1 chip along with four microphones (the WH-1000XM6 have 12 by comparison), so their noise-canceling performance is the same. Battery life has dipped a bit: The M4 2nd Gen are rated for up to 27 hours with noise canceling on, compared to the original’s 30 hours.

The original M4 headphones were known for having strong, dynamic bass and a slightly warmer sound profile than their successors. The foundation of that profile remains, but the new tuning helps deliver cleaner, more refined sound overall.

WH-CH730N is a true second-gen midrange model

I was fond of Sony’s over-ear CH-720N headphones because they were lightweight and comfortable while sounding good and offering decent noise-canceling performance for a reasonable price. (They listed for $150 but dipped to as low as $100 during flash sales.) While the list price for the new WH-CH730N has gone up $30 to $180, the model offers a similar value proposition in a new foldable design, along with improved performance all around. Plus, they promise better battery life at up to 50 hours with noise canceling on, according to Sony.

The WH-CH730N comes in white, pink, blue, black and a new oat color. David Carnoy/CNET

I like the new design, which looks and feels slightly more premium than their predecessor’s, and the headphones are quite comfortable. The new headphones’ sound is slightly improved, too. They lack the clarity and depth that you get with Sony’s more premium headphone offerings, but the sound is open and well-balanced with some nice warmth to it (the bass goes pretty deep, too). They’re pleasant headphones to listen to.

While the noise canceling certainly isn’t up to the level of what you get with Sony’s flagship WH-1000XM6, it has been upgraded with Sony’s Dual Noise Sensor technology and is pretty decent (Sony says it’s about 10% more effective). The bigger performance gain is arguably with the voice-calling performance, as the headphones have beamforming microphones with optimized microphone placement and AI noise reduction.

They, too, have a 10-band equalizer with a gaming EQ setting. And while they don’t support Sony’s advanced LDAC audio codec, they do support the LC3 audio codec, which is new (they support SBC and AAC). Alas, like their predecessor, while they come with a cable for wired listening, they do not come with a carry pouch or case.

The WH-CH730 in their new oat color on the left. David Carnoy/CNET

Entry-level on-ear WH-CH530 get small upgrades but cost more

Sony’s earlier CH-520 was a pretty basic on-ear model that didn’t have noise canceling, but sounded good for its relatively low price (the headphonea list for $60 but were often discounted to less than $50 and sometimes as low as $38, as they are now). Available in new color options, the new WH-CH520 list for $20 more and offer some small upgrades — most notably, improved voice-calling performance with AI noise reduction. However, they don’t seem like a true next-gen product like the CH-730N.

The CH-530 headphones are available in cobalt, coral, mint, pink, white and black. David Carnoy/CNET

The headphones are targeted at younger folks and now have a volume limiter feature, which should appeal to parents with young kids. Their battery life is rated at up to 55 hours. They don’t support wired listening, so you can’t plug them into an in-flight entertainment system. Nor do they come with a carrying pouch or case.

Priced for discounts

List prices for headphones have been creeping up, but all of Sony’s new so-called “value” models should see decent discounts heading into the holiday shopping season. The 1000XM5 headphones are currently selling at $198 at Amazon as part of a limited-time deal, so there’s no reason the M4 2nd Gen shouldn’t hit something close to that price in the not-so-distant future. Also, take the $180 price on the CH-730N with a grain of salt, as that model should see $50 discounts in flash sales, particularly around Black Friday.

I just received review samples of all three models, and I’ll have full reviews of the M4 2nd Gen and WH-CH730N later this month, including comparisons of their performance.

Tech.title: This New 360 Camera Won’t Come to the US. I Went to Berlin to Test It
Tech.content:
I traveled all the way to Berlin to test out DJI’s new 360 camera. OK, not just for that, but it was definitely one of the reasons. You see, due to the ongoing FCC block on new DJI products by the US government, it’s likely the new Osmo 360 II won’t be available in the US. Which is too bad because, as was the case with this camera’s predecessor, the hardware is top-tier.

The 360 II improves on the older Osmo 360 with new image sensors, dual, square 1-inch image sensors, as well as a maximum resolution and frame rate of 8K60. It bests Insta360’s X6, which maxes out at 8K50. Those 10 extra frames per second might not seem like a big deal, but in many situations, they can be the difference between having usable footage and not. Probably the biggest improvement, however, is the addition of user-replaceable lenses.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Unfortunately, the prospect of availability in the US through official channels is gray. As gray as the market where you’ll inevitably find this camera. With fingers crossed for future US availability, DJI loaned me a 360 II for a few days in Berlin to check it out.

The Osmo 360 II’s hardware is too different

On the outside, the second-gen model is similar to its predecessor. There are some exposed screwheads that give it a slightly tougher look, but the screen and buttons remain the same. There’s also a larger mic opening on the front.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The most notable change is the switch to user-replaceable lenses. As someone who’s used and ruined numerous 360 cameras over the years, I’d advise you not to overlook this feature. It’s all too easy to accidentally scratch a 360-degree camera lens since they stick out from the body. Repairs, when possible, can be costly, too. So being able to replace them yourself should be considered a must-have “feature” for most people.

The rest of the images in this story are from the Osmo 360 II and been reframed or cropped but otherwise unedited. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The other major change is new, square, 1-inch sensors. DJI says these have 14.5-stops of dynamic range. I didn’t get a chance to do much low-light testing, but it seemed solid. The earlier 360 was already good in this regard.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Thanks to these new sensors, better processing or both, the Osmo 360 II is capable of 8K60 video. This bests Insta360’s flagship X6, which maxes out at 8K50. For most people, this isn’t a big deal. Most phones can’t edit 8K video, and for social media, the lower 6K-resolution video is plenty unless you want to zoom in.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

That said, in the US, our displays are on multiples of 30 or 60. So 50 doesn’t work as well, potentially leading to stuttering movement or strobing background lights. Also, for more advanced users who can edit 8K, the extra resolution will help with more flexible framing and cropping options. If those same pros are recording sports or other fast movement, 60fps is far better than 30. Which is to say, for most people, 8K60 versus 8K50 isn’t a big deal, but for certain people, it will be a very big deal.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Despite this being a “first look” and not a full review, there are a few features found on other 360 cameras I wish the Osmo 360 II had. Being able to select the aspect ratio for single-lens photos would be great. Sure, you can do this in the editing process, but seeing your frame ahead of time helps, as does one less thing to edit later. Similarly, there are limited options to change the field of view with single-lens photos; the option is merely cropping in and reducing resolution if you don’t want an ultrawide, almost fisheye FOV. The X6 can double as a regular, wide-angle camera far more easily with these features.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The software

As with other DJI gear, the hardware isn’t the problem. You’ll need to download the DJI Mimo app from DJI directly on Android phones and disable some security settings. Not ideal. It is available on Apple’s App Store, so that’s one less issue if you’re on iOS. The app itself works well, letting you crop and edit photos and videos. There aren’t quite as many options here as there are on Insta360’s app, but it’s also not as bloated.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Full circle (well, sphere)

Competition is important. Insta360 is the biggest name in the 360 camera space, but with GoPro’s future uncertain and Kandao’s output slowing, we on the consumer side need Insta360 to have a big competitor to keep driving 360 camera development. While the X6’s 8K50 isn’t a huge deal for most people, it’s interesting that a camera released mere months later can do 8K60 just fine. I have no doubt that a future X7 will have 8K60, so why this interim step?

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The geopolitics of DJI in the US is far above my pay grade to write about. For now, it’s making getting this interesting camera overly difficult. If it does get approved for sale in the US, or is at least reasonably easy to get, we’ll give it a full review. For now, I guess we’ll have to wait and see.
